cards.front: How is matter classified at the macroscopic level?
cards.back: • Pure substances: elements and compounds (fixed composition) • Mixtures: homogeneous (uniform, e.g. air, sugar solution) or heterogeneous (non-uniform, e.g. salt + sand)

cards.front: How does a compound differ from a mixture?
cards.back: Compound: elements in a fixed ratio by mass, separable only by chemical methods, properties differ from its elements. Mixture: variable composition, separable by physical methods.

cards.front: Name the seven SI base quantities and their units.
cards.back: • length – metre (m) • mass – kilogram (kg) • time – second (s) • electric current – ampere (A) • temperature – kelvin (K) • amount of substance – mole (mol) • luminous intensity – candela (cd)
cards.hint: Kilogram is the only base unit whose name carries a prefix.

cards.front: What is the current SI definition of the mole?
cards.back: Amount containing exactly $6.02214076 \times 10^{23}$ elementary entities; this number is the Avogadro constant $N_A$ (unit $\text{mol}^{-1}$).
cards.hint: The old '12 g of carbon-12' definition is replaced; $N_A$ is now an exact fixed value.

cards.front: Mass vs weight: which stays constant from place to place?
cards.back: Mass (amount of matter) is constant. Weight is the force of gravity on it, so it can vary with location.

cards.front: SI unit of volume and its relation to the litre?
cards.back: SI unit: $\text{m}^3$. $1\ \text{L} = 1\ \text{dm}^3 = 1000\ \text{cm}^3$; $1\ \text{mL} = 1\ \text{cm}^3$.

cards.front: SI unit of density and its relation to $\text{g cm}^{-3}$?
cards.back: SI unit $\text{kg m}^{-3}$. $1\ \text{g cm}^{-3} = 1000\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$.

cards.front: Relations between kelvin, Celsius and Fahrenheit scales?
cards.back: • $T(\text{K}) = t(^\circ\text{C}) + 273.15$ • $t(^\circ\text{F}) = \dfrac{9}{5}\,t(^\circ\text{C}) + 32$
cards.hint: Trap: the kelvin scale has no degree sign and no negative values.

cards.front: At what temperature do Celsius and Fahrenheit readings coincide?
cards.hint: Put $F = C$ in $F = \dfrac{9}{5}C + 32$ and solve.

cards.front: Precision vs accuracy?
cards.back: • Precision: closeness of repeated measurements to one another • Accuracy: closeness of a measurement to the true value
cards.hint: Results can be precise but not accurate: consistent but all wrong.

cards.front: Write 0.00016 in scientific notation. How many significant figures?
cards.back: $1.6 \times 10^{-4}$; 2 significant figures (leading zeros are not significant).

cards.front: Which zeros are significant?
cards.back: • Leading zeros: never (0.003 has 1) • Zeros between non-zero digits: always (2.005 has 4) • Trailing zeros: only with a decimal point (0.200 has 3; 100 has 1; 100. has 3)

cards.front: Significant figures in $2.0 \times 10^3$ and in the count '20 students'?
cards.back: • $2.0 \times 10^3$: 2 (only the coefficient's digits count) • Exact counted numbers: infinite significant figures

cards.front: Significant-figure rule for addition and subtraction?
cards.back: Answer keeps as many decimal places as the term with the fewest decimal places: 12.11 + 18.0 + 1.012 = 31.1.

cards.front: Significant-figure rule for multiplication and division?
cards.back: Answer keeps as many significant figures as the least precise term: 2.5 × 1.25 = 3.125 → 3.1.

cards.front: NCERT rounding rule when the digit to be dropped is 5?
cards.back: Preceding digit is unchanged if even, increased by 1 if odd: 3.35 → 3.4 but 3.25 → 3.2.

cards.front: What is the factor-label (dimensional analysis) method?
cards.back: Multiply by unit factors (ratios equal to 1, e.g. $\dfrac{2.54\ \text{cm}}{1\ \text{in}}$) so unwanted units cancel and the required unit remains.

cards.front: State the law of conservation of mass. Who gave it?
cards.back: Matter can be neither created nor destroyed; total mass of reactants = total mass of products. Given by Antoine Lavoisier.

cards.front: State the law of definite proportions. Who gave it?
cards.back: A given compound always contains the same elements in the same proportion by mass, whatever its source. Given by Joseph Proust.
cards.hint: Proust: cupric carbonate from nature and from the lab had identical composition.

cards.front: State the law of multiple proportions with an example.
cards.back: When two elements form more than one compound, masses of one combining with a fixed mass of the other are in a simple whole-number ratio (Dalton). 2 g H: 16 g O in $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, 32 g in $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ → 1 : 2
cards.hint: Definite proportions: one compound. Multiple proportions: two or more compounds of the same elements.

cards.front: State Gay Lussac's law of gaseous volumes.
cards.back: Gases combine or are produced in a simple whole-number ratio by volume at the same T and P. e.g. 100 mL $\text{H}_2$ + 50 mL $\text{O}_2$ → 100 mL water vapour (2 : 1 : 2).

cards.front: State Avogadro's law.
cards.back: Equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.
cards.hint: Holds only for gases compared at the same T and P.

cards.front: Main postulates of Dalton's atomic theory?
cards.back: • Matter is made of indivisible atoms • Atoms of an element are identical, including mass • Compounds form when atoms combine in a fixed ratio • Reactions only reorganise atoms; atoms are not created or destroyed

cards.front: Which law could Dalton's atomic theory NOT explain?
cards.back: Gay Lussac's law of gaseous volumes. Avogadro explained it by distinguishing atoms from molecules (e.g. diatomic $\text{H}_2$, $\text{O}_2$).

cards.front: Define one atomic mass unit.
cards.back: Exactly 1/12th the mass of one carbon-12 atom; $1\ \text{amu} = 1.66056 \times 10^{-24}\ \text{g}$. Now written as u (unified mass).

cards.front: Mass of one carbon-12 atom in grams?
cards.back: $1.992648 \times 10^{-23}\ \text{g}$, assigned exactly 12 u.

cards.front: Why is the atomic mass of chlorine 35.5 u, not a whole number?
cards.back: It is a weighted average of isotopic masses by natural abundance: Cl-35 (~75.8%) and Cl-37 (~24.2%) → ≈35.5 u.

cards.front: Molecular mass vs formula mass?
cards.back: Molecular mass: sum of atomic masses in a molecule. Formula mass is used for ionic solids like NaCl that have no discrete molecules: 23.0 + 35.5 = 58.5 u.

cards.front: Molecular mass of glucose, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6$?
Value of the Avogadro constant?
cards.back: $N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$: number of entities in one mole.

cards.front: What is molar mass?
cards.back: Mass of one mole of a substance in grams; numerically equal to its atomic/molecular/formula mass in u. Unit $\text{g mol}^{-1}$ (e.g. $\text{H}_2\text{O}$: 18.02 $\text{g mol}^{-1}$).

cards.front: Formulae linking moles to mass and number of particles?
cards.back: $n = \dfrac{m}{M} = \dfrac{N}{N_A}$ • m = given mass, M = molar mass, N = number of particles
cards.hint: Moles are the bridge: mass ↔ moles ↔ particles.

cards.front: Molar volume of an ideal gas at STP as used in NCERT?
cards.back: 22.7 L at 273.15 K and 1 bar. The older 22.4 L applies at 273.15 K and 1 atm.
cards.hint: Trap: check whether the question defines STP with 1 bar or 1 atm.

cards.front: How many atoms are present in 1 mol of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$?
cards.back: 3 mol of atoms = $3 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}$ = $1.807 \times 10^{24}$ atoms.

cards.front: Molarity of pure water?
cards.back: 1000 g per litre ÷ 18 $\text{g mol}^{-1}$ ≈ 55.5 M.
cards.hint: Assumes density of water = 1 g/mL.

cards.front: Formula for mass per cent of an element in a compound?
cards.back: $\text{Mass }\% = \dfrac{\text{mass of element in 1 mol}}{\text{molar mass}} \times 100$

cards.front: Mass per cent of oxygen in water?
Empirical formula vs molecular formula?
cards.back: Empirical: simplest whole-number ratio of atoms. Molecular: exact number of each atom. Glucose: EF $\text{CH}_2\text{O}$, MF $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6$.
cards.hint: EF and MF can be identical, e.g. $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, $\text{CO}_2$.

cards.front: How is the molecular formula obtained from the empirical formula?
cards.back: $n = \dfrac{\text{molar mass}}{\text{empirical formula mass}}$; molecular formula = $(\text{EF})_n$.

cards.front: Steps to find an empirical formula from mass per cent data?
cards.back: • Take % values as grams (100 g sample) • Divide by atomic mass → moles • Divide all by the smallest mole value • Multiply to get whole numbers
cards.hint: Ratios like 1.5 or 1.33: multiply all by 2 or 3.

cards.front: C 40.0%, H 6.67%, O 53.3%. Empirical formula?
cards.back: Moles: C 3.33, H 6.62, O 3.33 → ratio 1 : 2 : 1 → $\text{CH}_2\text{O}$.

cards.front: What does $\text{CH}_4 + 2\text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{CO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ tell quantitatively?
cards.back: 1 mol $\text{CH}_4$ + 2 mol $\text{O}_2$ → 1 mol $\text{CO}_2$ + 2 mol $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, i.e. 16 g + 64 g → 44 g + 36 g (mass conserved).

cards.front: What is a limiting reagent?
cards.back: The reactant consumed completely first; it fixes the amount of product formed. Others are in excess.

cards.front: Is the reactant present in smaller mass always the limiting reagent?
cards.back: No. Compare moles ÷ stoichiometric coefficient for each reactant; the smallest value is limiting.
cards.hint: Trap: never compare raw masses or raw moles.

cards.front: 50.0 kg $\text{N}_2$ + 10.0 kg $\text{H}_2$ form $\text{NH}_3$. Which is limiting?
cards.back: $\text{H}_2$: 1786 mol $\text{N}_2$ needs 5357 mol $\text{H}_2$, but only 4960 mol present. $\text{NH}_3$ ≈ 3307 mol (≈56 kg).

cards.front: Formula for mass per cent of a solution?
cards.back: $\text{Mass }\% = \dfrac{\text{mass of solute}}{\text{mass of solution}} \times 100$

cards.front: Define mole fraction.
cards.back: $x_A = \dfrac{n_A}{n_A + n_B}$; unitless, and the sum of all mole fractions = 1.

cards.front: Define molarity and give its unit.
cards.back: $M = \dfrac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{volume of solution (L)}}$; unit $\text{mol L}^{-1}$.
cards.hint: Trap: volume of solution, not volume of solvent.

cards.front: Define molality and give its unit.
cards.back: $m = \dfrac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{mass of solvent (kg)}}$; unit $\text{mol kg}^{-1}$.
cards.hint: Trap: molality uses mass of solvent, molarity uses volume of solution.

cards.front: Which concentration term changes with temperature?
cards.back: Molarity, because volume changes with temperature. Molality, mass % and mole fraction are temperature-independent.

cards.front: Dilution formula and why it works?
cards.back: $M_1V_1 = M_2V_2$: adding solvent does not change the moles of solute.
cards.hint: Mixing two solutions: $M = \dfrac{M_1V_1 + M_2V_2}{V_1 + V_2}$.

cards.front: Mass of NaOH needed for 250 mL of 0.1 M solution?
cards.hint: Mass (g) = M × V (L) × molar mass.

cards.front: Relation between speed, frequency and wavelength of light?
cards.back: $c = \nu\lambda$; $c = 3.0 \times 10^8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ in vacuum.

cards.front: Define wavenumber and give its SI unit.
cards.back: $\bar{\nu} = \dfrac{1}{\lambda}$, number of wavelengths per unit length; SI unit $\text{m}^{-1}$ (often $\text{cm}^{-1}$).
cards.hint: Energy is directly proportional to wavenumber: $E = hc\bar{\nu}$.

cards.front: Order of EM radiation regions by increasing wavelength?
cards.back: γ-rays < X-rays < UV < visible < IR < microwaves < radio waves. Frequency and energy follow the reverse order.
cards.hint: Visible light spans about 400 nm (violet) to 750 nm (red).

cards.front: Which observations could the wave theory of light NOT explain?
cards.back: Black-body radiation, the photoelectric effect, and the variation of heat capacity of solids with temperature; line spectra of atoms too.

cards.front: Energy of one quantum (photon) of radiation?
cards.back: $E = h\nu = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$; $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$. Energy is emitted/absorbed in discrete packets (quanta).
cards.hint: $hc \approx 1.99 \times 10^{-25}$ J m.

cards.front: If the wavelength of light is halved, what happens to photon energy?
cards.back: Photon energy doubles, since $E \propto \dfrac{1}{\lambda}$.

cards.front: Einstein's photoelectric equation?
cards.back: $h u = h u_0 + \dfrac{1}{2}m_ev^2$; $h u_0 = W_0$ (work function), $ u_0$ = threshold frequency.
cards.hint: Threshold wavelength $\lambda_0 = \dfrac{c}{\nu_0}$; light with $\lambda > \lambda_0$ ejects no electrons.

cards.front: Effect of increasing light intensity (above threshold) on photoelectrons?
cards.back: More electrons are ejected; the kinetic energy of each electron is unchanged.

cards.front: Effect of increasing frequency of light on ejected electrons?
cards.back: Kinetic energy of ejected electrons increases linearly with frequency: $KE = h(\nu - \nu_0)$.

cards.front: Very intense light below threshold frequency falls on a metal. Result?
cards.back: No electrons are ejected, however intense or long the exposure. Above $\nu_0$, ejection is instantaneous.
cards.hint: Trap: intensity controls number of electrons, frequency controls whether they come out at all.

cards.front: Emission spectrum vs absorption spectrum?
cards.back: Emission: bright lines on a dark background, from excited atoms. Absorption: dark lines on a bright continuous background (photographic negative of emission).

cards.front: Why are line spectra called fingerprints of atoms?
cards.back: Each element has a unique line spectrum, so spectra identify elements (e.g. helium was discovered in the Sun this way).

cards.front: Rydberg formula for hydrogen spectral lines?
cards.hint: For hydrogen-like ions multiply by $Z^2$.

cards.front: Hydrogen spectral series: lower level $n_1$ and region?
cards.back: • Lyman, $n_1 = 1$: UV • Balmer, $n_1 = 2$: visible • Paschen, $n_1 = 3$: IR • Brackett, $n_1 = 4$: IR • Pfund, $n_1 = 5$: IR
cards.hint: Order L-B-P-B-P: 'Lazy Boys Play Brave Pranks'.

cards.front: Maximum spectral lines when electrons fall from level n to the ground state?
cards.back: $\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$ for many atoms; n = 4 gives 6 lines.
cards.hint: For a single atom, at most n − 1 lines.

cards.front: Bohr's quantisation condition for angular momentum?
cards.back: $m_evr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$, n = 1, 2, 3… Electrons move in stationary orbits without radiating energy.
cards.hint: Angular momentum is an integral multiple of $\dfrac{h}{2\pi}$.

cards.front: Bohr's frequency condition for an electron transition?
cards.back: $\nu = \dfrac{\Delta E}{h} = \dfrac{E_2 - E_1}{h}$: radiation is absorbed or emitted only when the electron jumps between orbits.

cards.front: Radius of the nth Bohr orbit of a hydrogen-like species?
cards.back: $r_n = \dfrac{52.9\,n^2}{Z}\ \text{pm}$; $a_0 = 52.9$ pm is the Bohr radius. $r \propto \dfrac{n^2}{Z}$.

cards.front: Energy of the nth orbit of a hydrogen-like species?
cards.back: $E_n = -2.18 \times 10^{-18}\left(\dfrac{Z^2}{n^2}\right)\ \text{J}$
cards.hint: $2.18 \times 10^{-18}$ J per atom = 13.6 eV.

cards.front: Why is the energy of an electron in a Bohr orbit negative?
cards.back: Zero energy is for an electron completely removed ($n = \infty$). A bound electron is more stable, so its energy is lower than zero.

cards.front: How does electron velocity in a Bohr orbit vary with Z and n?
cards.back: $v \propto \dfrac{Z}{n}$: increases with nuclear charge, decreases as n increases.
cards.hint: In the first orbit of H, $v \approx 2.2 \times 10^6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

cards.front: Ground-state energy of $\text{He}^+$ compared with H?
Ratio of first-orbit radii of H, $\text{He}^+$ and $\text{Li}^{2+}$?
Wavelength of the first Lyman line of hydrogen (n = 2 → 1)?
cards.back: $\Delta E = 2.18 \times 10^{-18}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{4}\right) = 1.64 \times 10^{-18}$ J → λ ≈ 122 nm (UV).

cards.front: For which species does Bohr's model work?
cards.back: Only one-electron species: H, $\text{He}^+$, $\text{Li}^{2+}$, $\text{Be}^{3+}$…

cards.front: Limitations of Bohr's model?
cards.back: • Fails for spectra of multi-electron atoms • Cannot explain fine structure, Zeeman (magnetic) and Stark (electric) effects • Cannot explain molecule formation • Ignores dual nature and uncertainty principle

cards.front: de Broglie relation?
cards.back: $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv} = \dfrac{h}{p}$: every moving particle has wave character.

cards.front: Why is the wave nature of a moving cricket ball not observed?
cards.back: $\lambda \propto \dfrac{1}{m}$; for large mass λ is far too small to detect.

cards.front: Which device uses the wave nature of electrons?
cards.back: The electron microscope (magnification up to about 15 million times).

cards.front: Link between de Broglie waves and Bohr's quantisation?
cards.back: A stable orbit holds a whole number of waves: $2\pi r = n\lambda$, which with $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv}$ gives $mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$.

cards.front: State Heisenberg's uncertainty principle.
cards.back: Exact position and momentum of an electron cannot be known simultaneously: $\Delta x \cdot \Delta p_x \ge \dfrac{h}{4\pi}$.
cards.hint: If Δx → 0, then Δp → ∞.

cards.front: Uncertainty principle in terms of velocity?
cards.back: $\Delta x \cdot \Delta v_x \ge \dfrac{h}{4\pi m}$; significant only for very small masses like electrons.

cards.front: Why does the uncertainty principle rule out Bohr's fixed orbits?
cards.back: A defined orbit needs exact position and velocity at the same time, which is impossible. Only the probability of finding the electron can be given.

cards.front: In $\hat{H}\psi = E\psi$, what is $\hat{H}$?
cards.back: The Hamiltonian operator (total energy: kinetic + potential). Solving gives allowed energies E and wave functions ψ.

cards.front: Physical meaning of ψ and $|\psi|^2$?
cards.back: ψ has no physical meaning. $|\psi|^2$ is the probability density of finding the electron at a point. An atomic orbital is a one-electron wave function.

cards.front: What does the principal quantum number n decide?
cards.back: Shell, size and largely the energy of the orbital. n = 1, 2, 3… (K, L, M…). Orbitals in a shell = $n^2$; max electrons = $2n^2$.
cards.hint: Shell n contains n subshells.

cards.front: What does the azimuthal quantum number l decide? Its range?
cards.back: Shape of the orbital (subshell). l = 0 to n − 1: s = 0, p = 1, d = 2, f = 3. Orbitals per subshell = $2l + 1$.
cards.hint: Max electrons in a subshell = 2(2l + 1): s 2, p 6, d 10, f 14.

cards.front: What does the magnetic quantum number $m_l$ decide?
cards.back: Spatial orientation of the orbital; values from −l to +l including 0 (2l + 1 values).

cards.front: Values and meaning of the spin quantum number?
cards.back: $m_s = +\dfrac{1}{2}$ or $-\dfrac{1}{2}$: two spin orientations of the electron about its own axis.

cards.front: Is n = 2, l = 2, $m_l$ = 0 an allowed set?
cards.back: Not allowed: l can be at most n − 1 = 1.
cards.hint: Quick check: $l < n$ and $|m_l| \le l$.

cards.front: Which of these subshells cannot exist: 1p, 2s, 2d, 3f, 4f?
cards.back: 1p, 2d, 3f do not exist, because l must be less than n.

cards.front: Orbital angular momentum of an electron in terms of l?
cards.back: $\sqrt{l(l+1)}\,\dfrac{h}{2\pi}$; zero for an s orbital (l = 0).

cards.front: Formulae for radial and angular nodes?
cards.back: • Radial nodes = n − l − 1 • Angular nodes = l • Total nodes = n − 1
cards.hint: 3s: 2 radial, 0 angular. 3d: 0 radial, 2 angular.

cards.front: Number of radial and angular nodes in a 3p orbital?
cards.back: Radial = 3 − 1 − 1 = 1; angular = 1; total = 2.

cards.front: Describe the plots of $\psi^2$ vs r for 1s and 2s orbitals.
cards.back: 1s: maximum at the nucleus, then decreases steadily. 2s: decreases to zero at one radial node, rises to a small maximum, then decreases.

cards.front: Shapes of s, p and d orbitals?
cards.back: • s: spherical • p: dumbbell, with a nodal plane through the nucleus • d: mostly double-dumbbell (cloverleaf)

cards.front: Which d orbital has a different shape from the other four?
cards.back: $d_{z^2}$: two lobes along the z-axis with a doughnut-shaped ring in the xy-plane. Still equal in energy to the other 3d orbitals.

cards.front: Which d orbitals have lobes along the axes?
cards.back: $d_{x^2-y^2}$ and $d_{z^2}$. $d_{xy}$, $d_{yz}$, $d_{zx}$ have lobes between the axes.

cards.front: Do 2s and 2p have the same energy?
cards.back: In hydrogen, yes (energy depends only on n; degenerate). In multi-electron atoms 2s < 2p, because s electrons penetrate more and are less shielded.

cards.front: State the (n + l) rule.
cards.back: Lower (n + l) fills first; if equal, the one with lower n fills first. 4s (4) before 3d (5); 3d (5) before 4p (5).

cards.front: Aufbau filling order up to 7s?
cards.hint: Follow the diagonal-arrow diagram, or the (n + l) rule.

cards.front: State Pauli's exclusion principle.
cards.back: No two electrons in an atom can have all four quantum numbers the same; an orbital holds at most 2 electrons of opposite spin.

cards.front: State Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity.
cards.back: In orbitals of equal energy (p, d, f), electrons do not pair until each orbital has one electron, all with parallel spins.
cards.hint: Applies only to degenerate (equal-energy) orbitals.

cards.front: Configurations of Cr (Z = 24) and Cu (Z = 29)?
cards.hint: Half-filled or fully filled d subshell wins.

cards.front: Why are half-filled and fully filled subshells extra stable?
cards.back: Symmetrical distribution of electrons and larger exchange energy (more exchanges between parallel-spin electrons).

cards.front: What are Dobereiner's triads?
cards.back: Groups of three similar elements where the middle element's atomic weight ≈ the average of the other two: Li, Na, K; Ca, Sr, Ba; Cl, Br, I.

cards.front: State Newlands' law of octaves. Its limitation?
cards.back: With elements in order of atomic weight, every eighth element resembles the first. It worked only up to calcium.
cards.hint: Named after the eight notes of a musical scale.

cards.front: State Mendeleev's periodic law.
cards.back: Properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic weights.
cards.hint: Mendeleev: atomic weight. Modern law: atomic number.

cards.front: Two key merits of Mendeleev's periodic table?
cards.back: • Left gaps for undiscovered elements and predicted their properties • Gave priority to similar properties over strict atomic-weight order, and corrected some atomic weights

cards.front: What are eka-aluminium and eka-silicon?
cards.back: Eka-aluminium = gallium; eka-silicon = germanium. Mendeleev predicted both before they were discovered.

cards.front: Why did Mendeleev place Te before I despite Te's higher atomic weight?
cards.back: To keep iodine with the halogens; the order is justified by atomic number (Te 52, I 53).

cards.front: State the modern periodic law.
cards.back: Physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.

cards.front: What did Moseley observe?
cards.back: A plot of $\sqrt{\nu}$ (characteristic X-ray frequency) against atomic number Z is a straight line; against atomic mass it is not.

cards.front: Number of elements in periods 1 to 7?
What does the period number correspond to?
cards.back: The principal quantum number (n) of the outermost (valence) shell. Elements in a period = 2 × orbitals being filled.

cards.front: Why does the 4th period have 18 elements?
cards.back: It fills 4s, 3d and 4p: 1 + 5 + 3 = 9 orbitals → 18 electrons.

cards.front: IUPAC group numbering in the long form of the table?
cards.back: Groups 1 to 18, replacing the older IA–VIIIA / IB–VIIIB notation.

cards.front: Range of lanthanoids and actinoids?
cards.back: Lanthanoids: Ce (58) – Lu (71), 4f series. Actinoids: Th (90) – Lr (103), 5f series. Both placed separately below the table.
cards.hint: La (57) and Ac (89) themselves sit in group 3.

cards.front: IUPAC numerical roots for naming elements with Z > 100?
cards.back: 0 nil, 1 un, 2 bi, 3 tri, 4 quad, 5 pent, 6 hex, 7 sept, 8 oct, 9 enn; join the roots and add -ium.

cards.front: IUPAC temporary name and symbol for Z = 120?
cards.back: Unbinilium (Ubn)
cards.hint: 1-2-0 → un + bi + nil + ium.

cards.front: IUPAC temporary name for Z = 104 and its official name?
cards.back: Unnilquadium (Unq); official name rutherfordium (Rf).
cards.hint: Symbol = first letters of the three roots.

cards.front: What decides the block of an element?
cards.back: The subshell that receives the last (differentiating) electron: s, p, d or f.

cards.front: General outer configuration of s-block and p-block elements?
cards.back: • s-block: $ns^{1-2}$ (groups 1, 2) • p-block: $ns^2np^{1-6}$ (groups 13–18)

cards.front: General outer configuration of d-block elements?
cards.hint: Pd ($4d^{10}5s^0$) is the classic ns⁰ case.

cards.front: General outer configuration of f-block elements?
Which element has an $ns^2$ (s-block) configuration but sits in group 18?
cards.back: Helium ($1s^2$): its completely filled valence shell gives noble-gas properties.

cards.front: Period and group of the element $[\text{Ne}]3s^2 3p^5$?
cards.back: Period 3; p-block group = 10 + valence electrons = 10 + 7 = 17 (chlorine).
cards.hint: p-block group = 10 + (ns + np electrons).

cards.front: Group of a d-block element with $3d^6 4s^2$?
cards.back: Group = (n−1)d + ns electrons = 6 + 2 = 8 (iron, period 4).

cards.front: Which elements are called representative (main group) elements?
cards.back: s-block and p-block elements.

cards.front: Name the metalloids (semi-metals).
cards.back: Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te: properties intermediate between metals and non-metals.

cards.front: How does metallic character vary in the periodic table?
cards.back: Decreases across a period, increases down a group. Metals form over 78% of known elements; non-metals are top right.

cards.front: Covalent vs metallic radius (with NCERT examples)?
cards.back: • Covalent: half the internuclear distance in a covalent molecule (Cl: 99 pm) • Metallic: half the distance between adjacent metal atoms (Cu: 128 pm)

cards.front: Trend of atomic radius in the periodic table?
cards.back: Decreases across a period (effective nuclear charge rises); increases down a group (new shells added).

cards.front: Why do noble gases appear to have large atomic radii in a period?
cards.back: Their value is a van der Waals (non-bonded) radius, which is larger than the covalent radii quoted for other elements.
cards.hint: Trap: don't compare van der Waals radius with covalent radius.

cards.front: Size of a cation and an anion compared with the parent atom?
cards.back: Cation is smaller (same nuclear charge holds fewer electrons). Anion is larger (extra electron repulsion, lower effective nuclear charge).

cards.front: In an isoelectronic series, what decides ionic size?
cards.back: Same number of electrons, so greater nuclear charge (Z) → smaller ion.
cards.hint: More protons pull the same number of electrons closer.

cards.front: Order of size: $\text{O}^{2-}$, $\text{F}^-$, $\text{Na}^+$, $\text{Mg}^{2+}$?
cards.back: $\text{O}^{2-} > \text{F}^- > \text{Na}^+ > \text{Mg}^{2+}$ (all have 10 electrons; Z = 8, 9, 11, 12).

cards.front: Define first ionization enthalpy.
cards.back: Energy to remove the outermost electron from an isolated gaseous atom in its ground state: $\text{X(g)} \rightarrow \text{X}^+\text{(g)} + e^-$. Always positive; unit $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.
cards.hint: Trap: 'isolated gaseous atom in ground state' is part of the definition.

cards.front: Why is second ionization enthalpy higher than the first?
cards.back: The second electron is removed from a positively charged ion, which holds its electrons more strongly.

cards.front: General trend of first ionization enthalpy?
cards.back: Increases across a period, decreases down a group.

cards.front: Exceptions to the IE trend in period 2?
cards.back: • Be > B: B loses a 2p electron, shielded by 2s and easier to remove • N > O: O has a paired 2p electron (repulsion); N is half-filled
cards.hint: Period 2 order: Li < B < Be < C < O < N < F < Ne.

cards.front: Order of first ionization enthalpy in period 3?
cards.back: Na < Al < Mg < Si < S < P < Cl < Ar
cards.hint: Same pattern as period 2: Mg > Al and P > S.

cards.front: Highest and lowest first ionization enthalpy among elements?
cards.back: Highest: He (≈2372 $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$). Lowest among stable elements: Cs.

cards.front: How do shielding and penetration affect ionization enthalpy?
cards.back: Inner electrons shield valence electrons from the nucleus. Penetration order s > p > d > f, so an s electron is held more tightly than a p electron of the same shell.

cards.front: Why is the second IE of Na much higher than that of Mg?
cards.back: $\text{Na}^+$ has a stable noble-gas (Ne) core; the next electron comes from an inner shell. $\text{Mg}^+$ still has a 3s electron.

cards.front: Define electron gain enthalpy.
cards.back: Enthalpy change when an electron is added to an isolated gaseous atom: $\text{X(g)} + e^- \rightarrow \text{X}^-\text{(g)}$; negative if energy is released.

cards.front: General trend of electron gain enthalpy?
cards.back: Becomes more negative across a period; less negative down a group.

cards.front: Which has the most negative electron gain enthalpy: F or Cl?
cards.back: Cl. F is very small, so the added electron faces strong repulsion in the compact 2p subshell. Likewise S is more negative than O.
cards.hint: Trap: F is the most electronegative, but Cl has the most negative $\Delta_{eg}H$.

cards.front: Why do noble gases have large positive electron gain enthalpies?
cards.back: The added electron must enter the next higher shell, giving a very unstable configuration.

cards.front: Sign of the second electron gain enthalpy of oxygen?
cards.back: Positive: adding an electron to $\text{O}^-$ is opposed by repulsion from the negative ion.

cards.front: Define electronegativity. Value for fluorine on the Pauling scale?
cards.back: Qualitative ability of an atom in a compound to attract shared electrons; not directly measurable, no unit. F = 4.0 (highest).
cards.hint: Electronegativity is for a bonded atom; electron gain enthalpy is for an isolated atom.

cards.front: Trend of electronegativity and link with metallic character?
cards.back: Increases across a period, decreases down a group. It is inversely related to metallic character.

cards.front: Usual valence of representative elements?
cards.back: Equal to the number of valence electrons, or 8 − valence electrons.

cards.front: Oxidation state of oxygen in $\text{OF}_2$ and in $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$?
cards.back: $\text{OF}_2$: +2 (F is more electronegative, −1 each). $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$: −2.
cards.hint: O shows positive states only with F: $\text{OF}_2$ (+2), $\text{O}_2\text{F}_2$ (+1).

cards.front: Why do second-period elements show anomalous behaviour?
cards.back: Small size, high charge/radius ratio, high electronegativity and no d orbitals → max covalency 4. e.g. B forms $[\text{BF}_4]^-$, Al forms $[\text{AlF}_6]^{3-}$.
cards.hint: Only 2s and 2p are available, so at most 4 bonds.

cards.front: Name the diagonal relationship pairs.
cards.back: Li–Mg, Be–Al, B–Si: the first element of a group resembles the second element of the next group.
cards.hint: Similar charge/radius ratio (polarising power) explains the resemblance.

cards.front: Which period-2 elements readily form $p\pi$–$p\pi$ multiple bonds?
cards.back: C, N, O (e.g. C=C, C≡C, N≡N, C=O), unlike heavier members of their groups.

cards.front: Nature of oxides across period 3 (Na to Cl)?
cards.back: $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ strongly basic → $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ amphoteric → $\text{Cl}_2\text{O}_7$ strongly acidic.

cards.front: Examples of amphoteric and neutral oxides?
cards.back: • Amphoteric: $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$, $\text{As}_2\text{O}_3$ • Neutral: CO, NO, $\text{N}_2\text{O}$
cards.hint: Amphoteric oxides react with both acids and bases.

cards.front: Where in a period is chemical reactivity highest?
cards.back: At the two extremes: alkali metals on the left (lose electrons easily) and halogens on the right (gain electrons easily). Lowest in the centre.

cards.front: State the octet rule.
cards.back: Atoms combine by losing, gaining or sharing electrons so that each attains eight electrons in its valence shell (noble gas configuration).

cards.front: Formula for formal charge on an atom in a Lewis structure?
cards.back:
$\text{FC} = V - L - \tfrac{1}{2}S$
• V = valence electrons in free atom
• L = non-bonding (lone pair) electrons
• S = bonding (shared) electrons
cards.hint: Preferred Lewis structure = one with the lowest formal charges on atoms.

cards.front: Formal charges on the three O atoms of ozone ($\text{O}_3$)?
cards.back: • Central O: +1 • Doubly bonded end O: 0 • Singly bonded end O: −1

cards.front: Three types of exceptions to the octet rule?
cards.back: • Incomplete octet: $\text{LiCl}$, $\text{BeH}_2$, $\text{BCl}_3$ • Odd-electron molecules: $\text{NO}$, $\text{NO}_2$ • Expanded octet: $\text{PF}_5$, $\text{SF}_6$, $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$

cards.front: Why can P, S, Cl expand their octet but N, O, F cannot?
cards.back: Third-period elements have vacant 3d orbitals available for bonding; second-period elements have no d orbitals in the valence shell.
cards.hint: Trap: $\text{NCl}_5$ does not exist, but $\text{PCl}_5$ does.

cards.front: Other limitations of the octet theory (besides exceptions)?
cards.back: • Cannot explain shapes of molecules • Gives no idea of relative energy/stability • Fails for noble gas compounds like $\text{XeF}_2$, $\text{XeF}_4$

cards.front: Factors favouring formation of an ionic bond?
cards.back: • Low ionisation enthalpy of the metal • Highly negative electron gain enthalpy of the non-metal • High lattice enthalpy of the solid formed

cards.front: Define lattice enthalpy. What is its value for NaCl?
cards.back: Energy required to completely separate one mole of a solid ionic compound into gaseous ions. For NaCl it is $+788\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

cards.front: Define bond length. Which is larger: covalent radius or van der Waals radius?
cards.back: Equilibrium distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms. van der Waals radius > covalent radius of the same atom.

cards.front: How do bond length and bond enthalpy vary with bond order?
cards.back: Higher bond order → shorter bond and higher bond enthalpy. e.g. $\text{N}\equiv\text{N}$ (946 $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$) > $\text{O=O}$ (498) > $\text{H–H}$ (435.8).

cards.front: Bond order of the isoelectronic species $\text{N}_2$, $\text{CO}$ and $\text{NO}^+$?
cards.back: All have bond order 3 (14 electrons each). Isoelectronic molecules/ions have the same bond order.
cards.hint: Likewise $\text{F}_2$ and $\text{O}_2^{2-}$ (18 e⁻) both have bond order 1.

cards.front: What is resonance? Does any single canonical structure exist?
cards.back: A molecule is represented by two or more canonical structures; the real molecule is their resonance hybrid. Canonical forms have no real existence.
cards.hint: Trap: the molecule does not oscillate between canonical forms.

cards.front: O–O bond lengths in ozone compared to O–O single and O=O double bonds?
cards.back: Both O–O bonds in $\text{O}_3$ are equal, 128 pm — between O–O single (148 pm) and O=O double (121 pm), due to resonance.

cards.front: Bond order of each C–O bond in the carbonate ion?
cards.back: All three C–O bonds are identical; bond order = 4/3 ≈ 1.33 (three equivalent resonance structures).
cards.hint: Same value (4/3) for each N–O bond in $\text{NO}_3^-$.

cards.front: Effect of resonance on stability of a molecule?
cards.back: Resonance stabilises the molecule: the energy of the resonance hybrid is lower than that of any single canonical structure. Bond lengths get averaged.

cards.front: Define dipole moment. Its units?
cards.back: $\mu = q \times d$ (charge × distance between charge centres). Unit: Debye (D); $1\ \text{D} = 3.33564 \times 10^{-30}\ \text{C m}$.
cards.hint: Dipole moment is a vector: arrow from positive to negative centre (chemistry convention).

cards.front: Name molecules with zero dipole moment despite polar bonds.
cards.back: $\text{CO}_2$, $\text{BeF}_2$ (linear), $\text{BF}_3$ (trigonal planar), $\text{CH}_4$, $\text{CCl}_4$ (tetrahedral): bond dipoles cancel due to symmetry.

cards.front: Why is $\mu$ of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ non-zero (1.85 D) while $\text{CO}_2$ is zero?
cards.back: $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ is bent (bond dipoles add up); $\text{CO}_2$ is linear (equal opposite O=C=O dipoles cancel).

cards.front: Why does $\text{NH}_3$ (1.47 D) have a higher dipole moment than $\text{NF}_3$ (0.24 D)?
cards.back: In $\text{NH}_3$, lone-pair moment is in the same direction as the N–H bond moments (adds up). In $\text{NF}_3$, N–F moments point towards F, opposing the lone-pair moment.
cards.hint: Both are pyramidal with one lone pair on N — the difference is only the direction of bond dipoles.

cards.front: State Fajans' rules for covalent character in ionic bonds.
cards.back: Covalent character increases with: • Smaller cation, larger anion • Higher charge on the ions • Cation with $(n-1)d^n ns^0$ config (more polarising than noble gas config)

cards.front: Which has more covalent character: LiCl or KCl? NaCl or $\text{AlCl}_3$?
cards.back: LiCl (smaller $\text{Li}^+$ is more polarising) and $\text{AlCl}_3$ (small, highly charged $\text{Al}^{3+}$).
cards.hint: Small + highly charged cation = high polarising power = more covalent.

cards.front: Order of electron-pair repulsions in VSEPR theory?
cards.back: lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair
cards.hint: Lone pairs are held by one nucleus only, so they occupy more space.

cards.front: Bond angles in $\text{CH}_4$, $\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$? Why do they decrease?
cards.back: 109.5° > 107° > 104.5°. Number of lone pairs increases (0, 1, 2); greater lp–bp and lp–lp repulsion squeezes the bond angle.

cards.front: Shapes of $\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ by VSEPR?
cards.back: • $\text{NH}_3$ ($\text{AB}_3\text{E}$): trigonal pyramidal • $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ($\text{AB}_2\text{E}_2$): bent (V-shaped) Both have electron pairs arranged tetrahedrally.

cards.front: Shape of $\text{SO}_2$ according to VSEPR?
cards.back: $\text{AB}_2\text{E}$ type (2 bond pairs + 1 lone pair, trigonal planar electron geometry) → bent shape.

cards.front: Shape of $\text{SF}_4$? Where is the lone pair?
cards.back: $\text{AB}_4\text{E}$ → see-saw (distorted tetrahedron). The lone pair sits in an equatorial position of the trigonal bipyramid.
cards.hint: Equatorial lone pair has only two 90° interactions — less repulsion than axial.

cards.front: Shape of $\text{ClF}_3$?
cards.back: $\text{AB}_3\text{E}_2$ (3 bp + 2 lp, both lone pairs equatorial) → T-shaped.

cards.front: Shapes of $\text{BrF}_5$ and $\text{XeF}_4$?
cards.back: • $\text{BrF}_5$ ($\text{AB}_5\text{E}$): square pyramidal • $\text{XeF}_4$ ($\text{AB}_4\text{E}_2$): square planar (lone pairs opposite each other)

cards.front: Why are axial bonds in $\text{PCl}_5$ longer than equatorial bonds?
cards.back: Each axial bond pair faces three bond pairs at 90°; equatorial ones face two. Greater repulsion makes axial bonds longer and weaker, so $\text{PCl}_5$ is very reactive.

cards.front: How does valence bond theory explain formation of $\text{H}_2$?
cards.back: Atomic orbitals of two H atoms overlap; attraction outweighs repulsion until energy reaches a minimum at 74 pm. Energy released: $435.8\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.
cards.hint: Greater the overlap, stronger the bond.

cards.front: Difference between a sigma and a pi bond?
cards.back: • σ bond: head-on (axial) overlap along the internuclear axis — stronger • π bond: sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals above and below the axis — weaker

cards.front: Number of σ and π bonds in ethene and ethyne?
cards.hint: Every multiple bond has exactly one σ; the rest are π.

cards.front: Why is there no free rotation about a C=C double bond?
cards.back: Rotation would destroy the sideways overlap of p orbitals, i.e. break the π bond. A σ bond (C–C) allows free rotation.

cards.front: Key features of hybridisation?
cards.back: • Orbitals of similar energy on the same atom mix • No. of hybrid orbitals = no. of atomic orbitals mixed • Hybrids are equivalent; form stronger σ bonds than pure orbitals
cards.hint: Trap: it is orbitals, not electrons, that hybridise.

cards.front: sp hybridisation: geometry, bond angle, % s-character, example?
cards.back: Linear, 180°, 50% s-character. Example: $\text{BeCl}_2$.

cards.front: $sp^2$ hybridisation: geometry, bond angle, % s-character, example?
cards.back: Trigonal planar, 120°, 33.3% s-character. Example: $\text{BCl}_3$.

cards.front: $sp^3$ hybridisation: geometry, bond angle, % s-character, examples?
cards.back: Tetrahedral, 109.5°, 25% s-character. Examples: $\text{CH}_4$; also N in $\text{NH}_3$ and O in $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

cards.front: Quick way to find hybridisation of a central atom?
cards.back: Count σ bonds + lone pairs on it: 2 → sp, 3 → $sp^2$, 4 → $sp^3$, 5 → $sp^3d$, 6 → $sp^3d^2$.
cards.hint: π bonds are not counted.

cards.front: Order of electronegativity of sp, $sp^2$, $sp^3$ carbon?
cards.back: $sp > sp^2 > sp^3$ — more s-character holds electrons closer to the nucleus.
cards.hint: So ethyne C–H is the most acidic among ethane, ethene, ethyne.

cards.front: Hybridisation of carbon in ethene and ethyne? Composition of the C–C multiple bond?
cards.back: • Ethene: $sp^2$; C=C = one σ ($sp^2$–$sp^2$) + one π (2p–2p) • Ethyne: sp; C≡C = one σ (sp–sp) + two π

cards.front: Which d orbitals are used in $sp^3d$ ($\text{PCl}_5$) and $sp^3d^2$ ($\text{SF}_6$)?
cards.back: • $sp^3d$: $d_{z^2}$ → trigonal bipyramidal • $sp^3d^2$: $d_{z^2}$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ → octahedral

cards.front: What is LCAO in molecular orbital theory?
cards.back: Molecular orbitals are formed by linear combination of atomic orbitals: addition gives a bonding MO (lower energy), subtraction an antibonding MO (higher energy).
cards.hint: Number of MOs formed = number of AOs combined.

cards.front: Conditions for combination of atomic orbitals to form MOs?
cards.back: • Comparable energies • Same symmetry about the molecular axis • Maximum overlap

cards.front: Formula for bond order in MO theory? What does bond order 0 mean?
cards.back: $\text{B.O.} = \tfrac{1}{2}(N_b - N_a)$. Bond order 0 → molecule does not exist (e.g. $\text{He}_2$, $\text{Be}_2$).
cards.hint: Positive bond order (even 1/2) means the species is stable, e.g. $\text{H}_2^+$.

cards.front: MO energy order for $\text{B}_2$, $\text{C}_2$, $\text{N}_2$ (beyond $\sigma^*2s$)?
cards.back: $(\pi 2p_x = \pi 2p_y) < \sigma 2p_z$ < $(\pi^* 2p_x = \pi^* 2p_y) < \sigma^* 2p_z$
cards.hint: π below σ2pz only up to N₂ (≤14 electrons) due to s–p mixing.

cards.front: MO energy order for $\text{O}_2$ and $\text{F}_2$ (beyond $\sigma^*2s$)?
cards.back: $\sigma 2p_z < (\pi 2p_x = \pi 2p_y)$ < $(\pi^* 2p_x = \pi^* 2p_y) < \sigma^* 2p_z$

cards.front: Bond order and magnetic nature of $\text{O}_2$ by MO theory?
cards.back: Bond order 2; two unpaired electrons in $\pi^*2p_x$ and $\pi^*2p_y$ → paramagnetic.
cards.hint: Lewis structure wrongly predicts O₂ to be diamagnetic — MOT explains it.

cards.front: Bond order and magnetism of $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{C}_2$?
cards.back: • $\text{N}_2$: BO 3, diamagnetic • $\text{C}_2$: BO 2, diamagnetic; its double bond has both π bonds (no σ)

cards.front: Order of bond order and bond length: $\text{O}_2^+$, $\text{O}_2$, $\text{O}_2^-$, $\text{O}_2^{2-}$?
cards.back: Bond order: 2.5 > 2 > 1.5 > 1 Bond length: reverse order ($\text{O}_2^{2-}$ longest). Only $\text{O}_2^{2-}$ is diamagnetic.
cards.hint: Electrons added to π* lower bond order; removing from π* raises it.

cards.front: Bond order of $\text{Li}_2$ and $\text{H}_2^+$? Do they exist?
cards.back: • $\text{Li}_2$: BO 1, exists, diamagnetic • $\text{H}_2^+$: BO ½, exists, paramagnetic

cards.front: What is a hydrogen bond? Give its two types.
cards.back: Weak attraction between H bonded to a highly electronegative atom (F, O, N) and another such atom. • Intermolecular: HF, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ • Intramolecular: o-nitrophenol
cards.hint: HF molecules form zig-zag chains via H-bonds.

cards.front: Why is o-nitrophenol more volatile than p-nitrophenol?
cards.back: o-Nitrophenol has intramolecular H-bonding (no association), while p-nitrophenol forms intermolecular H-bonds and associates → higher boiling point.

cards.front: Why is water a liquid while $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ is a gas at room temperature?
cards.back: Water molecules are associated by intermolecular hydrogen bonding (O is highly electronegative); S is not electronegative enough to form H-bonds.

cards.front: In which physical state is hydrogen bonding strongest?
cards.back: Strongest in the solid state, weakest in the gaseous state.

cards.front: Differentiate open, closed and isolated systems.
cards.back: • Open: exchanges matter and energy • Closed: exchanges energy only • Isolated: exchanges neither
cards.hint: Hot coffee in a sealed thermos ≈ isolated system.

cards.front: What is a state function? Name some.
cards.back: A property whose value depends only on the state of the system, not on the path. e.g. U, H, S, G, p, V, T.
cards.hint: Trap: q and w are path functions, but q + w (= ΔU) is a state function.

cards.front: Classify as extensive or intensive: mass, volume, U, H, heat capacity, T, p, density, molar heat capacity.
cards.back: • Extensive: mass, volume, U, H, heat capacity • Intensive: T, p, density, molar heat capacity
cards.hint: Ratio of two extensive properties is intensive (e.g. density = m/V).

cards.front: What is an adiabatic process?
cards.back: A process in which no heat is exchanged between system and surroundings ($q = 0$), so $\Delta U = w_{ad}$.

cards.front: What is a reversible process?
cards.back: One carried out infinitely slowly through a series of equilibrium states, so it can be reversed at any point by an infinitesimal change.

cards.front: State the first law of thermodynamics (mathematical form).
cards.back: $\Delta U = q + w$ — energy of an isolated system is constant; energy can be neither created nor destroyed.

cards.front: Sign conventions for q and w (IUPAC/NCERT)?
cards.back: • Heat absorbed by system: q positive • Work done on system: w positive • Work done by system: w negative
cards.hint: Trap: some old books write ΔU = q − w (work done by system positive).

cards.front: On what does the internal energy of an ideal gas depend?
cards.back: Only on temperature. Hence for an isothermal process of an ideal gas, $\Delta U = 0$.

cards.front: Work done when a gas expands against constant external pressure?
cards.back: $w = -p_{ex}\,\Delta V = -p_{ex}(V_f - V_i)$. Negative for expansion (work done by gas).

cards.front: Work done in reversible isothermal expansion of an ideal gas?
cards.back: $w_{rev} = -2.303\,nRT\log\dfrac{V_f}{V_i}$
cards.hint: Can also use $\log\dfrac{p_i}{p_f}$ since $p_iV_i = p_fV_f$.

cards.front: What are w, q and ΔU for free expansion of an ideal gas?
cards.back: Expansion into vacuum ($p_{ex} = 0$): w = 0. For an ideal gas also q = 0, ΔU = 0.
cards.hint: Free expansion does no work whether reversible or irreversible.

cards.front: For isothermal irreversible expansion of an ideal gas, what is q?
cards.back: $\Delta U = 0$, so $q = -w = p_{ex}(V_f - V_i)$.

cards.front: On a p–V graph, what does work correspond to? Which expansion gives maximum work?
cards.back: Work = area under the p–V curve. Reversible expansion gives the maximum work (largest area).

cards.front: Define enthalpy. What does ΔH equal?
cards.back: $H = U + pV$. $\Delta H = q_p$ (heat absorbed at constant pressure).
cards.hint: Similarly $\Delta U = q_V$ (heat at constant volume).

cards.front: Relation between ΔH and ΔU for a reaction involving gases?
cards.back:
$\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT$
$\Delta n_g$ = moles of gaseous products − moles of gaseous reactants
cards.hint: Use $R = 8.314\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$; watch kJ vs J.

cards.front: When is ΔH = ΔU for a reaction?
cards.back: When $\Delta n_g = 0$, e.g. $\text{H}_2(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\text{HCl}(g)$; also ≈ equal for reactions of only solids/liquids.

cards.front: For $\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\text{NH}_3(g)$, compare ΔH and ΔU.
cards.back: $\Delta n_g = 2 - 4 = -2$, so $\Delta H = \Delta U - 2RT$ → ΔH < ΔU.

cards.front: Is enthalpy extensive or intensive?
cards.back: Extensive. Molar enthalpy ($H_m = H/n$) is intensive.

cards.front: Relation between heat, heat capacity and temperature change?
cards.back: $q = C\,\Delta T$; $C = n\,C_m$ (molar) or $q = mc\,\Delta T$ (specific heat c).

cards.front: Relation between $C_p$ and $C_V$ for an ideal gas?
cards.back: $C_p - C_V = R$ (molar values). $C_p > C_V$ because at constant pressure heat is also used to do expansion work.

cards.front: Which quantity does a bomb calorimeter measure? A coffee-cup calorimeter?
cards.back: • Bomb calorimeter (constant volume): ΔU • Calorimeter at constant (atmospheric) pressure: ΔH
cards.hint: Bomb is sealed steel — no expansion work, w = 0.

cards.front: Define the standard state of a substance.
cards.back: Its pure form at 1 bar pressure at a specified temperature (usually 298 K). Standard values are marked with °.
cards.hint: Trap: standard state is not STP; temperature must be specified.

cards.front: Relation between enthalpies of sublimation, fusion and vaporisation?
cards.back: $\Delta_{sub}H^\circ = \Delta_{fus}H^\circ + \Delta_{vap}H^\circ$
cards.hint: Follows from Hess's law: solid → liquid → vapour.

cards.front: Why is $\Delta_{vap}H$ of water (≈ 40.8 $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$) larger than for most liquids of similar size?
cards.back: Strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding in water must be overcome.

cards.front: Define standard enthalpy of formation.
cards.back: Enthalpy change when 1 mol of a compound is formed from its elements in their most stable (reference) states under standard conditions.

cards.front: What is $\Delta_f H^\circ$ of an element in its reference state?
cards.back: Zero, e.g. C(graphite), $\text{O}_2(g)$, $\text{H}_2(g)$, $\text{Br}_2(l)$.
cards.hint: Trap: C(diamond) and $\text{O}_3(g)$ have non-zero $\Delta_f H^\circ$.

cards.front: Formula for $\Delta_r H^\circ$ from enthalpies of formation?
cards.back:
$\Delta_r H^\circ = \sum a_i\Delta_f H^\circ(\text{products}) - \sum b_i\Delta_f H^\circ(\text{reactants})$
a, b = stoichiometric coefficients

cards.front: How does ΔH change when a thermochemical equation is reversed or multiplied by 2?
cards.back: • Reversed: sign changes • Multiplied by 2: ΔH doubles

cards.front: Define enthalpy of combustion. What is its sign?
cards.back: Enthalpy change when 1 mol of a substance burns completely in oxygen. Always negative (exothermic).

cards.front: Which enthalpy of combustion equals $\Delta_f H^\circ$ of $\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$? Of $\text{CO}_2(g)$?
cards.back:
• $\Delta_c H^\circ[\text{H}_2(g)] = \Delta_f H^\circ[\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)]$
• $\Delta_c H^\circ[\text{C(graphite)}] = \Delta_f H^\circ[\text{CO}_2(g)]$
cards.hint: Same equation, so same ΔH.

cards.front: Define enthalpy of atomisation. Give its value for $\text{H}_2$.
cards.back: Enthalpy change to break all bonds in 1 mol of a substance into gaseous atoms. For $\text{H}_2$: 435.0 $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ (= bond dissociation enthalpy).

cards.front: Mean C–H bond enthalpy from atomisation of methane ($1665\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$)?
cards.back: $\dfrac{1665}{4} = $ 416 $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ — the four C–H bonds break with different energies, so the average is used.

cards.front: Formula for $\Delta_r H^\circ$ from bond enthalpies (gas phase)?
cards.back: $\Delta_r H^\circ = \sum \text{B.E.(reactants)} - \sum \text{B.E.(products)}$
cards.hint: Trap: this is reactants − products, the reverse of the formation-enthalpy formula.

cards.front: Why can lattice enthalpy not be measured directly? How is it found?
cards.back: Ions cannot be separated experimentally; it is found indirectly using Hess's law (Born–Haber cycle). NaCl: $+788\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

cards.front: Relation of enthalpy of solution to lattice and hydration enthalpies?
cards.back: $\Delta_{sol}H^\circ = \Delta_{lattice}H^\circ + \Delta_{hyd}H^\circ$. For NaCl ≈ 788 − 784 = +4 $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ (slightly endothermic).
cards.hint: If lattice enthalpy is very high, the salt may not dissolve at all.

cards.front: State Hess's law of constant heat summation.
cards.back: If a reaction occurs in several steps, the total enthalpy change is the sum of the enthalpy changes of the steps — same as for a one-step path.
cards.hint: Works because H is a state function.

cards.front: What is a spontaneous process? Does spontaneous mean fast?
cards.back: A process that occurs on its own without external help. Not necessarily fast — spontaneity says nothing about rate.
cards.hint: Trap: diamond → graphite is spontaneous but extremely slow.

cards.front: Is decrease in enthalpy a sufficient criterion for spontaneity?
cards.back: No. Many endothermic processes are spontaneous, e.g. melting of ice above 273 K, evaporation of water, dissolution of $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$.

cards.front: What is entropy? Formula for its change in a reversible process?
cards.back: Measure of degree of randomness (a state function). $\Delta S = \dfrac{q_{rev}}{T}$

cards.front: Order of entropy of solid, liquid and gas of the same substance?
cards.back: Solid < liquid < gas

cards.front: Entropy criterion for spontaneity?
cards.back: $\Delta S_{total} = \Delta S_{sys} + \Delta S_{surr} > 0$. For an isolated system, $\Delta S > 0$ for a spontaneous process.
cards.hint: Second law: entropy of the universe increases in every spontaneous process.

cards.front: Entropy change at a phase transition (e.g. melting at its melting point)?
cards.back: $\Delta S = \dfrac{\Delta H_{trans}}{T_{trans}}$; positive for fusion and vaporisation.

cards.front: Why does the same heat cause a larger entropy change at lower temperature?
cards.back: $\Delta S = q_{rev}/T$ — at low T the system is less disordered, so added heat raises randomness more.

cards.front: Define Gibbs energy and write ΔG at constant T and p.
cards.back:
$G = H - TS$
$\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$

cards.front: Criteria for spontaneity in terms of ΔG?
cards.back: • ΔG < 0: spontaneous • ΔG > 0: non-spontaneous • ΔG = 0: equilibrium

cards.front: Spontaneity when ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0? When ΔH > 0 and ΔS < 0?
cards.back: • ΔH −, ΔS +: spontaneous at all T • ΔH +, ΔS −: non-spontaneous at all T

cards.front: Spontaneity when ΔH and ΔS have the same sign?
cards.back: • ΔH −, ΔS −: spontaneous at low T • ΔH +, ΔS +: spontaneous at high T
cards.hint: High T makes the TΔS term dominate.

cards.front: Temperature at which spontaneity of a reaction changes?
cards.back: At ΔG = 0: $T = \dfrac{\Delta H}{\Delta S}$
cards.hint: Keep ΔH and ΔS in the same energy unit (J or kJ).

cards.front: Physical meaning of ΔG?
cards.back: $-\Delta G$ = maximum useful (non-expansion) work obtainable from the process.

cards.front: Relation between $\Delta_r G^\circ$ and equilibrium constant K?
cards.back: $\Delta_r G^\circ = -RT\ln K = -2.303\,RT\log K$

cards.front: What does $\Delta_r G^\circ < 0$ imply about K?
cards.back: K > 1: products are favoured at equilibrium. $\Delta_r G^\circ > 0$ → K < 1.

cards.front: Why is chemical equilibrium called dynamic?
cards.back: Forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates, so concentrations stay constant though reactions have not stopped.
cards.hint: Trap: at equilibrium concentrations are constant, not equal.

cards.front: What is the normal melting point of a substance?
cards.back: Temperature at which solid and liquid are in equilibrium at 1 atm pressure. For ice it is 273 K.

cards.front: What is constant at liquid–vapour equilibrium in a closed vessel at fixed T?
cards.back: The vapour pressure: rate of evaporation = rate of condensation.
cards.hint: Higher vapour pressure at a given T means a more volatile liquid.

cards.front: State Henry's law (gas–liquid equilibrium).
cards.back: The mass of a gas dissolved in a given mass of solvent at a given T is proportional to the pressure of the gas above the solvent.
cards.hint: Opening a soda bottle lowers CO₂ pressure → fizz.

cards.front: General characteristics of a system at equilibrium?
cards.back: • Possible only in a closed system at constant T • Can be approached from either direction • Measurable properties become constant

cards.front: Expression for $K_c$ for $aA + bB \rightleftharpoons cC + dD$?
cards.back: $K_c = \dfrac{[C]^c[D]^d}{[A]^a[B]^b}$ (equilibrium molar concentrations)

cards.front: How does K change if the equation is reversed, or multiplied by n?
cards.back:
• Reversed: $K' = \dfrac{1}{K}$
• Multiplied by n: $K' = K^n$
• Two equations added: $K = K_1 \times K_2$
cards.hint: Halving an equation → $\sqrt{K}$.

cards.front: Does $K_c$ depend on initial concentrations or on temperature?
cards.back: Independent of initial concentrations; depends only on temperature (for a given balanced equation).

cards.front: Relation between $K_p$ and $K_c$?
cards.back:
$K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n}$
$\Delta n$ = moles of gaseous products − gaseous reactants
cards.hint: Use $R = 0.0831\ \text{bar L mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$ when pressures are in bar.

cards.front: When is $K_p = K_c$? Give an example.
cards.back: When $\Delta n = 0$, e.g. $\text{H}_2(g) + \text{I}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{HI}(g)$.

cards.front: $K_p$ vs $K_c$ for $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NO}_2(g)$?
cards.back: $\Delta n = +1$ → $K_p = K_c\,RT$

cards.front: $K_p$ for $\text{CaCO}_3(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{CaO}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g)$?
cards.back: $K_p = p_{\text{CO}_2}$ — pure solids (and liquids) are omitted since their concentration/activity is constant (taken as 1).

cards.front: Units of $K_c$?
cards.back: $(\text{mol L}^{-1})^{\Delta n}$; no units when Δn = 0. Thermodynamic K (using activities) is dimensionless.

cards.front: What does the magnitude of K tell you?
cards.back: • $K > 10^3$: products predominate • $K < 10^{-3}$: reactants predominate • $10^{-3}$ to $10^3$: both in appreciable amounts

cards.front: How is the reaction quotient Q used to predict the direction of reaction?
cards.back: • $Q < K$: proceeds forward • $Q > K$: proceeds backward • $Q = K$: at equilibrium
cards.hint: Q has the same form as K but uses non-equilibrium concentrations.

cards.front: Relation of ΔG with Q and of ΔG° with K?
cards.back:
$\Delta G = \Delta G^\circ + RT\ln Q$
At equilibrium ($\Delta G = 0$): $\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K$

cards.front: State Le Chatelier's principle.
cards.back: If a system at equilibrium is disturbed by a change in concentration, pressure or temperature, it shifts in the direction that counteracts the change.

cards.front: Effect of adding a reactant or removing a product at equilibrium?
cards.back: Equilibrium shifts forward (more product formed); K is unchanged.

cards.front: Effect of increasing pressure on a gaseous equilibrium?
cards.back: Shifts towards the side with fewer moles of gas. No effect if $\Delta n_g = 0$.
cards.hint: $\text{N}_2 + 3\text{H}_2 \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3$: high pressure favours $\text{NH}_3$.

cards.front: Effect of adding an inert gas at constant volume?
cards.back: No effect — partial pressures/molar concentrations of reacting species are unchanged.

cards.front: Effect of raising temperature on K for exothermic and endothermic reactions?
cards.back: • Exothermic (ΔH < 0): K decreases • Endothermic (ΔH > 0): K increases
cards.hint: Temperature is the only factor that changes the value of K.

cards.front: Effect of a catalyst on equilibrium?
cards.back: Speeds up forward and backward reactions equally; equilibrium is reached faster but composition and K are unchanged.

cards.front: Why is the synthesis of ammonia not done at very low temperature even though it is exothermic?
cards.back: Low T favours yield but makes the rate too slow; an optimum temperature with an iron catalyst and high pressure is used.

cards.front: Define strong and weak electrolytes.
cards.back: • Strong: almost completely ionised in water (NaCl, HCl) • Weak: only partially ionised (acetic acid, $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$)

cards.front: Arrhenius definition of acid and base?
cards.back: Acid gives $\text{H}^+$ ($\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$) in water; base gives $\text{OH}^-$ in water.
cards.hint: Limitation: applies only to aqueous solutions.

cards.front: Brønsted–Lowry acid and base? What is a conjugate pair?
cards.back: Acid = proton donor; base = proton acceptor. A conjugate acid–base pair differs by one $\text{H}^+$.

cards.front: Conjugate acid and conjugate base of $\text{HCO}_3^-$?
cards.back: • Conjugate acid: $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$ • Conjugate base: $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ $\text{HCO}_3^-$ (like $\text{H}_2\text{O}$) is amphiprotic.

cards.front: Relation between strength of an acid and its conjugate base?
cards.back: Stronger the acid, weaker its conjugate base (e.g. HCl is strong, $\text{Cl}^-$ is a very weak base).

cards.front: Lewis acid and base? Give examples.
cards.back: • Lewis acid: electron-pair acceptor — $\text{BF}_3$, $\text{AlCl}_3$, $\text{Mg}^{2+}$, $\text{Co}^{3+}$ • Lewis base: electron-pair donor — $\text{NH}_3$, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, $\text{OH}^-$
cards.hint: Trap: $\text{BF}_3$ is an acid without any H.

cards.front: Ionic product of water $K_w$ at 298 K?
cards.back: $K_w = [\text{H}_3\text{O}^+][\text{OH}^-] = $ $1.0 \times 10^{-14}$; so $[\text{H}^+] = 10^{-7}$ M in pure water.
cards.hint: $K_w$ increases with temperature (ionisation is endothermic).

cards.front: Is pure water at 350 K acidic since its pH is below 7?
cards.back: No — it is still neutral because $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+] = [\text{OH}^-]$. $K_w$ rises with T, so neutral pH falls below 7.

cards.front: Define pH. Relation between pH and pOH at 298 K?
cards.back: $\text{pH} = -\log[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$ $\text{pH} + \text{pOH} = 14$ ($= pK_w$)

cards.front: pH of 0.001 M NaOH at 298 K?
pH of $1.0 \times 10^{-8}$ M HCl?
cards.back: Not 8! Add $\text{H}^+$ from water: $[\text{H}^+] \approx 1.05 \times 10^{-7}$ M → pH ≈ 6.98 (slightly acidic).
cards.hint: Trap: a very dilute acid can never give pH above 7.

cards.front: Ionisation constant of a weak acid in terms of degree of ionisation α?
cards.back: $K_a = \dfrac{c\alpha^2}{1-\alpha} \approx c\alpha^2$ (when α ≪ 1)

cards.front: $[\text{H}^+]$ of a weak monobasic acid of concentration c?
cards.back: $[\text{H}^+] = c\alpha = \sqrt{K_a\,c}$

cards.front: How does degree of ionisation of a weak electrolyte change on dilution?
cards.back: $\alpha \approx \sqrt{K_a/c}$ → α increases on dilution (as c decreases).

cards.front: Relation between pKa and acid strength?
cards.back: $pK_a = -\log K_a$. Smaller pKa → stronger acid.

cards.front: Relation between $K_a$ and $K_b$ of a conjugate acid–base pair?
cards.back: $K_a \times K_b = K_w$; $pK_a + pK_b = 14$ at 298 K.

cards.front: Order of successive ionisation constants of a polyprotic acid?
cards.back: $K_{a1} > K_{a2} > K_{a3}$ — it is harder to remove $\text{H}^+$ from a negatively charged ion.

cards.front: Acid strength order: HF, HCl, HBr, HI? And $\text{CH}_4$, $\text{NH}_3$, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, HF?
cards.back: • Down a group: HF < HCl < HBr < HI (H–A bond strength falls, size dominates) • Across a period: $\text{CH}_4 < \text{NH}_3 < \text{H}_2\text{O} < \text{HF}$ (electronegativity dominates)

cards.front: What is the common ion effect? Example?
cards.back: Suppression of ionisation of a weak electrolyte by adding a strong electrolyte having a common ion, e.g. adding $\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$ to $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ lowers its ionisation.

cards.front: Nature (acidic/basic/neutral) of aqueous NaCl, $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$?
cards.back: • NaCl (SA + SB): neutral, no hydrolysis • $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ (SA + WB): acidic • $\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$ (WA + SB): basic
cards.hint: Solution takes the nature of the stronger parent.

cards.front: pH of a solution of a salt of a weak acid and a weak base (e.g. $\text{CH}_3\text{COONH}_4$)?
cards.back: $\text{pH} = 7 + \tfrac{1}{2}(pK_a - pK_b)$ — independent of concentration.
cards.hint: pKa = pKb → pH 7 (neutral).

cards.front: What is a buffer solution? Give an acidic and a basic buffer.
cards.back: Resists change in pH on adding small amounts of acid or base. • Acidic: $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$ (pH ≈ 4.75) • Basic: $\text{NH}_4\text{OH} + \text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ (pH ≈ 9.25)

cards.front: Henderson–Hasselbalch equation for an acidic buffer?
cards.back: $\text{pH} = pK_a + \log\dfrac{[\text{Conjugate base}]}{[\text{Acid}]}$

cards.front: Henderson equation for a basic buffer?
cards.back: $\text{pOH} = pK_b + \log\dfrac{[\text{Conjugate acid}]}{[\text{Base}]}$

cards.front: pH of an acidic buffer when [salt] = [acid]?
cards.back: $\log 1 = 0$ → pH = pKa
cards.hint: Diluting a buffer leaves the ratio, and hence pH, unchanged.

cards.front: Define solubility product $K_{sp}$.
cards.back: Product of molar concentrations of ions in a saturated solution of a sparingly soluble salt, each raised to its stoichiometric coefficient.

cards.front: $K_{sp}$ in terms of molar solubility S for AgCl, $\text{CaF}_2$ and $\text{Ca}_3(\text{PO}_4)_2$?
cards.hint: General $\text{A}_x\text{B}_y$: $K_{sp} = x^x y^y S^{x+y}$.

cards.front: Ionic product $Q_{sp}$ vs $K_{sp}$: when does precipitation occur?
cards.back: • $Q_{sp} > K_{sp}$: precipitation • $Q_{sp} < K_{sp}$: more salt dissolves (unsaturated) • $Q_{sp} = K_{sp}$: saturated

cards.front: Effect of a common ion on solubility of a sparingly soluble salt?
cards.back: Solubility decreases, e.g. AgCl is less soluble in NaCl solution. Used to purify NaCl by passing HCl gas through its saturated solution.

cards.front: Can $K_{sp}$ values alone compare solubilities of AgCl and $\text{Ag}_2\text{CrO}_4$?
cards.back: No. Direct comparison is valid only for salts of the same type (same ion ratio). Otherwise calculate S from each $K_{sp}$.

cards.front: Effect of lowering pH on solubility of salts of weak acids (e.g. phosphates)?
cards.back: Solubility increases: $\text{H}^+$ combines with the anion (forming weak acid), lowering its concentration so more salt dissolves.

cards.front: Define oxidation in the classical sense.
cards.back: Addition of oxygen or an electronegative element to a substance, or removal of hydrogen or an electropositive element from it.
cards.hint: Example: $2\text{Mg} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{MgO}$ (Mg oxidised).

cards.front: Define reduction in the classical sense.
cards.back: Removal of oxygen or an electronegative element from a substance, or addition of hydrogen or an electropositive element to it.
cards.hint: Example: $2\text{HgO} \rightarrow 2\text{Hg} + \text{O}_2$ (HgO reduced).

cards.front: In $2\text{H}_2\text{S} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{S} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$, which species is oxidised?
cards.back: $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ is oxidised (hydrogen removed); $\text{O}_2$ is reduced (hydrogen added).

cards.front: In $2\text{FeCl}_3 + \text{H}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{FeCl}_2 + 2\text{HCl}$, why is $\text{FeCl}_3$ said to be reduced?
cards.back: An electronegative element (Cl) is removed from it. $\text{H}_2$ gains Cl, so $\text{H}_2$ is oxidised.

cards.front: Define oxidation and reduction in terms of electron transfer.
cards.back: • Oxidation: loss of electrons • Reduction: gain of electrons Both occur simultaneously in a redox reaction.
cards.hint: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain.

cards.front: What is an oxidising agent? What happens to it in a reaction?
cards.back: A species that accepts electrons; it is itself reduced (its oxidation number decreases).
cards.hint: Trap: the oxidising agent gets reduced, the reducing agent gets oxidised.

cards.front: In $2\text{Na} + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{NaCl}$, identify the oxidant and reductant.
cards.back: • Na loses $e^-$ (oxidised) → reductant • $\text{Cl}_2$ gains $e^-$ (reduced) → oxidant

cards.front: What is observed when a zinc rod is dipped in $\text{CuSO}_4$ solution?
cards.back: Blue colour of solution fades and reddish copper deposits on zinc: $\text{Zn} + \text{Cu}^{2+} \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+} + \text{Cu}$

cards.front: What happens when a copper rod is placed in $\text{AgNO}_3$ solution?
cards.back: Solution turns blue ($\text{Cu}^{2+}$ formed) and silver deposits: $\text{Cu} + 2\text{Ag}^+ \rightarrow \text{Cu}^{2+} + 2\text{Ag}$

cards.front: Order of tendency of Zn, Cu and Ag to release electrons?
cards.back: Zn > Cu > Ag. So Cu cannot displace Zn from $\text{ZnSO}_4$, but can displace Ag from $\text{AgNO}_3$.
cards.hint: A metal displaces only those metals that release electrons less readily.

cards.front: Define oxidation number.
cards.back: The charge an atom would carry in a compound if all its bonds were ionic, with shared electrons assigned to the more electronegative atom.

cards.front: Oxidation number of an element in the free (uncombined) state?
cards.back: Zero, whatever its form, e.g. $\text{O}_2$, $\text{O}_3$, $\text{P}_4$, $\text{S}_8$, Na.

cards.front: Rule for the sum of oxidation numbers in a molecule and in an ion?
cards.back: • Neutral molecule: sum = 0 • Polyatomic ion: sum = charge on the ion • Monoatomic ion: ON = its charge

cards.front: Which element shows −1 in all its compounds?
cards.back: Fluorine, the most electronegative element.

cards.front: Oxidation number of hydrogen in $\text{NaH}$ and in $\text{HCl}$?
cards.back: • Metal hydrides (NaH, $\text{CaH}_2$): −1 • With non-metals (HCl, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$): +1

cards.front: Oxidation number of oxygen in $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ and in $\text{KO}_2$?
cards.back: • Peroxide ($\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$, $\text{Na}_2\text{O}_2$): −1 • Superoxide ($\text{KO}_2$): $-\tfrac{1}{2}$

cards.front: Oxidation number of oxygen in $\text{OF}_2$ and $\text{O}_2\text{F}_2$?
cards.hint: F is always −1, so O is forced to be positive.

cards.front: Oxidation number of Mn in $\text{KMnO}_4$ and Cr in $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$?
cards.back: • Mn in $\text{KMnO}_4$: +7 • Cr in $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$: +6

cards.front: Oxidation number of Cr in $\text{CrO}_5$?
cards.back: +6. It has one Cr=O oxygen (−2) and two peroxo groups (four O at −1): $x - 2 - 4 = 0$.
cards.hint: Trap: taking every O as −2 gives +10, which is impossible for Cr.

cards.front: Oxidation number of Fe in $\text{Fe}_3\text{O}_4$?
cards.back: Average $+\tfrac{8}{3}$. Really a mixed oxide $\text{FeO}\cdot\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3$: one Fe at +2, two Fe at +3.
cards.hint: A fractional ON is always an average over atoms in different states.

cards.front: Oxidation numbers of carbon in $\text{C}_3\text{O}_2$ ($\text{O=C=C=C=O}$)?
cards.back: Average $+\tfrac{4}{3}$. • Two terminal C: +2 • Central C: 0

cards.front: Oxidation numbers of Br in $\text{Br}_3\text{O}_8$?
cards.back: Average $+\tfrac{16}{3}$. • Two terminal Br: +6 • Middle Br: +4

cards.front: Oxidation numbers of S in the tetrathionate ion $\text{S}_4\text{O}_6^{2-}$?
cards.back: Average +2.5. • Two terminal S (bonded to O): +5 • Two bridging S (S–S bonds): 0

cards.front: Oxidation numbers of N in $\text{NH}_4\text{NO}_3$?
cards.hint: Trap: the 'average' +1 is meaningless here; calculate each ion separately.

cards.front: What is Stock notation? Give the Stock names of FeO and $\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3$.
cards.back: Oxidation number of the metal written as a Roman numeral in brackets after its name/symbol. • FeO: iron(II) oxide • $\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3$: iron(III) oxide

cards.front: Stock name of $\text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2$?
cards.back: Mercury(I) chloride, $\text{Hg}_2(\text{I})\text{Cl}_2$; each Hg is +1.

cards.front: Define oxidation and reduction in terms of oxidation number.
cards.back: • Oxidation: increase in oxidation number • Reduction: decrease in oxidation number

cards.front: Which species can act only as oxidant, only as reductant, or as both?
cards.back: • Element in highest ON → only oxidant ($\text{KMnO}_4$, $\text{HNO}_3$) • Lowest ON → only reductant ($\text{H}_2\text{S}$, $\text{NH}_3$) • Intermediate ON → both ($\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$, $\text{SO}_2$, $\text{HNO}_2$)

cards.front: Maximum oxidation number shown by chlorine? Example?
cards.back: +7, as in $\text{HClO}_4$ and $\text{Cl}_2\text{O}_7$.
cards.hint: Highest ON of a p-block element is usually (group number − 10).

cards.front: Is $2\text{O}_3 \rightarrow 3\text{O}_2$ a redox reaction?
cards.back: No. Oxygen stays at oxidation number 0 on both sides.
cards.hint: Trap: allotropic changes are not redox.

cards.front: Are neutralisation and precipitation (e.g. $\text{AgNO}_3 + \text{NaCl}$) reactions redox?
cards.back: No. No element changes its oxidation number; they are simple ion-exchange (double decomposition) reactions.

cards.front: Four types of redox reactions?
cards.back: • Combination • Decomposition • Displacement (metal / non-metal) • Disproportionation

cards.front: When is a combination reaction $\text{A} + \text{B} \rightarrow \text{C}$ a redox reaction? Example?
cards.back: When A, B or both are in elemental form. e.g. $3\text{Mg} + \text{N}_2 \rightarrow \text{Mg}_3\text{N}_2$, $\text{C} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{CO}_2$

cards.front: Give two redox decomposition reactions. Is $\text{CaCO}_3 \rightarrow \text{CaO} + \text{CO}_2$ redox?
cards.back: • $2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2 + \text{O}_2$ • $2\text{KClO}_3 \rightarrow 2\text{KCl} + 3\text{O}_2$ $\text{CaCO}_3$ decomposition is not redox (no ON change).
cards.hint: Trap: not every decomposition is redox.

cards.front: General form of a displacement reaction and its two kinds?
cards.back: $\text{X} + \text{YZ} \rightarrow \text{XZ} + \text{Y}$ • Metal displacement • Non-metal displacement (e.g. $\text{H}_2$, $\text{O}_2$, halogens)

cards.front: Give metal displacement reactions used in metallurgy.
cards.back:
• $\text{V}_2\text{O}_5 + 5\text{Ca} \rightarrow 2\text{V} + 5\text{CaO}$
• $\text{TiCl}_4 + 2\text{Mg} \rightarrow \text{Ti} + 2\text{MgCl}_2$
• $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_3 + 2\text{Al} \rightarrow \text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 2\text{Cr}$
cards.hint: In each, a more reactive metal is the reductant.

cards.front: Which metals displace hydrogen from cold water, and which only from steam?
cards.back: • Cold water: alkali metals and Ca, Sr, Ba (very reactive) • Steam: less active metals like Mg and Fe
cards.hint: $2\text{Na} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{NaOH} + \text{H}_2$

cards.front: Name metals that do not liberate $\text{H}_2$ even from dilute HCl.
cards.back: Cu, Ag and Au: they are less reactive than hydrogen.

cards.front: Order of oxidising power of halogens? Example of halogen displacement.
cards.back: $\text{F}_2 > \text{Cl}_2 > \text{Br}_2 > \text{I}_2$ $\text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{KBr} \rightarrow 2\text{KCl} + \text{Br}_2$
cards.hint: A halogen displaces only the halide ions below it.

cards.front: Reaction of fluorine with water?
cards.back: $2\text{F}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 4\text{HF} + \text{O}_2$ F2 is so strong an oxidant that it displaces oxygen from water.

cards.front: Define a disproportionation reaction.
cards.back: A reaction in which an element in one oxidation state is simultaneously oxidised and reduced. The element must be in an intermediate state, with at least three states possible.

cards.front: Show disproportionation in the decomposition of $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$.
cards.back: $2\text{H}_2\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{O}_2$ O goes from −1 to −2 (in $\text{H}_2\text{O}$) and 0 (in $\text{O}_2$).

cards.front: Disproportionation of white phosphorus in alkali: products and oxidation states?
cards.back: $\text{P}_4 + 3\text{OH}^- + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{PH}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{PO}_2^-$ P: 0 → −3 ($\text{PH}_3$) and 0 → +1 ($\text{H}_2\text{PO}_2^-$)

cards.front: Disproportionation of sulphur ($\text{S}_8$) in alkali?
cards.back: $\text{S}_8 + 12\text{OH}^- \rightarrow 4\text{S}^{2-} + 2\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$ S: 0 → −2 and 0 → +2

cards.front: Reaction of chlorine with cold dilute alkali; oxidation states of Cl?
cards.back: $\text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{ClO}^- + \text{Cl}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$ Cl: 0 → +1 and 0 → −1 (disproportionation)

cards.front: Why does $\text{F}_2$ not disproportionate? Why can't $\text{ClO}_4^-$?
cards.back: • F is the most electronegative element and cannot show a positive ON. • Cl in $\text{ClO}_4^-$ is at its maximum (+7), so it cannot be oxidised further.
cards.hint: $\text{ClO}^-$, $\text{ClO}_2^-$, $\text{ClO}_3^-$ can disproportionate.

cards.front: Two methods of balancing redox equations?
cards.back: • Oxidation number method • Half-reaction (ion-electron) method

cards.front: Basic principle of the oxidation number method of balancing?
cards.back: Total increase in ON of the reductant = total decrease in ON of the oxidant; multiply species accordingly, then balance O and H.

cards.front: In the half-reaction method (acidic medium), how are O and H atoms balanced?
cards.back: • Add $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to the side short of O atoms • Then add $\text{H}^+$ to the side short of H atoms • Balance charge with electrons

cards.front: How is the half-reaction method changed for a basic medium?
cards.back: After balancing with $\text{H}^+$, add equal $\text{OH}^-$ to both sides; $\text{H}^+ + \text{OH}^-$ combine to $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, then cancel extra water.

cards.front: Balanced ionic equation for $\text{MnO}_4^-$ oxidising $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ in acidic medium?
cards.back: $\text{MnO}_4^- + 5\text{Fe}^{2+} + 8\text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{Mn}^{2+} + 5\text{Fe}^{3+} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$
cards.hint: Mn +7 → +2 gains 5 $e^-$; each Fe<sup>2+</sup> loses 1, so 1 : 5.

cards.front: Balanced ionic equation for $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$ oxidising $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ in acid?
cards.back: $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 6\text{Fe}^{2+} + 14\text{H}^+ \rightarrow 2\text{Cr}^{3+} + 6\text{Fe}^{3+} + 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$
cards.hint: Each Cr: +6 → +3, so the ion gains 6 $e^-$; colour orange → green.

cards.front: Balanced equation: $\text{MnO}_4^-$ oxidises $\text{I}^-$ in basic medium.
cards.back: $2\text{MnO}_4^- + \text{I}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{MnO}_2 + \text{IO}_3^- + 2\text{OH}^-$

cards.front: Product and electrons gained per $\text{MnO}_4^-$ in acidic, neutral/weakly basic and strongly basic media?
cards.back: • Acidic: $\text{Mn}^{2+}$, 5 $e^-$ • Neutral/weakly basic: $\text{MnO}_2$, 3 $e^-$ • Strongly basic: $\text{MnO}_4^{2-}$, 1 $e^-$

cards.front: General valence shell configuration of p-block elements?
cards.back: $ns^2np^{1-6}$ (helium is the exception, $1s^2$).

cards.front: What is the inert pair effect?
cards.back: Reluctance of the $ns^2$ electrons to take part in bonding down a group, due to poor shielding by d and f electrons. The lower oxidation state (group ON − 2) becomes more stable.

cards.front: Why do second-period p-block elements (B, C, N…) differ from the rest of their group?
cards.back: • Small size and high electronegativity • No d orbitals → maximum covalency 4 • Can form $p\pi$–$p\pi$ multiple bonds

cards.front: Group 13 elements and their valence configuration?
cards.back: B, Al, Ga, In, Tl (and Nh); $ns^2np^1$.

cards.front: Order of atomic radii in group 13?
cards.back: B < Ga < Al < In < Tl Ga (135 pm) is smaller than Al (143 pm).

cards.front: Why is the atomic radius of Ga less than that of Al?
cards.back: Ga has 10 extra 3d electrons that shield poorly, so the effective nuclear charge on its outer electrons is higher.
cards.hint: Same d-block contraction idea explains Ga IE1 (579) being slightly above Al (577).
