cards.front: Order of first ionisation enthalpy in group 13?
cards.back: B > Tl > Ga > Al > In It does not fall smoothly down the group because of poor shielding by d and f electrons.
cards.hint: B 801, Al 577, Ga 579, In 558, Tl 589 kJ/mol

cards.front: Trend in electronegativity down group 13?
cards.back: Decreases from B to Al, then increases slightly (Al < Ga < In < Tl) due to differences in atomic size.

cards.front: Which group 13 elements have the highest and lowest melting points?
cards.back: • Highest: boron (very high, giant covalent solid) • Lowest: gallium (about 303 K)
cards.hint: Ga can melt on a warm palm.

cards.front: Why is gallium used in high-temperature thermometers?
cards.back: It has an unusually low melting point (~303 K) but a very high boiling point (~2676 K), so it stays liquid over a wide range.

cards.front: Metallic character of group 13 elements?
cards.back: Boron is a non-metal (hard, black solid); Al to Tl are metals.

cards.front: Common oxidation states of group 13 elements?
cards.back: • B, Al: +3 only • Ga, In: +1 and +3 • Tl: +1 more stable than +3
cards.hint: Down the group, the +1 state gets steadily more stable.

cards.front: Order of stability of the +1 oxidation state in group 13?
cards.back: Ga < In < Tl (inert pair effect increases down the group).

cards.front: Why is $\text{Tl}^{3+}$ a good oxidising agent while $\text{Tl}^+$ is stable?
cards.back: Due to the inert pair effect, Tl prefers +1; so $\text{Tl}^{3+}$ readily gains 2 electrons → acts as an oxidising agent.

cards.front: Why are boron compounds covalent?
cards.back: Boron's small size and very high sum of the first three ionisation enthalpies prevent formation of $\text{B}^{3+}$ ions.

cards.front: Why do group 13 trihalides behave as Lewis acids?
cards.back: The central atom has only 6 valence electrons (electron deficient) and accepts a lone pair to complete its octet.
cards.hint: e.g. $\text{BF}_3 + \text{NH}_3 \rightarrow \text{F}_3\text{B}\leftarrow\text{NH}_3$

cards.front: Order of Lewis acid strength of boron trihalides?
cards.back: $\text{BF}_3 < \text{BCl}_3 < \text{BBr}_3 < \text{BI}_3$ $\text{BF}_3$ is weakest due to strong $p\pi$–$p\pi$ back bonding (F 2p → vacant B 2p).
cards.hint: Trap: opposite of the electronegativity order of the halogens.

cards.front: Lewis acid character of trichlorides down group 13?
cards.back: Decreases down the group as atomic size increases: $\text{BCl}_3 > \text{AlCl}_3 > \text{GaCl}_3$.

cards.front: In what form does $\text{AlCl}_3$ exist in vapour/non-polar solvents?
cards.back: As a dimer, $\text{Al}_2\text{Cl}_6$, with two Cl bridges, so each Al completes its octet.

cards.front: Reactivity of group 13 elements towards air?
cards.back: • Amorphous B burns to $\text{B}_2\text{O}_3$; crystalline B is unreactive • Al forms a protective oxide film • On heating with $\text{N}_2$ they form nitrides (BN, AlN)

cards.front: Acidic/basic nature of group 13 oxides?
cards.back: • $\text{B}_2\text{O}_3$: acidic • $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$, $\text{Ga}_2\text{O}_3$: amphoteric • $\text{In}_2\text{O}_3$, $\text{Tl}_2\text{O}_3$: basic
cards.hint: Basic character of oxides increases down the group.

cards.front: How does aluminium react with dilute HCl and with NaOH?
cards.back:
Dissolves in both (amphoteric) releasing $\text{H}_2$:
• $2\text{Al} + 6\text{HCl} \rightarrow 2\text{AlCl}_3 + 3\text{H}_2$
• $2\text{Al} + 2\text{NaOH} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{Na}[\text{Al(OH)}_4] + 3\text{H}_2$

cards.front: Why does concentrated $\text{HNO}_3$ not dissolve aluminium?
cards.back: It makes Al passive by forming a thin protective oxide layer on the surface.
cards.hint: So conc. $\text{HNO}_3$ can be transported in Al containers.

cards.front: Does boron react with acids and alkalis at moderate temperature?
cards.back: No. Boron does not react with acids or alkalis at moderate temperature, unlike aluminium.

cards.front: Maximum covalency of boron vs aluminium? Example.
cards.back: • B: 4 (no d orbitals), e.g. $[\text{BF}_4]^-$ • Al: 6 (d orbitals available), e.g. $[\text{AlF}_6]^{3-}$

cards.front: Why does boron behave anomalously in group 13?
cards.back: Small size, high ionisation enthalpy and electronegativity, and no d orbitals. So it is a non-metal forming covalent compounds with maximum covalency 4.

cards.front: Group 14 elements and their valence configuration?
cards.back: C, Si, Ge, Sn, Pb (and Fl); $ns^2np^2$.

cards.front: Trend in covalent radius down group 14?
cards.back: Increases: C < Si < Ge < Sn < Pb. Increase from Si onwards is small due to poorly shielding filled d and f orbitals.

cards.front: Order of first ionisation enthalpy in group 14?
cards.back: C > Si > Ge > Pb > Sn Pb is slightly higher than Sn because of poor shielding by 4f and 5d electrons.
cards.hint: C 1086, Si 786, Ge 761, Sn 708, Pb 715 kJ/mol

cards.front: Compare first ionisation enthalpy of group 14 with group 13.
cards.back: Group 14 is higher than group 13 in the same period, due to smaller size (higher nuclear charge).

cards.front: Metallic character of group 14 elements?
cards.back: • C, Si: non-metals • Ge: metalloid • Sn, Pb: soft metals with low melting points

cards.front: Trend in melting points of group 14?
cards.back: Very high for C and Si (giant covalent structures) and generally decrease down the group; Sn and Pb melt low. Higher than corresponding group 13 elements.

cards.front: Common oxidation states of group 14 elements?
cards.back: +4 and +2. Stability of +2 increases and of +4 decreases down the group.
cards.hint: Pb(+2) stable, Pb(+4) oxidant; Sn(+2) reductant, Sn(+4) stable.

cards.front: Compare stable oxidation states of Ge, Sn and Pb.
cards.back: • Ge: +4 stable, +2 rare • Sn: both; +4 more stable • Pb: +2 more stable (inert pair effect)

cards.front: Why is $\text{SnCl}_2$ a reducing agent but $\text{PbO}_2$ an oxidising agent?
cards.back: • $\text{Sn}^{2+}$ tends to go to the more stable +4 → reductant • $\text{Pb}^{4+}$ tends to go to the more stable +2 → oxidant

cards.front: Nature of group 14 dioxides?
cards.back: • $\text{CO}_2$, $\text{SiO}_2$, $\text{GeO}_2$: acidic • $\text{SnO}_2$, $\text{PbO}_2$: amphoteric

cards.front: Nature of group 14 monoxides?
cards.back: • CO: neutral • GeO: distinctly acidic • SnO, PbO: amphoteric
cards.hint: Trap: CO is neutral, not acidic like $\text{CO}_2$.

cards.front: Reactivity of group 14 elements with water?
cards.back: • C, Si, Ge: unaffected • Sn: decomposes steam → $\text{SnO}_2 + \text{H}_2$ • Pb: unaffected (protective oxide film)

cards.front: Why does $\text{SiCl}_4$ hydrolyse easily but $\text{CCl}_4$ does not?
cards.back: Si has vacant 3d orbitals to accept a lone pair from water; C has no d orbitals. $\text{SiCl}_4 + 4\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Si(OH)}_4 + 4\text{HCl}$
cards.hint: Trap: $\text{CCl}_4$ is inert to water even though its C–Cl bonds are polar.

cards.front: Which group 14 tetrahalide does not exist and why?
cards.back: $\text{PbI}_4$. The Pb–I bond formed initially does not release enough energy to unpair the $6s^2$ electrons; Pb prefers +2.

cards.front: Why does $[\text{SiF}_6]^{2-}$ exist but $[\text{SiCl}_6]^{2-}$ does not?
cards.back: • Six large Cl atoms cannot fit around small Si • Interaction of Cl lone pairs with Si is weak F is small enough.

cards.front: Define catenation. Order of catenation in group 14?
cards.back: Linking of atoms of the same element into chains or rings. C >> Si > Ge ≈ Sn; Pb shows none.
cards.hint: Follows bond enthalpy: C–C 348 > Si–Si 297 > Ge–Ge 260 > Sn–Sn 240 kJ/mol

cards.front: Why does carbon show strong catenation but silicon much less?
cards.back: The C–C bond is very strong (348 kJ/mol) due to small size; Si–Si (297 kJ/mol) is weaker.

cards.front: Why can carbon form $p\pi$–$p\pi$ multiple bonds but heavier group 14 elements cannot readily?
cards.back: Carbon is small with high electronegativity, so its 2p orbitals overlap well. Heavier atoms have large, diffuse orbitals that overlap poorly sideways.
cards.hint: Examples: C=C, C≡C, C=O, C≡N.

cards.front: Maximum covalency of carbon vs silicon and why?
cards.back: • C: 4 (only s and p orbitals in valence shell) • Si: up to 6 (vacant 3d), e.g. $[\text{SiF}_6]^{2-}$

decks.title: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles and Techniques

cards.front: Percentage s-character in $sp^3$, $sp^2$ and $sp$ hybrid orbitals of carbon?
cards.hint: More s-character → electrons held closer → carbon more electronegative.

cards.front: Shape and bond angle in $\text{CH}_4$, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$ and $\text{C}_2\text{H}_2$?
cards.back: • $\text{CH}_4$ ($sp^3$): tetrahedral, 109.5° • $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$ ($sp^2$): planar, 120° • $\text{C}_2\text{H}_2$ ($sp$): linear, 180°

cards.front: Order of C–C bond length for single, double and triple bonds?
cards.hint: More s-character and more bonds → shorter bond.

cards.front: Number of σ and π bonds in $\text{CH}_2\text{=CH–C}\equiv\text{N}$?
cards.back: 6 σ and 3 π bonds.
cards.hint: Every single bond = 1σ; double = 1σ + 1π; triple = 1σ + 2π.

cards.front: Hybridisation of each carbon in $\text{CH}_2\text{=C=CH}_2$ (allene)?
cards.back: Terminal carbons: $sp^2$; central carbon: $sp$.
cards.hint: A carbon with two double bonds is $sp$, like a triple-bonded carbon.

cards.front: In a wedge-dash formula, what do solid and dashed wedges show?
cards.back: • Solid wedge: bond projecting towards the observer • Dashed wedge: bond pointing away from the observer • Plain line: bond in the plane of paper

cards.front: Main classes of cyclic organic compounds with an example each?
cards.back: • Alicyclic: cyclohexane • Aromatic benzenoid: benzene • Non-benzenoid aromatic: tropolone • Heterocyclic: furan, thiophene, pyridine

cards.front: Define a homologous series.
cards.back: A series of compounds with the same functional group in which successive members differ by a $\text{–CH}_2$ unit (14 u) and show similar chemical properties.

cards.front: Basic IUPAC rules for naming a branched alkane?
cards.back: • Choose the longest carbon chain • Number to give substituents lowest locants • Write substituents in alphabetical order
cards.hint: Lowest locant rule: compare at the first point of difference.

cards.front: In alphabetising substituents, are di/tri, sec/tert, and iso/neo considered?
cards.back: • di, tri, tetra: ignored • sec-, tert-: ignored • iso, neo: counted (part of the name)
cards.hint: So 'isopropyl' is alphabetised under 'i'.

cards.front: IUPAC name of $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C–CH}_2\text{–CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$?
cards.back: 2,2,4-Trimethylpentane (iso-octane)

cards.front: IUPAC name of $\text{CH}_3\text{–CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{–CH}(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)\text{–CH}_2\text{–CH}_3$?
cards.back: 3-Ethyl-2-methylpentane
cards.hint: Locants {2,3} beat {3,4}; ethyl comes before methyl alphabetically.

cards.front: Priority order of principal functional groups (IUPAC)?
cards.back: –COOH > –SO3H > –COOR > –COCl > –CONH2 > –CN > –CHO > >C=O > –OH > –NH2 > C=C > C≡C
cards.hint: Halo, nitro, alkoxy and alkyl groups are always written as prefixes.

cards.front: IUPAC name of $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$?
cards.back: 4-Oxopentanoic acid. –COOH is the principal group (C-1); the ketone becomes the prefix 'oxo'.

cards.front: IUPAC name of $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$?
cards.back: Propanenitrile. The carbon of –CN is counted in the parent chain.
cards.hint: Trap: not 'ethyl cyanide' in IUPAC, and not ethanenitrile.

cards.front: Name the four types of structural isomerism with an example each.
cards.back: • Chain: pentane / 2-methylbutane • Position: propan-1-ol / propan-2-ol • Functional group: ethanol / methoxymethane • Metamerism: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OC}_2\text{H}_5$ / $\text{CH}_3\text{OC}_3\text{H}_7$

cards.front: What is stereoisomerism and its two types?
cards.back: Isomers with the same constitution (same atom connectivity) but different spatial arrangement of atoms. Types: geometrical and optical.

cards.front: Homolytic vs heterolytic cleavage: what does each produce?
cards.back: • Homolytic: each atom takes one electron → free radicals • Heterolytic: one atom takes both electrons → ions (carbocation + anion, or carbanion + cation)
cards.hint: Half-headed (fish-hook) arrow = one electron; full arrow = electron pair.

cards.front: Hybridisation and shape of a carbocation?
cards.back: $sp^2$, trigonal planar; carbon has only 6 valence electrons and a vacant p orbital perpendicular to the plane.

cards.front: Stability order of alkyl carbocations?
cards.back: 3° > 2° > 1° > $\text{CH}_3^+$ Due to +I effect and hyperconjugation of alkyl groups.

cards.front: Hybridisation, shape and stability order of carbanions?
cards.back: $sp^3$, pyramidal (one lone pair). Stability: $\text{CH}_3^- > 1° > 2° > 3°$ (alkyl +I effect destabilises the negative charge).
cards.hint: Trap: the order is the reverse of carbocations.

cards.front: Stability order of alkyl free radicals?
Why are benzyl and allyl carbocations unusually stable?
cards.back: The positive charge is delocalised by resonance with the adjacent π system.

cards.front: Define electrophile and give examples.
cards.back: An electron-seeking (electron-deficient) reagent that attacks an electron-rich site. e.g. $\text{H}^+$, $\text{NO}_2^+$, carbocations, $\text{BF}_3$, $\text{AlCl}_3$, carbonyl carbon

cards.front: Define nucleophile and give examples.
cards.back: A nucleus-seeking reagent that donates an electron pair. e.g. $\text{OH}^-$, $\text{CN}^-$, $\text{Cl}^-$, carbanions, and neutral $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, $\text{NH}_3$, $\text{R–NH}_2$
cards.hint: Trap: neutral molecules with lone pairs are nucleophiles too.

cards.front: State the inductive effect.
cards.back: Permanent polarisation of a σ bond, transmitted along the carbon chain, caused by an electronegative or electropositive group. It fades rapidly with distance (negligible beyond 3 bonds).

cards.front: Examples of −I and +I groups?
cards.back: • −I (withdraw): $\text{–NO}_2$, –CN, –COOH, –F, –Cl, –Br, –I • +I (donate): alkyl groups such as $\text{–CH}_3$, $\text{–C}_2\text{H}_5$

cards.front: Why is $\text{ClCH}_2\text{COOH}$ a stronger acid than $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$?
cards.back: The −I effect of Cl pulls electron density away, stabilising the carboxylate anion formed after loss of $\text{H}^+$.
cards.hint: Trend: $\text{FCH}_2\text{COOH} > \text{ClCH}_2\text{COOH} > \text{BrCH}_2\text{COOH} > \text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$

cards.front: What is resonance? Do canonical structures exist?
cards.back: When one Lewis structure cannot describe a molecule, it is shown as a resonance hybrid of several canonical structures. The canonical forms are hypothetical; only the hybrid exists.

cards.front: Which canonical structures contribute more to the resonance hybrid?
cards.back: • More covalent bonds • All atoms with complete octets • Less separation of opposite charges • Negative charge on the more electronegative atom
cards.hint: Canonical forms differ only in electrons, never in positions of nuclei.

cards.front: Examples of +R and −R groups?
cards.back: • +R (donate to π system): halogens, –OH, $\text{–OR}$, $\text{–NH}_2$, $\text{–NHCOCH}_3$ • −R (withdraw): –COOH, –CHO, >C=O, –CN, $\text{–NO}_2$

cards.front: State the electromeric effect. +E vs −E?
cards.back: Temporary complete shift of a π electron pair in a multiple bond, only in the presence of an attacking reagent. • +E: electrons move to the atom the reagent attaches to • −E: electrons move away from it

cards.front: What is hyperconjugation?
cards.back: Delocalisation of σ electrons of a C–H bond of an alkyl group into an adjacent vacant p orbital or π system. Also called no-bond resonance; it is a permanent effect.

cards.front: Why is $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+$ more stable than $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2^+$ by hyperconjugation?
cards.back: Stability rises with the number of α-hydrogens: tert-butyl cation has 9 α-H, ethyl cation only 3.
cards.hint: $\text{CH}_3^+$ has no α-H, so no hyperconjugation.

cards.front: Four main types of organic reactions?
cards.back: • Substitution • Addition • Elimination • Rearrangement

cards.front: Principle of crystallisation; how are coloured impurities removed?
cards.back: Based on a difference in solubility of compound and impurities in a solvent. Coloured impurities are removed by activated charcoal.

cards.front: When is simple distillation used vs fractional distillation?
cards.back: • Simple: boiling points differ widely (chloroform 334 K / aniline 457 K) • Fractional: boiling points are close; uses a fractionating column (crude oil)

cards.front: When is distillation under reduced pressure used? Example?
cards.back: For liquids that decompose at or below their boiling point. Lower pressure lowers the boiling point. e.g. glycerol from spent-lye in the soap industry

cards.front: Steam distillation: which compounds and why do they boil below 373 K?
cards.back: For steam-volatile compounds immiscible with water (e.g. aniline). The liquid boils when $p_1 + p_2$ = atmospheric pressure, so it distils below its own boiling point.

cards.front: Define retardation factor $R_f$ in chromatography.
cards.back: $R_f = \dfrac{\text{distance moved by substance}}{\text{distance moved by solvent front}}$ Always less than 1.

cards.front: Column chromatography and TLC are based on which principle? Common adsorbents?
cards.back: Adsorption chromatography (different adsorption of components). Adsorbents: silica gel or alumina.

cards.front: Paper chromatography is which type, and what is the stationary phase?
cards.back: Partition chromatography. Stationary phase: water held in the paper; the mobile phase is the solvent.
cards.hint: Trap: the paper itself is only the support, not the stationary phase.

cards.front: Test for carbon and hydrogen in an organic compound?
cards.back: Heat with CuO: • C → $\text{CO}_2$ turns lime water milky • H → $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ turns anhydrous $\text{CuSO}_4$ blue

cards.front: Why is the organic compound fused with sodium in Lassaigne's test?
cards.back: To convert covalently bonded N, S and halogens into ionic forms: NaCN, $\text{Na}_2\text{S}$, NaX.

cards.front: Lassaigne's test for nitrogen: reagent and observation?
cards.back: Sodium extract + $\text{FeSO}_4$, boil, acidify with conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ → Prussian blue, $\text{Fe}_4[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]_3\cdot x\text{H}_2\text{O}$

cards.front: Two tests for sulphur in Lassaigne's extract?
cards.back: • Sodium nitroprusside → violet colour • Acetic acid + lead acetate → black ppt of PbS

cards.front: Observation when both N and S are present (Lassaigne's test)?
cards.back: NaSCN forms, giving a blood-red colour with $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ (no Prussian blue).
cards.hint: With excess sodium, NaSCN breaks into NaCN and $\text{Na}_2\text{S}$, giving the separate tests.

cards.front: Halogen test: precipitates with $\text{AgNO}_3$ and their solubility in ammonia?
cards.back: • AgCl: white, soluble in $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ • AgBr: pale yellow, sparingly soluble • AgI: yellow, insoluble

cards.front: Why is the sodium extract boiled with $\text{HNO}_3$ before the halogen test?
cards.back: To decompose NaCN and $\text{Na}_2\text{S}$, which would otherwise interfere with the $\text{AgNO}_3$ test.

cards.front: Why does hydrazine ($\text{NH}_2\text{NH}_2$) not give Lassaigne's test for nitrogen?
cards.back: It contains no carbon, so NaCN cannot form during sodium fusion.

cards.front: Formulae for % C and % H (Liebig method)?
cards.back:
$\%\text{C} = \dfrac{12 \times m_{\text{CO}_2} \times 100}{44 \times m}$
$\%\text{H} = \dfrac{2 \times m_{\text{H}_2\text{O}} \times 100}{18 \times m}$
m = mass of compound

cards.front: Formula for % N by Dumas method?
cards.back:
$\%\text{N} = \dfrac{28 \times V \times 100}{22400 \times m}$
V = volume of $\text{N}_2$ at STP (mL), m = mass of compound (g)
cards.hint: $\text{N}_2$ is collected over KOH solution, which absorbs $\text{CO}_2$.

cards.front: Principle of Kjeldahl's method and its limitation?
cards.back: N is converted to $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4$ by conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$; NaOH releases $\text{NH}_3$, absorbed in standard acid. Not applicable to nitro, azo compounds and N in rings (pyridine).

cards.front: Formula for % halogen by Carius method?
cards.back: $\%\text{X} = \dfrac{\text{At. mass of X} \times m_{\text{AgX}} \times 100}{\text{Mol. mass of AgX} \times m}$ Compound heated with fuming $\text{HNO}_3$ and $\text{AgNO}_3$.

cards.front: Formula for % sulphur; how is oxygen usually estimated?
cards.back: $\%\text{S} = \dfrac{32 \times m_{\text{BaSO}_4} \times 100}{233 \times m}$ Oxygen: usually found by difference (100 − sum of other %).

cards.front: General formulae of alkanes, alkenes and alkynes?
cards.back: • Alkanes: $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+2}$ • Alkenes: $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n}$ • Alkynes: $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n-2}$

cards.front: How are alkanes prepared from alkenes/alkynes?
cards.back: Catalytic hydrogenation: $\text{H}_2$ with finely divided Pt, Pd or Ni. Pt and Pd work at room temperature; Ni needs higher temperature and pressure.

cards.front: Reduction of alkyl halides to alkanes: reagent?
cards.back: Zn and dilute HCl (except fluorides): $\text{CH}_3\text{Cl} + \text{H}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Zn, H}^+} \text{CH}_4 + \text{HCl}$

cards.front: Wurtz reaction: reagents and product?
cards.back: Alkyl halide + Na in dry ether → alkane with double the carbons: $2\text{RX} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow \text{R–R} + 2\text{NaX}$
cards.hint: Trap: methane cannot be made by Wurtz; two different halides give a mixture.

cards.front: Decarboxylation of sodium salts of carboxylic acids: reagent and product?
cards.back: Heat with soda lime (NaOH + CaO): $\text{RCOONa} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{R–H} + \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ Alkane has one carbon less.
cards.hint: Sodium ethanoate + soda lime → methane.

cards.front: Kolbe's electrolytic method: product from sodium acetate and at which electrode?
cards.back: Ethane is formed at the anode: $2\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^- \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_6 + 2\text{CO}_2 + 2e^-$
cards.hint: Trap: methane cannot be made by Kolbe's method (even-carbon alkanes only).

cards.front: Effect of branching on boiling point of isomeric alkanes?
cards.back: Branching lowers boiling point: smaller surface area, weaker van der Waals forces. n-pentane (309 K) > isopentane (301 K) > neopentane (282.5 K)

cards.front: Conditions and mechanism of halogenation of alkanes?
cards.back: In diffused sunlight / UV light or heat; proceeds by a free radical chain mechanism (initiation, propagation, termination).

cards.front: Reactivity order of halogens and of H atoms in alkane halogenation?
cards.back: • Halogens: $\text{F}_2 > \text{Cl}_2 > \text{Br}_2 > \text{I}_2$ • Hydrogens replaced: 3° > 2° > 1°

cards.front: Why is iodination of alkanes carried out with $\text{HIO}_3$ or $\text{HNO}_3$?
cards.back: Iodination is reversible; the oxidising agent removes the HI formed, driving the reaction forward.
cards.hint: Fluorination, at the other end, is too violent to control.

cards.front: Balanced general equation for complete combustion of an alkane?
cards.back: $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+2} + \dfrac{3n+1}{2}\text{O}_2 \rightarrow n\text{CO}_2 + (n+1)\text{H}_2\text{O}$

cards.front: Products of controlled oxidation of methane with Cu and with $\text{Mo}_2\text{O}_3$?
cards.back: • $\text{Cu}$, 523 K, 100 atm → methanol • $\text{Mo}_2\text{O}_3$, heat → methanal (HCHO)

cards.front: Product of oxidation of $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CH}$ by $\text{KMnO}_4$?
cards.back: $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C–OH}$ (2-methylpropan-2-ol); the tertiary H is oxidised to –OH.

cards.front: Isomerisation of n-hexane: reagent and products?
cards.back: Anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$ + HCl → 2-methylpentane and 3-methylpentane.

cards.front: What is aromatisation of alkanes? Example and catalyst?
cards.back: Alkanes with ≥ 6 C are converted to aromatic hydrocarbons on oxides of V, Mo or Cr at 773 K, 10–20 atm. n-Hexane → benzene

cards.front: Conformations of ethane: which is most stable and why?
cards.back: Staggered is most stable (H atoms farthest apart, minimum torsional strain); eclipsed is least stable.

cards.front: Energy difference between staggered and eclipsed ethane? Can they be isolated?
cards.back: About $12.5\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. Cannot be isolated at room temperature since rotation about C–C is almost free.

cards.front: Structural isomers of $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$ (alkenes)?
cards.back: Three: but-1-ene, but-2-ene, 2-methylpropene. But-2-ene also shows cis–trans isomerism.
cards.hint: Cyclobutane and methylcyclopropane are also $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$ (ring isomers).

cards.front: Condition for geometrical (cis–trans) isomerism in alkenes?
cards.back: Each doubly bonded carbon must carry two different atoms or groups.
cards.hint: Trap: but-1-ene and 2-methylpropene show no cis–trans isomerism.

cards.front: Compare cis- and trans-but-2-ene in polarity, boiling point and melting point.
cards.back: • Cis is polar, trans is non-polar • Boiling point: cis > trans (277 K vs 274 K) • Melting point: trans > cis (better packing)

cards.front: Partial reduction of alkynes: reagents giving cis and trans alkenes?
cards.back: • Lindlar's catalyst (Pd on $\text{CaCO}_3$ poisoned with S compounds/quinoline) → cis • Na in liquid $\text{NH}_3$ → trans
cards.hint: Catalyst on a surface → syn addition (cis); dissolving metal → trans.

cards.front: Preparation of alkenes from alkyl halides: reagent, type of reaction?
cards.back: Alcoholic KOH, heat → dehydrohalogenation (β-elimination). Rate: halogen I > Br > Cl; alkyl 3° > 2° > 1°

cards.front: Preparation of alkenes from vicinal dihalides and from alcohols?
cards.back: • Vicinal dihalide + zinc dust → alkene (dehalogenation) • Alcohol + conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, heat → alkene (acidic dehydration)

cards.front: Test for unsaturation using bromine?
cards.back: Reddish-orange bromine in $\text{CCl}_4$ is decolourised as it adds across C=C or C≡C.

cards.front: Reactivity order of hydrogen halides towards alkenes?
cards.back: HI > HBr > HCl (H–X bond strength decreases down the group).

cards.front: State Markovnikov's rule.
cards.back: In addition of HX to an unsymmetrical alkene, the negative part (X) goes to the doubly bonded carbon carrying fewer hydrogen atoms.
cards.hint: The rich get richer: H goes to the carbon that already has more H.

cards.front: Product of propene + HBr, without and with peroxide?
cards.back: • Without peroxide: 2-bromopropane (Markovnikov) • With peroxide: 1-bromopropane (anti-Markovnikov, Kharasch effect)

cards.front: Mechanism basis of Markovnikov addition of HBr to propene?
cards.back: Electrophilic addition: $\text{H}^+$ adds first to give the more stable 2° carbocation, which is then attacked by $\text{Br}^-$.

cards.front: Why is the peroxide effect not seen with HCl and HI?
cards.back: • H–Cl bond (430.5 kJ/mol) is too strong to be broken by free radicals • H–I bond is weak, but iodine radicals combine to form $\text{I}_2$
cards.hint: Peroxide effect: HBr only.

cards.front: Acid-catalysed hydration of alkenes: product and rule followed?
cards.back: Alkene + $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ / $\text{H}^+$ → alcohol, following Markovnikov's rule. e.g. 2-methylpropene → tert-butyl alcohol

cards.front: Baeyer's reagent: what is it and what does it give with alkenes?
cards.back: Cold, dilute, aqueous $\text{KMnO}_4$. Adds to C=C to give vicinal glycols; pink/purple colour is discharged (test for unsaturation).
cards.hint: Pink colour disappearing = unsaturation present.

cards.front: Products of oxidation by acidic $\text{KMnO}_4$: 2-methylpropene and but-2-ene?
cards.back: • 2-Methylpropene → propan-2-one + $\text{CO}_2$ + $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ • But-2-ene → 2 ethanoic acid

cards.front: What is ozonolysis and its use?
cards.back: Addition of $\text{O}_3$ to form an ozonide, then cleavage with Zn + $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to give aldehydes/ketones. Used to locate the double bond.

cards.front: Ozonolysis products of propene and of 2-methylpropene?
cards.back: • Propene → ethanal + methanal • 2-Methylpropene → propanone + methanal
cards.hint: Reverse trick: join the two C=O carbons by a C=C to get the alkene back.

cards.front: Polymerisation of ethene: product and conditions?
cards.back: Polythene, formed at high temperature and pressure with a catalyst: $n\,\text{CH}_2\text{=CH}_2 \rightarrow (\text{–CH}_2\text{–CH}_2\text{–})_n$

cards.front: C≡C bond: length, bond enthalpy and shape around it?
cards.back: 120 pm, $823\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$; one σ + two π bonds; linear (180°), carbons are $sp$.

cards.front: Preparation of ethyne from calcium carbide?
cards.back: $\text{CaC}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Ca(OH)}_2 + \text{C}_2\text{H}_2$

cards.front: Preparation of alkynes from vicinal dihalides?
cards.back: Two successive dehydrohalogenations: alcoholic KOH gives a vinylic halide, then sodamide ($\text{NaNH}_2$) gives the alkyne.

cards.front: Why are terminal alkyne hydrogens acidic?
cards.back: The ≡C–H carbon is $sp$ (50% s-character), most electronegative, so the H is released as $\text{H}^+$. $\text{HC}\equiv\text{CH} + \text{Na} \rightarrow \text{HC}\equiv\text{C}^-\text{Na}^+ + \tfrac{1}{2}\text{H}_2$

cards.front: Order of acidic character: ethyne, ethene, ethane; and ethyne, propyne, but-2-yne?
cards.back: • $\text{HC}\equiv\text{CH} > \text{H}_2\text{C=CH}_2 > \text{CH}_3\text{–CH}_3$ • $\text{HC}\equiv\text{CH} > \text{CH}_3\text{C}\equiv\text{CH} \gg \text{CH}_3\text{C}\equiv\text{CCH}_3$
cards.hint: But-2-yne has no acidic H at all.

cards.front: Product of propyne with excess HBr?
cards.back: 2,2-Dibromopropane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CBr}_2\text{CH}_3$ (Markovnikov addition twice; a gem-dihalide).

cards.front: Hydration of ethyne and propyne: reagents and products?
cards.back: $\text{HgSO}_4$ / dil. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, 333 K: • Ethyne → ethanal • Propyne → propanone (via an unstable enol)
cards.hint: Only ethyne gives an aldehyde; other terminal alkynes give methyl ketones.

cards.front: Other laboratory routes to benzene?
cards.back: • Sodium benzoate + soda lime (decarboxylation) • Phenol + zinc dust (reduction) • Cyclic polymerisation of ethyne

cards.front: Hückel's rule for aromaticity?
cards.back: • Planar cyclic molecule • Complete delocalisation of π electrons • $(4n+2)$ π electrons, n = 0, 1, 2…
cards.hint: Benzene: 6 π electrons, n = 1.

cards.front: Is cyclooctatetraene aromatic? Why?
cards.back: No. It has 8 π electrons (not $4n+2$) and is non-planar (tub shaped).

cards.front: Three steps of electrophilic substitution in benzene?
cards.back: • Generation of the electrophile • Formation of arenium ion (σ-complex; one C becomes $sp^3$) • Loss of $\text{H}^+$ to restore aromaticity

cards.front: Nitration of benzene: reagents and electrophile?
cards.back: Conc. $\text{HNO}_3$ + conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ (nitrating mixture), 323–333 K. Electrophile: nitronium ion, $\text{NO}_2^+$.

cards.front: Halogenation of benzene: reagents and role of the catalyst?
cards.back: $\text{Cl}_2$ with anhydrous $\text{FeCl}_3$ or $\text{AlCl}_3$ in the dark; the Lewis acid generates the electrophile $\text{Cl}^+$.

cards.front: Sulphonation of benzene: reagent and electrophile?
cards.back: Fuming $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ (oleum); electrophile $\text{SO}_3$. Product: benzenesulphonic acid.

cards.front: Friedel–Crafts alkylation and acylation of benzene: reagents and products?
cards.back: • $\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}$ + anhyd. $\text{AlCl}_3$ → toluene • $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$ + anhyd. $\text{AlCl}_3$ → acetophenone

cards.front: Product of benzene + $\text{Cl}_2$ in UV light at 500 K?
cards.back: Benzene hexachloride (BHC, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_6\text{Cl}_6$), an addition product (gammaxane).
cards.hint: Trap: with $\text{FeCl}_3$ in the dark it is substitution (chlorobenzene).

cards.front: Name ortho/para directing groups and say whether they activate the ring.
cards.back: –OH, $\text{–NH}_2$, –NHR, $\text{–NHCOCH}_3$, $\text{–OCH}_3$, $\text{–CH}_3$: o/p directing and activating (raise ring electron density).
cards.hint: Usually the ring-attached atom carries a lone pair (or is an alkyl group).

cards.front: Name meta directing groups and their effect on ring reactivity.
cards.back: $\text{–NO}_2$, –CN, –CHO, –COR, –COOH, –COOR, $\text{–SO}_3\text{H}$: meta directing and deactivating.
cards.hint: Ring-attached atom is bonded by a multiple bond to an electronegative atom.

cards.front: Halogens on benzene: directing effect and activation?
cards.back: Ortho/para directing (+R effect) but deactivating (strong −I effect outweighs +R).
cards.hint: The classic exception NEET loves.

cards.front: Which hydrocarbons are carcinogenic, and how are they formed?
cards.back: Benzene and polynuclear hydrocarbons with more than two fused benzene rings (e.g. 3-methylcholanthrene). Formed by incomplete combustion of tobacco, coal, petroleum.

cards.front: What is a binary solution? Which component is the solvent?
cards.back: A homogeneous mixture of two components. The component present in the larger amount is the solvent; it decides the physical state of the solution.

cards.front: Give an example of a solution of a gas in a solid.
cards.back: Hydrogen dissolved in palladium. Other types: amalgam of mercury with sodium (liquid in solid), camphor in nitrogen gas (solid in gas).
cards.hint: Trap: amalgam of Hg with Na is liquid-in-solid, not solid-in-liquid.

cards.front: Define mass percentage (w/w) of a component.
cards.back: $\text{Mass \%} = \dfrac{\text{mass of component}}{\text{total mass of solution}} \times 100$ E.g. commercial bleach is ~3.62% w/w NaOCl in water.

cards.front: When is concentration expressed in parts per million (ppm)?
cards.back: When a solute is present in trace amounts. $\text{ppm} = \dfrac{\text{parts of component}}{\text{total parts of solution}} \times 10^6$
cards.hint: Used for pollutants in water/air, e.g. fluoride in drinking water.

cards.front: Define mole fraction. What is the sum of mole fractions in a solution?
cards.back: $x_A = \dfrac{n_A}{n_A + n_B + \ldots}$ Sum of all mole fractions $= \textbf{1}$, so in a binary solution $x_A + x_B = 1$.
cards.hint: Mole fraction is dimensionless and temperature-independent.

cards.front: Define molarity (M). Does it depend on temperature?
cards.back: Moles of solute per litre of solution: $M = \dfrac{n_{solute}}{V_{solution}(\text{L})}$ Yes, it changes with temperature because volume changes.
cards.hint: Molarity: per litre of SOLUTION. Molality: per kg of SOLVENT.

cards.front: Define molality (m). Why is it preferred over molarity for colligative properties?
cards.back: Moles of solute per kg of solvent: $m = \dfrac{n_{solute}}{W_{solvent}(\text{kg})}$ It involves only masses, so it is independent of temperature.
cards.hint: Mass-based terms (molality, mole fraction, w/w, ppm by mass) are temperature-independent.

cards.front: Molarity of a solution with 4 g NaOH in 250 mL solution?
How does the solubility of a solid in a liquid change with temperature?
cards.back: Follows Le Chatelier's principle: • Endothermic dissolution ($\Delta_{sol}H > 0$): solubility increases with T • Exothermic dissolution ($\Delta_{sol}H < 0$): solubility decreases with T

cards.front: Effect of pressure on the solubility of a solid in a liquid?
cards.back: No significant effect, because solids and liquids are highly incompressible.

cards.front: State Henry's law.
cards.back: Partial pressure of a gas in the vapour phase is proportional to its mole fraction in solution: $p = K_H\,x$ At constant T, solubility of a gas is proportional to its pressure.

cards.front: Higher the Henry's constant $K_H$ of a gas, its solubility is…?
cards.back: Lower. $K_H$ has pressure units (e.g. kbar); larger $K_H$ means a larger pressure is needed for the same mole fraction.
cards.hint: Trap: high $K_H$ = LESS soluble.

cards.front: How does the $K_H$ of a gas change with temperature, and what does that mean for solubility?
cards.back: $K_H$ increases with temperature, so gas solubility decreases on heating. That is why aquatic species are more comfortable in cold water.

cards.front: Why are soft drink bottles sealed under high pressure?
cards.back: To increase the solubility of $\text{CO}_2$ (Henry's law).
cards.hint: Opening the bottle lowers pressure, so $\text{CO}_2$ escapes as fizz.

cards.front: What causes 'bends' in scuba divers, and how is it avoided?
cards.back: At depth, high pressure dissolves more $\text{N}_2$ in blood; on rapid ascent it forms bubbles in capillaries. Tanks use air diluted with helium (11.7% He, 56.2% $\text{N}_2$, 32.1% $\text{O}_2$).

cards.front: What is anoxia and where does it occur?
cards.back: Low partial pressure of oxygen at high altitudes gives low blood $\text{O}_2$; climbers become weak and unable to think clearly.

cards.front: State Raoult's law for a solution of two volatile liquids.
cards.back: Partial vapour pressure of each component is proportional to its mole fraction: $p_1 = p_1^\circ x_1$, $p_2 = p_2^\circ x_2$ $p_{total} = p_1 + p_2$

cards.front: Express total vapour pressure of an ideal binary solution in terms of $x_2$.
cards.back: $p_{total} = p_1^\circ + (p_2^\circ - p_1^\circ)\,x_2$ A plot of $p_{total}$ vs $x_2$ is a straight line.

cards.front: Mole fraction of component 1 in the vapour phase ($y_1$)?
cards.back: $y_1 = \dfrac{p_1}{p_{total}}$ (Dalton's law of partial pressures) The vapour is richer in the more volatile component.

cards.front: How is Raoult's law a special case of Henry's law?
cards.back: Both say $p \propto x$. Henry's law: $p = K_H\,x$; Raoult's law: $p_1 = p_1^\circ x_1$. Raoult's law is the special case of Henry's law in which $K_H = p_1^\circ$.
cards.hint: Trap: it is Raoult's law that is the special case (NCERT wording).

cards.front: Raoult's law for a solution of a non-volatile solute?
cards.back: Only solvent contributes to vapour pressure: $p_1 = x_1\,p_1^\circ$ So vapour pressure of solution is lower than that of pure solvent.

cards.front: Conditions for an ideal solution?
cards.back: • Obeys Raoult's law at all concentrations • $\Delta_{mix}H = 0$ and $\Delta_{mix}V = 0$ • A–B interactions ≈ A–A and B–B interactions
cards.hint: Ideal: zero heat change and zero volume change on mixing.

cards.front: Features of a solution showing positive deviation from Raoult's law?
cards.back: • A–B interactions weaker than A–A/B–B • Vapour pressure higher than expected • $\Delta_{mix}H > 0$, $\Delta_{mix}V > 0$

cards.front: Examples of positive deviation from Raoult's law?
cards.back: Ethanol + acetone, ethanol + water, carbon disulphide + acetone.
cards.hint: Ethanol's H-bonds get broken on mixing → escapes easily → higher vapour pressure.

cards.front: Features of a solution showing negative deviation from Raoult's law?
cards.back: • A–B interactions stronger than A–A/B–B • Vapour pressure lower than expected • $\Delta_{mix}H < 0$, $\Delta_{mix}V < 0$
cards.hint: Negative deviation: mixing releases heat and volume contracts.

cards.front: Why does chloroform + acetone show negative deviation?
cards.back: Hydrogen bond forms between H of $\text{CHCl}_3$ and O of acetone, giving stronger A–B attraction and lower vapour pressure.

cards.front: Examples of negative deviation from Raoult's law?
cards.back: Chloroform + acetone, phenol + aniline, nitric acid + water.

cards.front: What is an azeotrope?
cards.back: A binary mixture with the same composition in liquid and vapour that boils at a constant temperature; components cannot be separated by fractional distillation.

cards.front: Minimum boiling azeotropes are formed by solutions showing which deviation? Example?
cards.back: Large positive deviation. E.g. ethanol–water at about 95% ethanol by volume.
cards.hint: Positive deviation → higher vapour pressure → lower boiling point → minimum boiling.

cards.front: Maximum boiling azeotropes are formed by solutions showing which deviation? Example?
cards.back: Large negative deviation. E.g. nitric acid–water at about 68% $\text{HNO}_3$ by mass.

cards.front: What are colligative properties? Name the four.
cards.back: Properties depending only on the number of solute particles, not their nature: • Relative lowering of vapour pressure • Elevation of boiling point • Depression of freezing point • Osmotic pressure

cards.front: Formula for relative lowering of vapour pressure.
cards.back: $\dfrac{p_1^\circ - p_1}{p_1^\circ} = x_2$ equal to the mole fraction of solute.
cards.hint: Relative lowering depends only on the solute's mole fraction, not its identity.

cards.front: Relative lowering of vapour pressure in terms of masses (dilute solution)?
cards.back: $\dfrac{p_1^\circ - p_1}{p_1^\circ} = \dfrac{w_2 M_1}{M_2 w_1}$ Used to find molar mass of solute $M_2$.
cards.hint: For dilute solutions $n_2 \ll n_1$, so $x_2 \approx n_2/n_1$.

cards.front: Why does adding a non-volatile solute raise the boiling point?
cards.back: Vapour pressure is lowered, so a higher temperature is needed to make vapour pressure equal to external pressure (1.013 bar).

cards.front: Formula for elevation of boiling point.
cards.back: $\Delta T_b = K_b\,m$ $K_b$ = ebullioscopic (molal elevation) constant, $m$ = molality.

cards.front: Unit of $K_b$ and $K_f$? Values for water?
cards.back: Unit: $\text{K kg mol}^{-1}$ Water: $K_b = 0.52$, $K_f = 1.86\ \text{K kg mol}^{-1}$

cards.front: Formula for molar mass of solute from boiling point elevation.
cards.back: $M_2 = \dfrac{1000 \times K_b \times w_2}{\Delta T_b \times w_1}$ $w_1$ = mass of solvent (g), $w_2$ = mass of solute (g).

cards.front: Formula for depression of freezing point.
cards.back: $\Delta T_f = K_f\,m$ $K_f$ = cryoscopic (molal depression) constant.
cards.hint: $K_f$ of water (1.86) is larger than its $K_b$ (0.52).

cards.front: Why is ethylene glycol added to car radiator water?
cards.back: It depresses the freezing point of water, acting as antifreeze in cold climates.

cards.front: Relation of $K_f$ and $K_b$ with solvent properties?
cards.back: $K_b = \dfrac{R\,M_1\,T_b^2}{1000\,\Delta_{vap}H}$, $K_f = \dfrac{R\,M_1\,T_f^2}{1000\,\Delta_{fus}H}$ They depend only on the solvent, not the solute.
cards.hint: $M_1$ in g/mol here; constants are a solvent's fingerprint.

cards.front: Define osmosis.
cards.back: Net flow of solvent molecules through a semipermeable membrane from pure solvent (or dilute solution) to the more concentrated solution.
cards.hint: Solvent moves from low to high solute concentration.

cards.front: Define osmotic pressure. Formula?
cards.back: Excess pressure applied on the solution side to just stop osmosis. $\pi = CRT$ or $\pi = \dfrac{n_2 RT}{V}$ ($C$ = molarity)
cards.hint: Same form as ideal gas law: $\pi V = n_2RT$.

cards.front: Why is osmotic pressure preferred for finding molar masses of proteins and polymers?
cards.back: • Measured at room temperature (biomolecules not damaged) • Uses molarity, and gives a large measurable value even for very dilute solutions

cards.front: What are isotonic solutions? What is the isotonic NaCl concentration for blood?
cards.back: Solutions with the same osmotic pressure at a given temperature; no osmosis occurs between them. Blood is isotonic with 0.9% (w/V) NaCl (normal saline).

cards.front: What happens to red blood cells placed in hypertonic and hypotonic solutions?
cards.back: • Hypertonic (>0.9% NaCl): water flows out, cells shrink • Hypotonic (<0.9% NaCl): water flows in, cells swell/burst

cards.front: What is reverse osmosis? Give one use.
cards.back: Applying pressure greater than osmotic pressure on the solution side makes solvent flow from solution to pure solvent. Use: desalination of sea water (cellulose acetate membrane).
cards.hint: RO: pressure on solution side must exceed $\pi$.

cards.front: What is abnormal molar mass?
cards.back: A molar mass from colligative measurement that is lower or higher than the true value, due to dissociation or association of solute in solution.

cards.front: Define van't Hoff factor $i$.
cards.back: $i = \dfrac{\text{normal molar mass}}{\text{abnormal molar mass}}$ $= \dfrac{\text{observed colligative property}}{\text{calculated colligative property}}$

cards.front: Value of $i$ for association, dissociation and neither?
cards.back: • Dissociation: $i > 1$ • Association: $i < 1$ • No change (e.g. glucose, urea): $i = 1$
cards.hint: Dissociation → more particles → $i > 1$; association → fewer → $i < 1$.

cards.front: Why does ethanoic acid show molar mass ~120 in benzene?
cards.back: It forms dimers via hydrogen bonding, halving particle number; so $i \approx 0.5$ and molar mass appears about double (60 → 120).

cards.front: Modified colligative property expressions with $i$?
cards.back:
• $\Delta T_b = i\,K_b\,m$
• $\Delta T_f = i\,K_f\,m$
• $\pi = i\,CRT$
• $\dfrac{\Delta p}{p_1^\circ} = i\,x_2$

cards.front: Ideal van't Hoff factor for NaCl, $\text{K}_2\text{SO}_4$ and $\text{CaCl}_2$ (complete dissociation)?
cards.back: NaCl: 2; $\text{K}_2\text{SO}_4$: 3; $\text{CaCl}_2$: 3

cards.front: Arrange 0.1 m aqueous glucose, NaCl, $\text{CaCl}_2$ by freezing point.
cards.back: Depression $\propto i$: glucose (1) < NaCl (2) < $\text{CaCl}_2$ (3). Freezing point: glucose > NaCl > $\text{CaCl}_2$
cards.hint: Trap: largest $\Delta T_f$ means LOWEST freezing point.

cards.front: Relation between degree of dissociation $\alpha$ and $i$ for an electrolyte giving $n$ ions?
cards.back: $i = 1 + (n-1)\alpha$ So $\alpha = \dfrac{i - 1}{n - 1}$

cards.front: Relation between degree of association $\alpha$ and $i$ when $n$ molecules associate into one?
cards.back: $i = 1 - \alpha + \dfrac{\alpha}{n}$ For dimerisation ($n = 2$): $i = 1 - \alpha/2$

cards.front: Difference between a galvanic cell and an electrolytic cell?
cards.back: • Galvanic: chemical → electrical energy (spontaneous redox) • Electrolytic: electrical → chemical energy (non-spontaneous reaction driven by current)
cards.hint: Galvanic: spontaneous, $\Delta G < 0$. Electrolytic: needs external energy.

cards.front: Cell reaction and $E^\circ_{cell}$ of the Daniell cell?
cards.back: $\text{Zn(s)} + \text{Cu}^{2+}\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + \text{Cu(s)}$ $E^\circ_{cell} = 1.1\ \text{V}$ when ion concentrations are 1 mol/L.

cards.front: What happens in a Daniell cell if external opposing potential exceeds 1.1 V?
cards.back: Current flows in the reverse direction; it works as an electrolytic cell: Zn deposits at the zinc electrode and Cu dissolves.
cards.hint: Below 1.1 V: still galvanic; exactly 1.1 V: no current.

cards.front: Anode and cathode in a galvanic cell: sign and process?
cards.back: • Anode: oxidation, negative terminal • Cathode: reduction, positive terminal Electrons flow anode → cathode in the external circuit.
cards.hint: Trap: in an electrolytic cell the anode is positive, but oxidation still occurs at the anode.

cards.front: Functions of a salt bridge?
cards.back: • Completes the internal circuit • Maintains electrical neutrality of both half-cells Usually agar-agar gel with KCl or $\text{NH}_4\text{NO}_3$.

cards.front: How is a galvanic cell represented (cell notation)?
cards.back: Anode on the left, cathode on the right, salt bridge as a double vertical line: $\text{Zn|Zn}^{2+}\text{(aq)}\,||\,\text{Cu}^{2+}\text{(aq)|Cu}$
cards.hint: Oxidation on the Left, Reduction on the Right.

cards.front: Formula for standard emf of a cell from electrode potentials?
cards.back: $E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ_{right} - E^\circ_{left}$ $= E^\circ_{cathode} - E^\circ_{anode}$ (both as standard reduction potentials)

cards.front: What is the standard hydrogen electrode (SHE)? Its potential?
cards.back: Pt electrode coated with platinum black, dipped in acid with $[\text{H}^+] = 1\ \text{M}$, $\text{H}_2$ gas at 1 bar. $E^\circ = 0\ \text{V}$ at all temperatures (by convention).
cards.hint: SHE is the reference zero for all standard electrode potentials.

cards.front: Why can't the absolute potential of a single electrode be measured?
cards.back: Only a potential difference between two electrodes can be measured; so electrode potentials are measured relative to the SHE.

cards.front: What does a negative standard reduction potential indicate?
cards.back: The electrode is a stronger reducing agent than $\text{H}^+/\text{H}_2$; its ions are harder to reduce than $\text{H}^+$. E.g. $E^\circ_{\text{Zn}^{2+}/\text{Zn}} = -0.76\ \text{V}$

cards.front: Strongest oxidising agent and strongest reducing agent in the electrochemical series?
cards.back: • Strongest oxidising agent: $\text{F}_2$ ($E^\circ = +2.87\ \text{V}$) • Strongest reducing agent: Li ($E^\circ_{\text{Li}^+/\text{Li}} = -3.05\ \text{V}$)
cards.hint: Higher $E^\circ$ = better oxidising agent; lower $E^\circ$ = better reducing agent.

cards.front: Can $\text{CuSO}_4$ solution be stored in a zinc pot?
cards.back: No. $E^\circ_{\text{Zn}^{2+}/\text{Zn}} (-0.76) < E^\circ_{\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}} (+0.34)$, so Zn reduces $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ and the pot dissolves.
cards.hint: A metal with lower $E^\circ$ displaces from solution the ions of a metal with higher $E^\circ$.

cards.front: Can a metal with positive $E^\circ$ (e.g. Cu) liberate $\text{H}_2$ from dilute acids?
cards.back: No. Only metals with negative standard reduction potential (below H in the series) displace $\text{H}_2$ from dilute acids.

cards.front: Nernst equation for the electrode $\text{M}^{n+}\text{(aq)} + ne^- \rightarrow \text{M(s)}$?
cards.back: $E = E^\circ - \dfrac{RT}{nF}\ln\dfrac{1}{[\text{M}^{n+}]}$ Concentration of the pure solid M is taken as unity.

cards.front: Nernst equation at 298 K in log form?
cards.back: $E = E^\circ - \dfrac{0.059}{n}\log Q$ (from $2.303RT/F = 0.059\ \text{V}$ at 298 K)

cards.front: Nernst equation for the Daniell cell at 298 K?
What happens to $E_{cell}$ of the Daniell cell if $[\text{Cu}^{2+}]$ increases?
cards.back: $E_{cell}$ increases (Q = $[\text{Zn}^{2+}]/[\text{Cu}^{2+}]$ decreases). Increasing $[\text{Zn}^{2+}]$ decreases $E_{cell}$.

cards.front: Potential of a hydrogen electrode in a solution of pH 10 at 298 K?
cards.back: $E = -0.059 \times \text{pH}$ (with $p_{\text{H}_2}$ = 1 bar) $E = -0.59\ \text{V}$

cards.front: Relation between $E^\circ_{cell}$ and equilibrium constant $K_c$ at 298 K?
cards.back: $E^\circ_{cell} = \dfrac{0.059}{n}\log K_c$ At equilibrium $E_{cell} = 0$ and $Q = K_c$.
cards.hint: At equilibrium $E_{cell} = 0$, so $E^\circ_{cell}$ is fixed by $K_c$.

cards.front: Large positive $E^\circ_{cell}$ means $K_c$ is…?
cards.back: Very large: the reaction goes almost to completion. E.g. Daniell cell $K_c \approx 2 \times 10^{37}$.

cards.front: Relation between Gibbs energy change and cell emf?
cards.back: $\Delta_r G = -nFE_{cell}$ Standard: $\Delta_r G^\circ = -nFE^\circ_{cell}$
cards.hint: n = moles of electrons transferred in the balanced cell reaction.

cards.front: Sign of $E_{cell}$ and $\Delta G$ for a spontaneous cell reaction?
cards.back: $E_{cell} > 0$ and $\Delta G < 0$.

cards.front: Relation between $\Delta_r G^\circ$ and equilibrium constant?
cards.back: $\Delta_r G^\circ = -RT\ln K$ $= -2.303RT\log K$

cards.front: Value of Faraday constant (F) as used by NCERT?
cards.back: Charge on 1 mol of electrons: $F = 96487\ \text{C mol}^{-1}$ (≈ 96500)

cards.front: Trap: Does $\Delta_r G$ depend on how the cell reaction is balanced?
cards.back: Yes, $\Delta_r G$ is extensive: doubling the equation doubles $n$ and $\Delta_r G$. $E_{cell}$ is intensive and does not change.

cards.front: Define resistivity and give its SI unit.
cards.back: $R = \rho\dfrac{l}{A}$; $\rho$ = resistance of a conductor of unit length and unit area. SI unit: $\Omega\ \text{m}$ (often $\Omega$ cm).

cards.front: Define conductivity ($\kappa$). SI unit?
cards.back: Reciprocal of resistivity: $\kappa = \dfrac{1}{\rho} = \dfrac{l}{RA}$ SI unit: $\text{S m}^{-1}$ ($\text{1 S cm}^{-1} = 100\ \text{S m}^{-1}$)

cards.front: What is the cell constant? Formula?
cards.back: $G^* = \dfrac{l}{A} = R\,\kappa$ Unit: $\text{m}^{-1}$ (or $\text{cm}^{-1}$). Found using a KCl solution of known conductivity.
cards.hint: Cell constant depends only on the cell geometry, not the solution.

cards.front: Why is AC (not DC) used to measure resistance of an electrolyte solution?
cards.back: DC would cause electrolysis, changing the solution composition. AC (with a Wheatstone bridge) avoids this.

cards.front: Factors affecting electrolytic (ionic) conductance?
cards.back: • Nature of electrolyte and size/solvation of ions • Nature and viscosity of solvent • Concentration • Temperature (conductance increases with T)
cards.hint: Metallic conductance decreases with T; electrolytic conductance increases.

cards.front: Define molar conductivity. Formula and unit?
cards.back: $\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa}{c}$ With $\kappa$ in $\text{S cm}^{-1}$ and c in mol/L: $\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{M}$ Unit: $\text{S cm}^2\text{mol}^{-1}$
cards.hint: Use 1000 when $\kappa$ is in S cm⁻¹ and M in mol L⁻¹.

cards.front: How do conductivity and molar conductivity vary with dilution?
cards.back: • Conductivity $\kappa$ decreases (fewer ions per unit volume) • Molar conductivity $\Lambda_m$ increases (volume containing 1 mol increases)
cards.hint: Trap: these two move in OPPOSITE directions on dilution.

cards.front: Debye–Hückel–Onsager equation for strong electrolytes?
cards.back: $\Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^\circ - A\sqrt{c}$ Plot of $\Lambda_m$ vs $\sqrt{c}$ is a straight line with slope $-A$ and intercept $\Lambda_m^\circ$.
cards.hint: Linear $\Lambda_m$ vs $\sqrt{c}$ only for strong electrolytes.

cards.front: How does A in $\Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^\circ - A\sqrt{c}$ compare for NaCl, $\text{CaCl}_2$, $\text{MgSO}_4$ in water?
cards.back: A depends on the type of electrolyte (charges on ions): same for all 1-1 electrolytes, larger for 2-1 and 2-2. So $A$: NaCl < $\text{CaCl}_2$ < $\text{MgSO}_4$

cards.front: Graph of $\Lambda_m$ vs $\sqrt{c}$ for a weak electrolyte (e.g. acetic acid)?
cards.back: $\Lambda_m$ rises steeply at low concentration (degree of dissociation increases); curve is not linear, so $\Lambda_m^\circ$ cannot be found by extrapolation.

cards.front: State Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions.
cards.back: Limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte is the sum of the limiting molar conductivities of its cation and anion: $\Lambda_m^\circ = \nu_+\lambda_+^\circ + \nu_-\lambda_-^\circ$
cards.hint: Each ion contributes a fixed share at infinite dilution.

cards.front: How is $\Lambda_m^\circ$ of acetic acid found using Kohlrausch's law?
cards.back: $\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}) = \Lambda_m^\circ(\text{HCl}) + \Lambda_m^\circ(\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}) - \Lambda_m^\circ(\text{NaCl})$

cards.front: Degree of dissociation of a weak electrolyte from conductivity?
cards.back: $\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^\circ}$
cards.hint: Weak electrolyte: $\Lambda_m^\circ$ comes from Kohlrausch's law, not extrapolation.

cards.front: Dissociation constant of a weak acid in terms of molar conductivity?
cards.back: $K_a = \dfrac{c\alpha^2}{1-\alpha}$ with $\alpha = \Lambda_m/\Lambda_m^\circ$ $K_a = \dfrac{c\Lambda_m^2}{\Lambda_m^\circ(\Lambda_m^\circ - \Lambda_m)}$

cards.front: Which cation has the highest limiting molar conductivity in water and why?
cards.back: $\text{H}^+$ (~349.6 $\text{S cm}^2\text{mol}^{-1}$), because it moves by rapid proton transfer between H-bonded water molecules; $\text{OH}^-$ is highest among anions.

cards.front: State Faraday's first law of electrolysis.
cards.back: Mass of substance deposited/liberated is proportional to the charge passed: $w = Z\,I\,t$ ($Z$ = electrochemical equivalent)

cards.front: State Faraday's second law of electrolysis.
cards.back: For the same charge passed through different electrolytes, masses liberated are proportional to their chemical equivalent weights: $\dfrac{w_1}{w_2} = \dfrac{E_1}{E_2}$

cards.front: Charge needed to deposit 1 mol of Al from $\text{Al}^{3+}$?
cards.back: $3F$ $= 3 \times 96487 \approx 2.89 \times 10^5\ \text{C}$
cards.hint: Charge needed = (change in oxidation state) × F per mole.

cards.front: Charge needed to reduce 1 mol of $\text{MnO}_4^-$ to $\text{Mn}^{2+}$?
cards.back: Mn goes from +7 to +2, so 5 mol e⁻: $5F$ $\approx 4.82 \times 10^5\ \text{C}$

cards.front: Products of electrolysis of molten NaCl?
cards.back: • Cathode: Na metal • Anode: $\text{Cl}_2$ gas

cards.front: Products of electrolysis of aqueous NaCl (inert electrodes)?
cards.back: • Cathode: $\text{H}_2$ (water is reduced, $E^\circ$ of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ higher than $\text{Na}^+$) • Anode: $\text{Cl}_2$ (due to overpotential of $\text{O}_2$) Solution becomes NaOH.
cards.hint: Trap: by $E^\circ$, $\text{O}_2$ (1.23 V) should form before $\text{Cl}_2$ (1.36 V), but $\text{O}_2$ overpotential makes $\text{Cl}_2$ form.

cards.front: Products of electrolysis of aqueous $\text{CuSO}_4$ with Pt vs Cu electrodes?
cards.back: • Pt: cathode Cu, anode $\text{O}_2$ • Cu: cathode Cu deposits, anode Cu dissolves (as $\text{Cu}^{2+}$)

cards.front: Products of electrolysis of dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ with Pt? What about concentrated?
cards.back: • Dilute: anode $\text{O}_2$, cathode $\text{H}_2$ • Concentrated: anode gives $\text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-}$ (peroxodisulphate), cathode $\text{H}_2$

cards.front: Primary vs secondary battery?
cards.back: • Primary: reaction occurs only once, cannot be recharged (e.g. dry cell) • Secondary: rechargeable by passing current in reverse (e.g. lead storage battery)
cards.hint: Primary = use once; Secondary = recharge.

cards.front: Anode, cathode and potential of the dry (Leclanché) cell?
cards.back: • Anode: zinc container • Cathode: carbon (graphite) rod surrounded by $\text{MnO}_2$ + C • Electrolyte: moist paste of $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ and $\text{ZnCl}_2$ Potential ≈ 1.5 V

cards.front: Cathode reaction in a dry cell?
cards.back: $\text{MnO}_2 + \text{NH}_4^+ + e^- \rightarrow \text{MnO(OH)} + \text{NH}_3$ Mn goes from +4 to +3.

cards.front: Electrodes and electrolyte of a lead storage battery?
cards.back: • Anode: Pb • Cathode: grid of lead packed with $\text{PbO}_2$ • Electrolyte: ~38% $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$

cards.front: Overall discharge reaction of a lead storage battery?
cards.back: $\text{Pb} + \text{PbO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow 2\text{PbSO}_4 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ On charging the reaction reverses.
cards.hint: Both electrodes form $\text{PbSO}_4$ on discharge; acid density falls.

cards.front: What is a fuel cell? Electrode reactions of the $\text{H}_2$–$\text{O}_2$ fuel cell?
cards.back:
Galvanic cell converting combustion energy of fuels directly into electricity.
• Cathode: $\text{O}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + 4e^- \rightarrow 4\text{OH}^-$
• Anode: $2\text{H}_2 + 4\text{OH}^- \rightarrow 4\text{H}_2\text{O} + 4e^-$

cards.front: Advantages of the $\text{H}_2$–$\text{O}_2$ fuel cell? Where was it used?
cards.back: • High efficiency (~70% vs ~40% for thermal plants) • Pollution-free; product water Used in the Apollo space programme (water used for drinking by astronauts).

cards.front: Define rate of a reaction.
cards.back: Change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time. Unit: $\text{mol L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$ (gas phase: $\text{atm s}^{-1}$).
cards.hint: Rate is always positive; reactant terms get a minus sign.

cards.front: Average vs instantaneous rate?
cards.back: • Average: $r_{av} = -\dfrac{\Delta[\text{R}]}{\Delta t}$ over a time interval • Instantaneous: $r = -\dfrac{d[\text{R}]}{dt}$, slope of the tangent to the concentration–time curve at that instant

cards.front: Rate expression for $\text{2HI} \rightarrow \text{H}_2 + \text{I}_2$ in terms of each species?
cards.back: $r = -\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{d[\text{HI}]}{dt} = \dfrac{d[\text{H}_2]}{dt} = \dfrac{d[\text{I}_2]}{dt}$
cards.hint: Divide each rate by its stoichiometric coefficient; minus sign for reactants.

cards.front: For $\text{N}_2 + 3\text{H}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{NH}_3$, relate rate of disappearance of $\text{H}_2$ to formation of $\text{NH}_3$.
cards.back: $-\dfrac{1}{3}\dfrac{d[\text{H}_2]}{dt} = \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{d[\text{NH}_3]}{dt}$ So $-\dfrac{d[\text{H}_2]}{dt} = \dfrac{3}{2}\dfrac{d[\text{NH}_3]}{dt}$

cards.front: Why is a negative sign used with the rate of change of reactant concentration?
cards.back: Reactant concentration decreases, so $\Delta[\text{R}]$ is negative; the minus sign makes the rate positive.

cards.front: Factors affecting rate of a reaction?
cards.back: • Concentration (pressure for gases) • Temperature • Catalyst • Nature of reactants, surface area

cards.front: What is a rate law (rate equation)?
cards.back: Rate expressed in terms of reactant concentrations raised to powers determined experimentally: $\text{Rate} = k[\text{A}]^x[\text{B}]^y$
cards.hint: Trap: x and y need not equal the stoichiometric coefficients.

cards.front: What is the rate constant (specific reaction rate)?
cards.back: Rate of reaction when all reactant concentrations are unity. It depends on temperature (and catalyst), not on concentration.
cards.hint: k changes with temperature and catalyst only.

cards.front: Define order of a reaction.
cards.back: Sum of the powers of concentration terms in the experimentally determined rate law. For rate $= k[\text{A}]^x[\text{B}]^y$, order $= x + y$.
cards.hint: Order is found by experiment, never from the balanced equation alone.

cards.front: Can order of a reaction be zero or fractional?
cards.back: Yes: order can be 0, fractional, or an integer (NCERT: 0, 1, 2, 3 and fractions). It is an experimental quantity.

cards.front: General unit of rate constant for an n-th order reaction?
cards.hint: Plug n: n=0 → mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹; n=1 → s⁻¹; n=2 → L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.

cards.front: Units of k for zero, first and second order reactions?
cards.back: • Zero: $\text{mol L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$ • First: $\text{s}^{-1}$ • Second: $\text{L mol}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$

cards.front: Define molecularity of a reaction.
cards.back: Number of reacting species (atoms, ions, molecules) that must collide simultaneously in an elementary reaction. Unimolecular, bimolecular, termolecular.
cards.hint: Molecularity applies only to single-step (elementary) reactions.

cards.front: Why is molecularity greater than three rare?
cards.back: Probability of more than three molecules colliding simultaneously is very small.

cards.front: Key differences between order and molecularity?
cards.back: • Order: experimental; can be 0 or fractional; for overall reaction • Molecularity: theoretical; always a whole number, never zero; only for elementary steps

cards.front: What is the rate-determining step?
cards.back: The slowest step in a complex reaction mechanism; it decides the overall rate.
cards.hint: The slowest step limits the overall speed, like the narrowest neck of a funnel.

cards.front: Rate law of $2\text{H}_2\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{O}_2$ (in alkaline medium with $\text{I}^-$)?
cards.back: Rate $= k[\text{H}_2\text{O}_2][\text{I}^-]$: first order in each, overall second order. Slow step: $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2 + \text{I}^- \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{IO}^-$

cards.front: If rate $= k[\text{A}]^2[\text{B}]$, what happens to rate when [A] is doubled and [B] halved?
cards.back: Rate becomes $2^2 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = $ 2 times.

cards.front: Integrated rate equation for a zero order reaction?
cards.back: $[\text{R}] = [\text{R}]_0 - kt$ so $k = \dfrac{[\text{R}]_0 - [\text{R}]}{t}$

cards.front: Graph of [R] vs t for a zero order reaction?
cards.back: Straight line with slope $-k$ and intercept $[\text{R}]_0$.

cards.front: Half-life of a zero order reaction?
cards.back: $t_{1/2} = \dfrac{[\text{R}]_0}{2k}$ Directly proportional to initial concentration.
cards.hint: Zero order: half-life gets shorter as reaction proceeds.

cards.front: Examples of zero order reactions?
cards.back: • Decomposition of $\text{NH}_3$ on hot platinum surface at high pressure • Thermal decomposition of HI on gold surface
cards.hint: Surface fully covered → rate independent of concentration.

cards.front: Why does $\text{NH}_3$ decomposition on Pt become zero order at high pressure?
cards.back: The metal surface gets saturated with gas molecules; further increase in concentration cannot increase rate.

cards.front: Time for a zero order reaction to go to completion?
cards.back: $t = \dfrac{[\text{R}]_0}{k}$ (= $2\,t_{1/2}$). Zero order reactions do reach completion.

cards.front: Integrated rate equation for a first order reaction?
cards.back: $k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log\dfrac{[\text{R}]_0}{[\text{R}]}$ or $[\text{R}] = [\text{R}]_0 e^{-kt}$
cards.hint: Use base-10 log with the 2.303 factor.

cards.front: Graph of $\ln[\text{R}]$ vs t for a first order reaction?
cards.back: Straight line with slope $-k$ and intercept $\ln[\text{R}]_0$. (For $\log$: slope $= -k/2.303$)

cards.front: Graph of $\log\dfrac{[\text{R}]_0}{[\text{R}]}$ vs t for a first order reaction?
cards.back: Straight line through the origin with slope $\dfrac{k}{2.303}$.

cards.front: Half-life of a first order reaction?
cards.back: $t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k}$ Independent of initial concentration.
cards.hint: 0.693 = ln 2. Radioactive decay is the classic example.

cards.front: Relation between half-life and initial concentration for zero vs first order?
cards.back: • Zero order: $t_{1/2} \propto [\text{R}]_0$ • First order: $t_{1/2}$ independent of $[\text{R}]_0$

cards.front: Fraction of reactant left after n half-lives in a first order reaction?
cards.back: $\dfrac{[\text{R}]}{[\text{R}]_0} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^n$ E.g. after 3 half-lives, 1/8 remains.

cards.front: For a first order reaction, time for 99.9% completion vs half-life?
For a first order reaction, time for 99% completion vs 90% completion?
First order rate constant for a gas-phase reaction $\text{A(g)} \rightarrow \text{B(g)} + \text{C(g)}$ from pressures?
cards.back: $k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log\dfrac{p_i}{2p_i - p_t}$ $p_i$ = initial pressure, $p_t$ = total pressure at time t

cards.front: Examples of first order reactions?
cards.back: • All natural and artificial radioactive decay • Decomposition of $\text{N}_2\text{O}_5$, $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ • Hydrogenation of ethene

cards.front: What is a pseudo first order reaction?
cards.back: A reaction of higher molecularity/order that behaves as first order because one reactant is in large excess, so its concentration stays nearly constant.
cards.hint: Excess reactant (usually water) disappears from the rate law.

cards.front: Give two examples of pseudo first order reactions.
cards.back: • Acid hydrolysis of ethyl acetate: rate $= k[\text{CH}_3\text{COOC}_2\text{H}_5]$ • Inversion of cane sugar: rate $= k[\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{11}]$ Water is in large excess.

cards.front: How does rate change with a 10 °C rise in temperature?
cards.back: Rate constant nearly doubles for every 10 °C rise. Ratio $\dfrac{k_{T+10}}{k_T}$ is the temperature coefficient.

cards.front: Write the Arrhenius equation.
cards.back: $k = A\,e^{-E_a/RT}$ A = Arrhenius (frequency) factor, $E_a$ = activation energy, R = gas constant
cards.hint: Higher $E_a$ or lower T → smaller k.

cards.front: What is activation energy?
cards.back: Minimum extra energy reactants must absorb to form the activated complex (energy of activated complex minus energy of reactants).
cards.hint: Think of $E_a$ as the energy hill reactants must climb.

cards.front: Logarithmic form of the Arrhenius equation and its graph?
cards.back: $\ln k = \ln A - \dfrac{E_a}{RT}$ $\ln k$ vs $1/T$: straight line, slope $-E_a/R$, intercept $\ln A$.

cards.front: Slope of the $\log k$ vs $1/T$ plot?
cards.hint: Trap: with log (base 10) divide by 2.303; with ln, slope is $-E_a/R$.

cards.front: Arrhenius equation relating rate constants at two temperatures?
cards.back: $\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303R}\left(\dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1T_2}\right)$

cards.front: What does $e^{-E_a/RT}$ represent?
cards.back: Fraction of molecules having kinetic energy ≥ $E_a$ (from the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution).

cards.front: Effect of increasing temperature on the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve?
cards.back: Curve broadens and shifts right; peak (most probable KE) moves to higher energy and fraction of molecules with energy ≥ $E_a$ increases. Total area stays constant.

cards.front: Rate constant when $E_a = 0$, and when $T \rightarrow \infty$?
cards.back: In both cases $k = A$.

cards.front: Which reaction is more sensitive to temperature: high or low $E_a$?
cards.back: Reaction with higher $E_a$: its rate constant changes more for the same temperature rise (steeper $\ln k$ vs $1/T$ line).

cards.front: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?
cards.back: Provides an alternate pathway with lower activation energy; it forms a temporary intermediate with reactants and is regenerated.
cards.hint: Catalyst lowers the hill; it does not change the start or end levels.

cards.front: Does a catalyst change $\Delta G$ or the equilibrium constant?
cards.back: No. It does not alter $\Delta G$ or $K$; it only helps reach equilibrium faster by speeding up forward and backward reactions equally.

cards.front: Can a catalyst make a non-spontaneous reaction occur?
cards.back: No. It catalyses only spontaneous reactions (those with $\Delta G < 0$).

cards.front: State the two conditions for an effective collision (collision theory).
cards.back: Colliding molecules must have • energy ≥ threshold energy • proper orientation
cards.hint: Enough energy + right orientation = effective collision.

cards.front: Rate expression according to collision theory?
cards.back: Rate $= P\,Z_{AB}\,e^{-E_a/RT}$ $Z_{AB}$ = collision frequency, $P$ = probability (steric) factor accounting for orientation.

cards.front: Relation between threshold energy and activation energy?
cards.back: Threshold energy = activation energy + average energy of reactant molecules.

cards.front: Which elements make up group 15 and what is their valence shell configuration?
cards.back: • N, P, As, Sb, Bi (pnictogens) • Valence configuration $ns^2np^3$

cards.front: Classify the group 15 elements as non-metal, metalloid or metal.
cards.back: • N, P: non-metals • As, Sb: metalloids • Bi: metal
cards.hint: Metallic character increases down every p-block group.

cards.front: How does atomic radius change down group 15?
cards.back: Increases down the group; a big jump from N to P, but only a small increase from As to Bi because filled d and f orbitals shield poorly.

cards.front: Why is the ionisation enthalpy of group 15 elements higher than that of group 16 elements of the same period?
cards.back: Group 15 has an extra-stable half-filled $np^3$ configuration, so removing an electron is harder. e.g. $IE_1$: N > O, P > S.
cards.hint: Trap: IE generally rises across a period, but N > O is the classic exception.

cards.front: Common oxidation states of group 15 elements?
cards.back: −3, +3 and +5. Tendency to show −3 decreases down the group; Bi hardly forms any −3 compound.

cards.front: How does the stability of +5 and +3 oxidation states change down group 15?
cards.back: +5 becomes less stable and +3 more stable down the group, due to the inert pair effect.
cards.hint: The only well-characterised Bi(V) compound is BiF5.

cards.front: What is the inert pair effect?
cards.back: Reluctance of the $ns^2$ electrons to take part in bonding in heavier p-block elements, because intervening d and f electrons shield poorly. Lower oxidation state (group number − 2) becomes more stable.

cards.front: Range of oxidation states shown by nitrogen?
cards.back: From −3 to +5 (e.g. −3 in $\mathrm{NH_3}$, +5 in $\mathrm{HNO_3}$, intermediate states in its oxides).

cards.front: Why does nitrogen differ from the rest of group 15?
cards.back: • Small size, high electronegativity, high IE • No d orbitals (max covalency 4) • Forms $p\pi-p\pi$ multiple bonds (e.g. $\mathrm{N\equiv N}$)

cards.front: Why is nitrogen a diatomic gas while phosphorus exists as solid $\mathrm{P_4}$?
cards.back: N forms a strong $p\pi-p\pi$ triple bond giving discrete $\mathrm{N_2}$; P is too large for effective $p\pi-p\pi$ overlap, so it forms single bonds in tetrahedral $\mathrm{P_4}$.

cards.front: Why does nitrogen show weaker catenation than phosphorus?
cards.back: The N–N single bond is weaker than P–P: the short bond brings the non-bonding lone pairs close, causing strong repulsion.
cards.hint: Trap: N–N single bond is weak, but N≡N triple bond is very strong.

cards.front: Why is dinitrogen chemically inert at room temperature?
cards.back: Very high $\mathrm{N\equiv N}$ bond dissociation enthalpy (about $941\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$).

cards.front: Heavier group 15 elements form multiple bonds of which type, unlike nitrogen?
cards.back: $d\pi-p\pi$ bonds using vacant d orbitals, e.g. P=O in phosphorus oxoacids. Nitrogen has no d orbitals.

cards.front: Order of thermal stability and basicity of group 15 hydrides $\mathrm{EH_3}$?
cards.back: Both decrease down the group: $\mathrm{NH_3 > PH_3 > AsH_3 > SbH_3 > BiH_3}$
cards.hint: E–H bond weakens as E gets bigger; lone pair becomes more diffuse, so less basic.

cards.front: Order of reducing character of group 15 hydrides?
cards.back: Increases down the group: $\mathrm{NH_3 < PH_3 < AsH_3 < SbH_3 < BiH_3}$; $\mathrm{BiH_3}$ is the strongest reducing agent.

cards.front: Order of H–E–H bond angle in group 15 hydrides?
cards.back: $\mathrm{NH_3}\ (107.8^\circ) > \mathrm{PH_3}\ (93.6^\circ) > \mathrm{AsH_3} > \mathrm{SbH_3} > \mathrm{BiH_3}\ (\approx 90^\circ)$
cards.hint: Larger, less electronegative central atom: bond pairs move away, repel less, angle shrinks toward 90°.

cards.front: Order of boiling points of group 15 hydrides?
cards.back: $\mathrm{PH_3 < AsH_3 < NH_3 < SbH_3 < BiH_3}$ $\mathrm{NH_3}$ is raised by H-bonding but is still below $\mathrm{SbH_3}$ and $\mathrm{BiH_3}$.
cards.hint: Trap: NH3 is NOT the highest-boiling group 15 hydride.

cards.front: Trend in acidic character of group 15 oxides?
cards.back: Oxide in the higher oxidation state is more acidic ($\mathrm{E_2O_5 > E_2O_3}$). Down the group acidity falls: N, P oxides acidic; As, Sb oxides amphoteric; Bi oxide basic.

cards.front: Why does nitrogen not form a pentahalide while phosphorus forms $\mathrm{PCl_5}$?
cards.back: Nitrogen has no vacant d orbitals, so it cannot expand its octet beyond covalency 4.

cards.front: Which is more covalent: group 15 trihalides or pentahalides?
cards.back: Pentahalides: the higher (+5) oxidation state is more polarising than +3.

cards.front: Which nitrogen trihalide is stable?
cards.back: Only $\mathrm{NF_3}$. The other trihalides of heavier group 15 elements are all stable.

cards.front: Which elements make up group 16 and what is their valence shell configuration?
cards.back: • O, S, Se, Te, Po (chalcogens; Po is radioactive) • Valence configuration $ns^2np^4$

cards.front: Classify the group 16 elements as non-metal, metalloid or metal.
cards.back: • O, S: non-metals • Se, Te: metalloids • Po: metal

cards.front: Why is the electron gain enthalpy of oxygen less negative than that of sulfur?
cards.back: O is very small and compact, so the incoming electron faces strong inter-electronic repulsion. From S onward, $\Delta_{eg}H$ becomes less negative down to Po.
cards.hint: Same idea as F vs Cl in group 17.

cards.front: In which compounds does oxygen show a positive oxidation state?
cards.back: Only with fluorine: +2 in $\mathrm{OF_2}$ and +1 in $\mathrm{O_2F_2}$.
cards.hint: F is the only element more electronegative than O.

cards.front: Oxidation states of S, Se, Te and the trend in their stability?
cards.back: −2, +2, +4, +6. Down the group −2 becomes less stable; +4 becomes more stable than +6 (inert pair effect).

cards.front: Why does oxygen behave anomalously in group 16?
cards.back: • Small size, very high electronegativity • Strong H-bonding ($\mathrm{H_2O}$ liquid, $\mathrm{H_2S}$ gas) • No d orbitals: covalency limited to 4 (mostly 2)

cards.front: Why is oxygen a diatomic gas while sulfur is a solid $\mathrm{S_8}$?
cards.back: O forms strong $p\pi-p\pi$ double bonds (O=O). S is larger, prefers single S–S bonds and strong catenation, giving puckered $\mathrm{S_8}$ rings.

cards.front: Order of acidic character of group 16 hydrides?
cards.back: $\mathrm{H_2O < H_2S < H_2Se < H_2Te}$, because the H–E bond dissociation enthalpy decreases down the group.

cards.front: Order of thermal stability and reducing character of group 16 hydrides?
cards.back: • Thermal stability: $\mathrm{H_2O > H_2S > H_2Se > H_2Te}$ • Reducing character: the reverse ($\mathrm{H_2Te}$ strongest)

cards.front: Order of H–E–H bond angle in group 16 hydrides?
cards.back: $\mathrm{H_2O}\ (104.5^\circ) > \mathrm{H_2S}\ (92^\circ) > \mathrm{H_2Se}\ (91^\circ) > \mathrm{H_2Te}\ (90^\circ)$

cards.front: Order of boiling points of group 16 hydrides?
cards.back: $\mathrm{H_2S < H_2Se < H_2Te < H_2O}$; water is highest due to extensive H-bonding.
cards.hint: Trap: the order is not simply by molar mass.

cards.front: Shape and hybridisation of $\mathrm{SF_6}$? Why is it so unreactive?
cards.back: Octahedral, $sp^3d^2$. Six F atoms sterically shield S, blocking attack, so it is exceptionally stable.

cards.front: Trend in reducing property of group 16 dioxides $\mathrm{EO_2}$?
cards.back: Decreases from $\mathrm{SO_2}$ to $\mathrm{TeO_2}$: $\mathrm{SO_2}$ is a reducing agent, $\mathrm{TeO_2}$ is an oxidising agent.
cards.hint: +4 grows more stable down the group, so E(IV) holds less tendency to go to +6.

cards.front: Which elements make up group 17 and what is their valence shell configuration?
cards.back: • F, Cl, Br, I, At (halogens) • Valence configuration $ns^2np^5$, one electron short of a noble gas

cards.front: Which element has the highest electronegativity?
cards.back: Fluorine (4.0 on the Pauling scale). Electronegativity decreases down group 17.

cards.front: Order of negative electron gain enthalpy of the halogens?
cards.back: Cl > F > Br > I. F is below Cl because its small 2p shell causes strong repulsion to the added electron.
cards.hint: Chlorine has the most negative electron gain enthalpy in the periodic table.

cards.front: Order of bond dissociation enthalpy of the halogens?
cards.back: $\mathrm{Cl_2 > Br_2 > F_2 > I_2}$. $\mathrm{F_2}$ is anomalously low due to lone pair–lone pair repulsion across the short F–F bond.
cards.hint: Trap: F2 is NOT the strongest halogen bond.

cards.front: Physical state and colour of the halogens?
cards.back: • $\mathrm{F_2}$: pale yellow gas • $\mathrm{Cl_2}$: greenish-yellow gas • $\mathrm{Br_2}$: red-brown liquid • $\mathrm{I_2}$: violet-black solid
cards.hint: Colour arises from absorption of visible light that excites outer electrons.

cards.front: Order of oxidising power of the halogens? Why is $\mathrm{F_2}$ strongest?
cards.back: $\mathrm{F_2 > Cl_2 > Br_2 > I_2}$. F₂ wins due to low F–F bond dissociation enthalpy and very high hydration enthalpy of $\mathrm{F^-}$ (despite F's less negative electron gain enthalpy than Cl).

cards.front: What does fluorine give with water?
cards.back: It oxidises water to oxygen: $\mathrm{2F_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow 4H^+ + 4F^- + O_2}$
cards.hint: Cl2 and Br2 instead give HX + HOX; I2 does not react with water.

cards.front: Oxidation states of halogens?
cards.back: • F: only −1 • Cl, Br, I: −1 and also +1, +3, +5, +7 (using d orbitals, mainly in oxides, oxoacids, interhalogens)

cards.front: Why does fluorine differ from other halogens?
cards.back: • Very small size, highest electronegativity • Low F–F bond enthalpy • No d orbitals: shows only −1 and forms only one oxoacid (HOF) • Strong H-bonding in HF
