cards.front: Order of acid strength and thermal stability of hydrogen halides?
cards.back: • Acid strength: HF < HCl < HBr < HI • Thermal stability: HF > HCl > HBr > HI Both follow the H–X bond dissociation enthalpy.

cards.front: Order of boiling points of hydrogen halides?
cards.back: HCl < HBr < HI < HF; HF is highest because of strong H-bonding.

cards.front: Which elements make up group 18 and what is their valence shell configuration?
cards.back: • He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn (Rn radioactive) • $ns^2np^6$, except He: $1s^2$

cards.front: Ionisation enthalpy and electron gain enthalpy of noble gases?
cards.back: • Very high IE (stable closed shell), decreasing down the group • Large positive electron gain enthalpy

cards.front: Why do noble gases have very low melting and boiling points?
cards.back: They are monoatomic with only weak dispersion (London) forces. He has the lowest boiling point of any known substance (about 4.2 K).

cards.front: Why does a noble gas seem larger than the halogen of the same period?
cards.back: For noble gases the van der Waals radius is quoted (no bonds), while halogen values are smaller covalent radii.
cards.hint: Trap: it is a difference in how radius is measured, not a real reversal of the trend.

cards.front: How was the first noble gas compound made?
cards.back: Bartlett made $\mathrm{O_2^+PtF_6^-}$, noticed IE of Xe (about $1170\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$) ≈ IE of $\mathrm{O_2}$, and made $\mathrm{Xe^+PtF_6^-}$ (1962).

cards.front: Which noble gas forms the most compounds, and with which elements?
cards.back: Xenon, mainly with the most electronegative elements F and O. Kr forms few (e.g. $\mathrm{KrF_2}$); He, Ne, Ar form no stable compounds.
cards.hint: Large Xe has the lowest IE of the stable noble gases.

cards.front: Where are d-block elements placed and how many series are there?
cards.back: Groups 3–12, between s- and p-blocks. Four series: 3d (Sc–Zn), 4d (Y–Cd), 5d (La, Hf–Hg), 6d (Ac, Rf–Cn).

cards.front: Define a transition element.
cards.back: An element with an incompletely filled d subshell in its ground state or in any of its common oxidation states.
cards.hint: Definition hinges on the d subshell being partly filled, in the atom or a common ion.

cards.front: Why are Zn, Cd and Hg not regarded as transition metals?
cards.back: They have a full $d^{10}$ configuration both in the ground state and in their common +2 state.
cards.hint: Cu counts: Cu²⁺ is 3d⁹.

cards.front: General electronic configuration of d-block elements?
Configurations of Cr and Cu (3d series exceptions)?
cards.back: • Cr: $[\mathrm{Ar}]3d^5 4s^1$ • Cu: $[\mathrm{Ar}]3d^{10} 4s^1$ Half-filled and fully-filled d subshells are extra stable.

cards.front: Why do transition metals have high melting points?
cards.back: Strong metallic bonding from participation of (n−1)d electrons along with ns electrons. Melting points peak around the middle of the series ($d^5$).
cards.hint: Zn, Cd, Hg (d¹⁰) have low m.p.; Hg is liquid.

cards.front: How do enthalpies of atomisation of 4d and 5d metals compare with 3d metals?
cards.back: Higher for 4d and 5d, giving much more frequent metal–metal bonding in compounds of heavier transition metals.
cards.hint: Metals with very high atomisation enthalpy tend to be noble in reactions.

cards.front: How does atomic radius vary across a 3d series?
cards.back: Decreases from Sc but becomes nearly constant in the middle, as increased nuclear charge is offset by shielding from added d electrons.

cards.front: Why are the atomic radii of Zr and Hf almost identical?
cards.back: Lanthanoid contraction: filling of poorly-shielding 4f orbitals before 5d cancels the expected size increase. (Zr 160 pm, Hf 159 pm)
cards.hint: Hence 4d and 5d members of a group resemble each other closely.

cards.front: How does density change from Ti to Cu?
cards.back: Increases: atomic radius falls while atomic mass rises.

cards.front: Why is the third ionisation enthalpy of Mn very high?
cards.back: $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$ is $3d^5$ (half-filled); removing an electron destroys this stable arrangement.

cards.front: Which 3d metals have unusually high second ionisation enthalpy, and why?
cards.back: Cr and Cu: their $\mathrm{M^+}$ ions are $3d^5$ and $3d^{10}$, which are especially stable.

cards.front: Why do transition metals show variable oxidation states?
cards.back: The (n−1)d and ns orbitals are close in energy, so different numbers of electrons from both can take part in bonding.
cards.hint: Oxidation states usually differ by one unit in transition metals (vs two in p-block).

cards.front: Which 3d element shows the largest number and the highest oxidation state?
cards.back: Mn: +2 to +7 (e.g. $\mathrm{KMnO_4}$). Sc shows only +3 and Zn only +2.

cards.front: Why is the highest oxide of Mn $\mathrm{Mn_2O_7}$ but the highest fluoride only $\mathrm{MnF_4}$?
cards.back: Oxygen can form multiple bonds with the metal, stabilising higher oxidation states more than F can.

cards.front: Why is $\mathrm{Cu^+}$ unstable in aqueous solution?
cards.back: It disproportionates: $\mathrm{2Cu^+ \rightarrow Cu^{2+} + Cu}$, because the much more negative hydration enthalpy of $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ outweighs its second IE.

cards.front: Which 3d metal has a positive $E^\circ(\mathrm{M^{2+}/M})$ and what does it imply?
cards.back: Cu (+0.34 V). It cannot liberate $\mathrm{H_2}$ from dilute non-oxidising acids; its high atomisation + ionisation enthalpy is not balanced by hydration enthalpy.

cards.front: Why is $\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}$ a strong oxidant?
cards.back: $E^\circ(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}/Mn^{2+}})$ is highly positive (+1.57 V) because $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$ is stable $3d^5$, so $\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}$ readily gains an electron.

cards.front: Both $\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}$ are $d^4$. Which is reducing and which oxidising?
cards.back: • $\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}$ is reducing: goes to $\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$ ($t_{2g}^3$, stable) • $\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}$ is oxidising: goes to $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$ ($d^5$, stable)
cards.hint: Each moves toward its more stable configuration.

cards.front: Why is $E^\circ(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}})$ (+0.77 V) much lower than $E^\circ(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}/Mn^{2+}})$ (+1.57 V)?
cards.back: $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$ is $3d^5$ (half-filled, extra stable), so it has less tendency to gain an electron; $\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}$ ($d^4$) readily gains one to become stable $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$ ($d^5$).

cards.front: Formula for spin-only magnetic moment?
cards.back: $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}$ BM, where n = number of unpaired electrons and BM = Bohr magneton.
cards.hint: Check: n = 3 gives √15 ≈ 3.87 BM; n = 5 gives √35 ≈ 5.92 BM.

cards.front: Spin-only moments for n = 1 to 5 unpaired electrons?
Which 3d ion has the highest spin-only magnetic moment among M²⁺ ions?
cards.back: $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$ ($3d^5$, 5 unpaired): $\mu = \sqrt{35} \approx 5.92$ BM. ($\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$ has the same value.)

cards.front: What causes paramagnetism in transition metal ions?
cards.back: Unpaired electrons; each has spin (and orbital) magnetic moment. $d^0$ and $d^{10}$ ions are diamagnetic.

cards.front: Why are most transition metal ions coloured?
cards.back: d–d transitions: an electron absorbs visible light and jumps to a higher d level; the complementary colour is seen. Needs partly-filled d orbitals.

cards.front: Which of these are colourless: $\mathrm{Sc^{3+}, Ti^{3+}, Cu^{+}, Zn^{2+}, Ti^{4+}}$?
cards.back: $\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}$, $\mathrm{Ti^{4+}}$ ($d^0$), $\mathrm{Cu^+}$, $\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}$ ($d^{10}$) are colourless. $\mathrm{Ti^{3+}}$ ($d^1$) is purple.

cards.front: Colours of aqueous $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}, Fe^{2+}, Fe^{3+}, Ni^{2+}, Cu^{2+}}$?
cards.back: • $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$: pink • $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$: green • $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$: yellow • $\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}$: green • $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$: blue

cards.front: Why do transition metals form many complexes?
cards.back: Small, highly charged ions and vacant d orbitals of suitable energy to accept ligand lone pairs.
cards.hint: Small size + high charge + vacant d orbitals.

cards.front: Why are transition metals and their compounds good catalysts?
cards.back: • Variable oxidation states allow easy electron transfer • Surface provides sites to adsorb and bond reactants
cards.hint: e.g. Fe³⁺ catalyses I⁻ + S₂O₈²⁻ by cycling Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺.

cards.front: What are interstitial compounds? Give their key properties.
cards.back: Small atoms (H, C, N, B) trapped in metal lattice voids, e.g. TiC, $\mathrm{Fe_3H}$, $\mathrm{Mn_4N}$. Usually non-stoichiometric, harder, higher m.p. than the metal, retain conductivity, chemically inert.

cards.front: Why do transition metals readily form alloys?
cards.back: Their atomic radii are similar (within about 15%), so atoms substitute in each other's lattice. e.g. brass (Cu–Zn), bronze (Cu–Sn).

cards.front: Ore and first step in preparing $\mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7}$?
cards.back: Chromite $\mathrm{FeCr_2O_4}$ fused with $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$ in air: $\mathrm{4FeCr_2O_4 + 8Na_2CO_3 + 7O_2 \rightarrow 8Na_2CrO_4 + 2Fe_2O_3 + 8CO_2}$

cards.front: How is sodium chromate converted to $\mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7}$?
cards.back: • Acidify: $\mathrm{2Na_2CrO_4 + 2H^+ \rightarrow Na_2Cr_2O_7 + 2Na^+ + H_2O}$ • Add KCl: less soluble $\mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7}$ crystallises out

cards.front: Effect of pH on chromate and dichromate?
cards.back: Interconvertible: acid → orange $\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}$, base → yellow $\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}}$. Cr stays +6 throughout.
cards.hint: Trap: this is NOT a redox change.

cards.front: Structures of chromate and dichromate ions?
cards.back: • $\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}}$: tetrahedral • $\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}$: two tetrahedra sharing one corner, Cr–O–Cr angle about $126^\circ$
cards.hint: Dichromate = two CrO4 tetrahedra joined through one shared O.

cards.front: Half-reaction of acidified dichromate as oxidant?
cards.back: $\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-} + 14H^+ + 6e^- \rightarrow 2Cr^{3+} + 7H_2O}$, $E^\circ = 1.33$ V. Orange → green.

cards.front: What do $\mathrm{I^-}$, $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$, $\mathrm{H_2S}$, $\mathrm{Sn^{2+}}$ give with acidified $\mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7}$?
cards.back:
• $\mathrm{I^- \rightarrow I_2}$ • $\mathrm{Fe^{2+} \rightarrow Fe^{3+}}$
• $\mathrm{H_2S \rightarrow S}$ • $\mathrm{Sn^{2+} \rightarrow Sn^{4+}}$

cards.front: How is $\mathrm{KMnO_4}$ prepared from $\mathrm{MnO_2}$?
cards.back: • Fuse $\mathrm{MnO_2}$ with KOH and an oxidant ($\mathrm{KNO_3}$) → green $\mathrm{K_2MnO_4}$ • Manganate disproportionates in neutral/acidic solution to $\mathrm{MnO_4^-}$ + $\mathrm{MnO_2}$
cards.hint: Commercially, manganate is oxidised electrolytically.

cards.front: Disproportionation of manganate in acid?
cards.back: $\mathrm{3MnO_4^{2-} + 4H^+ \rightarrow 2MnO_4^- + MnO_2 + 2H_2O}$

cards.front: Shape and magnetic nature of manganate vs permanganate?
cards.back: Both tetrahedral. Green $\mathrm{MnO_4^{2-}}$ (Mn +6, $d^1$) is paramagnetic; purple $\mathrm{MnO_4^-}$ (Mn +7, $d^0$) is diamagnetic.

cards.front: Why is $\mathrm{KMnO_4}$ intensely coloured despite Mn being $d^0$?
cards.back: Charge transfer (ligand O to metal) transitions, not d–d transitions.
cards.hint: Trap: d⁰ does not always mean colourless.

cards.front: Reduction of $\mathrm{MnO_4^-}$ in acidic vs neutral/weakly alkaline medium?
cards.back:
• Acidic: $\mathrm{MnO_4^- + 8H^+ + 5e^- \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + 4H_2O}$
• Neutral: $\mathrm{MnO_4^- + 2H_2O + 3e^- \rightarrow MnO_2 + 4OH^-}$
cards.hint: Equivalent mass = M/5 in acid, M/3 in neutral medium.

cards.front: Products of acidified $\mathrm{KMnO_4}$ with oxalate, $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$, $\mathrm{I^-}$ and $\mathrm{NO_2^-}$?
cards.back:
• $\mathrm{C_2O_4^{2-} \rightarrow CO_2}$ (at 333 K) • $\mathrm{Fe^{2+} \rightarrow Fe^{3+}}$
• $\mathrm{I^- \rightarrow I_2}$ • $\mathrm{NO_2^- \rightarrow NO_3^-}$

cards.front: What does iodide give with $\mathrm{KMnO_4}$ in neutral or faintly alkaline solution?
cards.back: Iodate: $\mathrm{I^- \rightarrow IO_3^-}$ (vs $\mathrm{I_2}$ in acid). Thiosulphate gives sulphate.

cards.front: Why is HCl not used to acidify $\mathrm{KMnO_4}$ in titrations?
cards.back: $\mathrm{KMnO_4}$ oxidises HCl to $\mathrm{Cl_2}$, consuming extra oxidant. Dilute $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ is used.

cards.front: General electronic configuration and common oxidation state of lanthanoids?
cards.back: $[\mathrm{Xe}]4f^{1-14}5d^{0-1}6s^2$; most common oxidation state +3.
cards.hint: La³⁺ (4f⁰) and Lu³⁺ (4f¹⁴) are colourless.

cards.front: Define lanthanoid contraction and its cause.
cards.back: Steady decrease in atomic and $\mathrm{Ln^{3+}}$ radii from La to Lu, due to imperfect shielding by 4f electrons of the rising nuclear charge.
cards.hint: Shielding power of orbitals: s > p > d > f (4f shields worst).

cards.front: Consequences of lanthanoid contraction?
cards.back: • 4d and 5d elements of a group have near-identical radii (Zr/Hf) • Lanthanoids are hard to separate • Basicity of $\mathrm{Ln(OH)_3}$ decreases from La to Lu

cards.front: Why is $\mathrm{Ce^{4+}}$ an oxidant while $\mathrm{Eu^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Yb^{2+}}$ are reductants?
cards.back: All tend toward the common +3 state. $\mathrm{Ce^{4+}}$ ($f^0$) gains an electron; $\mathrm{Eu^{2+}}$ ($f^7$) and $\mathrm{Yb^{2+}}$ ($f^{14}$) lose one.
cards.hint: Tb⁴⁺ (f⁷) is also an oxidant.

cards.front: General electronic configuration of actinoids?
cards.back: $[\mathrm{Rn}]5f^{1-14}6d^{0-1}7s^2$. All are radioactive.

cards.front: Why do actinoids show a wider range of oxidation states than lanthanoids?
cards.back: 5f, 6d and 7s levels are comparable in energy, and 5f orbitals are less buried, so more electrons can bond (up to +7 for Np, Pu).

cards.front: State the two types of valence in Werner's theory.
cards.back: • Primary valence: ionisable, equals oxidation state, satisfied by anions • Secondary valence: non-ionisable, equals coordination number, satisfied by ligands

cards.front: Moles of AgCl per mole of $\mathrm{CoCl_3\cdot6NH_3}$, $\mathrm{CoCl_3\cdot5NH_3}$, $\mathrm{CoCl_3\cdot4NH_3}$ (excess $\mathrm{AgNO_3}$)?
cards.back: 3, 2 and 1: $\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]Cl_3}$, $\mathrm{[CoCl(NH_3)_5]Cl_2}$, $\mathrm{[CoCl_2(NH_3)_4]Cl}$
cards.hint: Only Cl⁻ outside the square brackets precipitates.

cards.front: How does a double salt differ from a complex compound in water?
cards.back: A double salt dissociates completely into simple ions (e.g. Mohr's salt, carnallite, potash alum). A complex ion does not: $\mathrm{K_4[Fe(CN)_6]}$ gives no free $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ or $\mathrm{CN^-}$.

cards.front: Define coordination number.
cards.back: Number of ligand donor atoms directly bonded to the central metal atom/ion. e.g. 6 in $\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}$.
cards.hint: Count donor atoms, not ligands: en counts 2.

cards.front: Coordination number of the metal in $\mathrm{[Fe(C_2O_4)_3]^{3-}}$ and $\mathrm{[Co(en)_3]^{3+}}$?
cards.back: 6 in both: oxalate and en are each didentate, and 3 × 2 = 6.

cards.front: What is a ligand? Classify by denticity with examples.
cards.back: Ion/molecule donating electron pair(s) to the metal. • Unidentate: $\mathrm{Cl^-, H_2O, NH_3}$ • Didentate: en, $\mathrm{C_2O_4^{2-}}$ • Hexadentate: $\mathrm{EDTA^{4-}}$

cards.front: Donor atoms in $\mathrm{EDTA^{4-}}$?
cards.back: Two N and four O atoms, making it hexadentate.

cards.front: What is an ambidentate ligand? Give examples.
cards.back: A ligand that can bind through two different donor atoms, but only one at a time: • $\mathrm{NO_2^-}$ (via N: nitrito-N; via O: nitrito-O) • $\mathrm{SCN^-}$ (via S: thiocyanato-S; via N: thiocyanato-N)

cards.front: What is a chelate?
cards.back: A complex in which a di- or polydentate ligand binds one metal through two or more donor atoms, forming a ring. Chelates are more stable than similar unidentate complexes.
cards.hint: Chelate effect: ring formation increases stability.

cards.front: Define homoleptic and heteroleptic complexes.
cards.back: • Homoleptic: only one type of ligand, e.g. $\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}$ • Heteroleptic: more than one type, e.g. $\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_4Cl_2]^+}$
cards.hint: Homo = same: one kind of ligand only.

cards.front: Oxidation number of the metal in $\mathrm{[Cu(CN)_4]^{3-}}$ and $\mathrm{Ni(CO)_4}$?
cards.back: • Cu: x + 4(−1) = −3, so +1 • Ni: CO is neutral, so 0

cards.front: What is the coordination sphere?
cards.back: The central atom and its attached ligands, written inside square brackets; ions outside are counter ions. e.g. in $\mathrm{K_4[Fe(CN)_6]}$, $\mathrm{K^+}$ is the counter ion.

cards.front: Order of naming in a coordination compound?
cards.back: • Cation first, then anion • Inside the entity: ligands first in alphabetical order, then the metal with its oxidation state in Roman numerals
cards.hint: Prefixes di, tri, bis, tris are ignored when alphabetising.

cards.front: IUPAC names of ligands $\mathrm{Cl^-, CN^-, OH^-, H_2O, NH_3, CO, NO}$?
cards.back: • chlorido, cyanido, hydroxido • aqua, ammine, carbonyl, nitrosyl
cards.hint: Anionic ligands end in -o; neutral ones keep special names.

cards.front: When are bis, tris, tetrakis used instead of di, tri, tetra?
cards.back: When the ligand name already contains a numerical prefix or is complex; the name goes in brackets, e.g. tris(ethane-1,2-diamine).

cards.front: How is the metal named in an anionic complex? Give Fe, Cu, Ag, Pb, Sn.
cards.back: Metal name ends in -ate, often using the Latin root: ferrate, cuprate, argentate, plumbate, stannate.

cards.front: IUPAC name of $\mathrm{K_4[Fe(CN)_6]}$?
cards.back: Potassium hexacyanidoferrate(II)

cards.front: IUPAC name of $\mathrm{[CoCl(NH_3)_5]Cl_2}$?
cards.back: Pentaamminechloridocobalt(III) chloride
cards.hint: 'ammine' comes before 'chlorido' alphabetically.

cards.front: IUPAC name of $\mathrm{K_3[Fe(C_2O_4)_3]}$?
cards.back: Potassium trioxalatoferrate(III)

cards.front: IUPAC name of $\mathrm{[Co(en)_3]_2(SO_4)_3}$?
cards.back: Tris(ethane-1,2-diamine)cobalt(III) sulphate

cards.front: IUPAC name of $\mathrm{[Ag(NH_3)_2][Ag(CN)_2]}$?
cards.back: Diamminesilver(I) dicyanidoargentate(I)
cards.hint: Same metal, but -ate only in the anionic entity.

cards.front: IUPAC name of $\mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)_2Cl(NO_2)]}$?
cards.back: Diamminechloridonitrito-N-platinum(II)

cards.front: What is linkage isomerism? Give the classic example.
cards.back: Arises from an ambidentate ligand. $\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5(NO_2)]Cl_2}$: red form is O-bonded (nitrito-O), yellow form is N-bonded (nitrito-N).

cards.front: What is coordination isomerism? Example?
cards.back: Interchange of ligands between cationic and anionic entities of different metals: $\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6][Cr(CN)_6]}$ and $\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_6][Co(CN)_6]}$

cards.front: What is ionisation isomerism? Example?
cards.back: Counter ion itself is a potential ligand and swaps with a ligand, giving different ions in solution: $\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5(SO_4)]Br}$ and $\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5Br]SO_4}$
cards.hint: Test: one gives a precipitate with BaCl₂, the other with AgNO₃.

cards.front: What is solvate (hydrate) isomerism? Example?
cards.back: Differs in whether solvent is a ligand or free molecule: $\mathrm{[Cr(H_2O)_6]Cl_3}$ (violet) vs $\mathrm{[Cr(H_2O)_5Cl]Cl_2\cdot H_2O}$ (grey-green).

cards.front: Which complexes show cis–trans isomerism?
cards.back: • Square planar $\mathrm{MX_2L_2}$, e.g. $\mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)_2Cl_2]}$ • Octahedral $\mathrm{MX_2L_4}$, e.g. $\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_4Cl_2]^+}$
cards.hint: Trap: tetrahedral complexes show NO geometrical isomerism.

cards.front: How many geometrical isomers does square planar $\mathrm{[MABXL]}$ have?
cards.back: Three (e.g. $\mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)(Br)(Cl)(py)]}$).

cards.front: What are fac and mer isomers?
cards.back: Geometrical isomers of octahedral $\mathrm{[Ma_3b_3]}$, e.g. $\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_3(NO_2)_3]}$: • fac: three identical ligands on one face • mer: three identical ligands on a meridian

cards.front: Is $\mathrm{[Co(en)_3]^{3+}}$ optically active?
cards.back: Yes; it exists as a pair of non-superimposable mirror images (d and l enantiomers).

cards.front: Which isomer of $\mathrm{[PtCl_2(en)_2]^{2+}}$ is optically active?
cards.back: Only the cis isomer (it has no plane of symmetry); trans is optically inactive. Total isomers = 3.
cards.hint: Trap: count cis-d, cis-l and trans.

cards.front: Hybridisation and shape for coordination numbers 4, 5 and 6 (VBT)?
cards.back: • 4: $sp^3$ tetrahedral or $dsp^2$ square planar • 5: $sp^3d$ trigonal bipyramidal • 6: $d^2sp^3$ or $sp^3d^2$ octahedral

cards.front: Inner orbital vs outer orbital complex?
cards.back: • Inner orbital (low spin): uses (n−1)d, $d^2sp^3$ • Outer orbital (high spin): uses nd, $sp^3d^2$
cards.hint: Strong-field ligands give inner orbital (low spin) complexes.

cards.front: Hybridisation and magnetism of $\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}$?
cards.back: $\mathrm{Co^{3+}}$ ($3d^6$) pairs up: $d^2sp^3$, octahedral, diamagnetic (inner orbital).
cards.hint: NH₃ acts as a strong field ligand for Co³⁺.

cards.front: Hybridisation and magnetism of $\mathrm{[CoF_6]^{3-}}$?
cards.back: $sp^3d^2$, octahedral, paramagnetic with 4 unpaired electrons (outer orbital, high spin).
cards.hint: F⁻ is a weak field ligand: no pairing.

cards.front: Compare $\mathrm{[NiCl_4]^{2-}}$ and $\mathrm{[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}}$.
cards.back: • $\mathrm{[NiCl_4]^{2-}}$: $sp^3$, tetrahedral, paramagnetic (2 unpaired) • $\mathrm{[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}}$: $dsp^2$, square planar, diamagnetic

cards.front: Hybridisation, shape and magnetism of $\mathrm{Ni(CO)_4}$?
cards.back: Ni(0), $3d^{10}$: $sp^3$, tetrahedral, diamagnetic.

cards.front: Number of unpaired electrons in $\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}}$?
cards.back: One. $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$ ($3d^5$) pairs up under strong-field $\mathrm{CN^-}$: $d^2sp^3$, $\mu \approx 1.73$ BM.

cards.front: Limitations of valence bond theory?
cards.back: • No explanation of colour • No quantitative magnetic data or thermodynamic/kinetic stability • Cannot distinguish weak vs strong ligands • Cannot predict tetrahedral vs square planar for CN 4

cards.front: Basic assumption of crystal field theory?
cards.back: Metal–ligand bond is purely ionic; ligands are point charges (or dipoles) that lift the degeneracy of metal d orbitals.

cards.front: How do d orbitals split in an octahedral field?
cards.back: • $e_g$ ($d_{x^2-y^2}, d_{z^2}$): raised, point at ligands • $t_{2g}$ ($d_{xy}, d_{yz}, d_{xz}$): lowered Gap = $\Delta_o$
cards.hint: e_g lobes point along the axes, straight at the ligands.

cards.front: Energy shifts of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ relative to the barycentre (octahedral)?
cards.back: $t_{2g}$: $-0.4\Delta_o$ each; $e_g$: $+0.6\Delta_o$ each.

cards.front: Spectrochemical series (weak to strong field)?
cards.back: $\mathrm{I^- < Br^- < SCN^- < Cl^- < S^{2-} < F^- < OH^- < C_2O_4^{2-} < H_2O}$ $\mathrm{< NCS^- < edta^{4-} < NH_3 < en < CN^- < CO}$
cards.hint: Ends: halides weakest, CN⁻ and CO strongest.

cards.front: $d^4$ ion: configuration when $\Delta_o < P$ vs $\Delta_o > P$ (P = pairing energy)?
cards.back: • $\Delta_o < P$ (weak field): $t_{2g}^3e_g^1$, high spin • $\Delta_o > P$ (strong field): $t_{2g}^4e_g^0$, low spin

cards.front: How do d orbitals split in a tetrahedral field and how big is $\Delta_t$?
cards.back: Order is inverted: $t_2$ higher, $e$ lower. $\Delta_t = \dfrac{4}{9}\Delta_o$, so low-spin tetrahedral complexes are rarely seen.

cards.front: Why is $\mathrm{[Ti(H_2O)_6]^{3+}}$ violet?
cards.back: $d^1$: the electron absorbs visible (blue-green) light for the $t_{2g} \rightarrow e_g$ (d–d) transition; the transmitted complementary colour looks violet.

cards.front: Why is anhydrous $\mathrm{CuSO_4}$ white but $\mathrm{CuSO_4\cdot5H_2O}$ blue?
cards.back: Without water ligands there is no crystal field splitting, so no d–d transition. Water ligands split the d orbitals.

cards.front: Colour change of $\mathrm{[Ni(H_2O)_6]^{2+}}$ on adding en?
cards.back: Green → violet $\mathrm{[Ni(en)_3]^{2+}}$: stronger-field en raises $\Delta_o$, so shorter wavelength light is absorbed.

cards.front: Limitations of crystal field theory?
cards.back: • Treats ligands as point charges, yet anionic ligands are weak-field (should be strongest) • Ignores covalent character of metal–ligand bonds

cards.front: Test for $\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}$ in qualitative analysis?
cards.back: Dimethylglyoxime in ammoniacal solution gives a red precipitate.

cards.front: Role of complexes in extraction and purification of metals?
cards.back: • Au/Ag extracted as cyanide complexes, e.g. $\mathrm{[Au(CN)_2]^-}$, then reduced by Zn • Ni purified via volatile $\mathrm{Ni(CO)_4}$ (Mond process)

cards.front: Metal in chlorophyll, haemoglobin and vitamin $\mathrm{B_{12}}$?
cards.back: • Chlorophyll: Mg • Haemoglobin: Fe • Vitamin $\mathrm{B_{12}}$ (cyanocobalamin): Co
cards.hint: Mg-Fe-Co: plants, blood, vitamin.

cards.front: How are monohalo compounds with an $sp^3$ C–X bond classified?
cards.back: • Alkyl halides (1°, 2°, 3°) • Allylic halides: X on $sp^3$ C next to C=C • Benzylic halides: X on $sp^3$ C attached to an aromatic ring

cards.front: Which compounds have an $sp^2$ C–X bond?
cards.back: • Vinylic halides: X on a C=C carbon, e.g. CH2=CH–Cl • Aryl halides: X directly on the aromatic ring, e.g. C6H5Cl
cards.hint: Trap: CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–CH<sub>2</sub>Cl is allylic, not vinylic.

cards.front: IUPAC name of (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCl?
cards.back: 2-Chloropropane (common name: isopropyl chloride)

cards.front: IUPAC name of (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CBr?
cards.back: 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane (common name: tert-butyl bromide)

cards.front: Geminal vs vicinal dihalides: what is the difference?
cards.back: • Gem: both X on the same C, e.g. CH3CHCl2 (1,1-dichloroethane, ethylidene chloride) • Vic: X on adjacent C, e.g. ClCH2CH2Cl (1,2-dichloroethane, ethylene dichloride)
cards.hint: Gem = 'twins' on one carbon; vic = 'neighbours'.

cards.front: Why is the C–X bond polar?
cards.back: Halogen is more electronegative than carbon, so C carries $\delta^+$ and X carries $\delta^-$.

cards.front: Trend of C–X bond length and bond enthalpy from C–F to C–I?
cards.back: • Bond length: C–F < C–Cl < C–Br < C–I • Bond enthalpy: C–F > C–Cl > C–Br > C–I (size of X increases)

cards.front: Order of dipole moments of CH<sub>3</sub>F, CH<sub>3</sub>Cl, CH<sub>3</sub>Br, CH<sub>3</sub>I?
cards.back: CH3Cl > CH3F > CH3Br > CH3I CH3F has larger charge separation but a much shorter bond, so its dipole is slightly less than CH3Cl.
cards.hint: Trap: CH<sub>3</sub>F is not the highest despite F being most electronegative.

cards.front: Best reagent to convert an alcohol into an alkyl chloride, and why?
cards.back: Thionyl chloride, SOCl2 $\text{ROH} + \text{SOCl}_2 \rightarrow \text{RCl} + \text{SO}_2 + \text{HCl}$ Both by-products are gases and escape, leaving pure RCl.

cards.front: Reagent for alcohol → alkyl chloride using HCl, and reactivity order of alcohols?
cards.back: • Dry HCl with anhydrous ZnCl2 (for 1° and 2°); 3° alcohols react with conc. HCl at room temperature • Reactivity: 3° > 2° > 1°

cards.front: Products when an alcohol reacts with PCl<sub>3</sub> and with PCl<sub>5</sub>?
cards.back:
• $3\text{ROH} + \text{PCl}_3 \rightarrow 3\text{RCl} + \text{H}_3\text{PO}_3$
• $\text{ROH} + \text{PCl}_5 \rightarrow \text{RCl} + \text{POCl}_3 + \text{HCl}$
cards.hint: PCl<sub>3</sub> gives phosphorous acid; PCl<sub>5</sub> gives POCl<sub>3</sub>.

cards.front: Why can these alcohol methods not make aryl halides from phenol?
cards.back: The C–O bond in phenol has partial double bond character (resonance), so it is hard to break.

cards.front: Why is free-radical halogenation of alkanes a poor method for haloalkanes?
cards.back: It gives a mixture of isomeric mono- and polyhalo products that is hard to separate, e.g. butane + Cl2 gives 1- and 2-chlorobutane.

cards.front: Addition of HBr to propene gives which major product?
cards.back: 2-Bromopropane (Markovnikov addition: Br goes to the carbon with fewer H atoms).

cards.front: State the Finkelstein reaction.
cards.back: $\text{R–X} + \text{NaI} \rightarrow \text{R–I} + \text{NaX}$ (X = Cl, Br) in dry acetone NaCl/NaBr precipitate in acetone, driving the reaction forward.
cards.hint: Le Chatelier: removing NaX shifts the equilibrium to R–I.

cards.front: State the Swarts reaction.
cards.back: Alkyl chloride/bromide heated with a metallic fluoride such as AgF, Hg2F2, CoF2 or SbF3 gives an alkyl fluoride.
cards.hint: Swarts makes fluorides; Finkelstein makes iodides.

cards.front: Aryl chloride by electrophilic substitution: reagents and products from toluene?
cards.back: Cl2 with Lewis acid (Fe or FeCl3) in the dark gives o- and p-chlorotoluene.

cards.front: Why does direct iodination of benzene need an oxidising agent like HNO<sub>3</sub> or HIO<sub>4</sub>?
cards.back: Iodination is reversible; the oxidising agent removes the HI formed, pushing the reaction forward.
cards.hint: Fluorination is the opposite problem: far too reactive to control.

cards.front: What is the Sandmeyer reaction?
cards.back: Benzene diazonium salt + Cu2Cl2/HCl or Cu2Br2/HBr $\rightarrow$ chlorobenzene or bromobenzene + N2

cards.front: How is iodobenzene made from a diazonium salt?
cards.back: Shake the diazonium salt solution with KI; no cuprous salt is needed.

cards.front: Boiling point order of RF, RCl, RBr, RI (same R)?
cards.back: RI > RBr > RCl > RF Larger, more polarisable halogen gives stronger van der Waals forces.

cards.front: Order of boiling points of isomeric bromobutanes?
cards.back: 1-Bromobutane > 2-bromobutane > 2-bromo-2-methylpropane More branching gives smaller surface area, so weaker forces.

cards.front: Which dichlorobenzene isomer has the highest melting point, and why?
cards.back: p-Dichlorobenzene; its symmetry lets it fit better in the crystal lattice. Boiling points of the three isomers are nearly the same.
cards.hint: Para = symmetric = packs best = highest m.p.

cards.front: Why are haloalkanes only slightly soluble in water?
cards.back: Energy released by new haloalkane–water attractions is less than the energy needed to break water's H-bonds. They dissolve well in organic solvents.

cards.front: Product of R–X with KCN vs AgCN?
cards.back: • KCN $\rightarrow$ alkyl cyanide R–CN (ionic; C attacks, C–C bond is stronger) • AgCN $\rightarrow$ isocyanide R–NC (covalent; N lone pair attacks)
cards.hint: CN<sup>−</sup> is an ambident nucleophile.

cards.front: Product of R–X with KNO<sub>2</sub> vs AgNO<sub>2</sub>?
cards.back: • KNO2 $\rightarrow$ alkyl nitrite R–O–N=O • AgNO2 $\rightarrow$ nitroalkane R–NO2
cards.hint: Silver salts (covalent) attack through N: AgCN gives –NC, AgNO<sub>2</sub> gives –NO<sub>2</sub>.

cards.front: Key features of the S<sub>N</sub>2 mechanism?
cards.back: • One step; rate $= k[\text{RX}][\text{Nu}^-]$ (second order) • Nucleophile attacks from the back side, 180° to X • Gives inversion of configuration

cards.front: Order of reactivity of alkyl halides in S<sub>N</sub>2?
cards.back: CH3X > 1° > 2° > 3° Bulky groups hinder back-side attack (steric hindrance).
cards.hint: S<sub>N</sub>2 hates crowding.

cards.front: Key features of the S<sub>N</sub>1 mechanism?
cards.back: • Two steps; rate $= k[\text{RX}]$ (first order) • Slow step: C–X ionises to a carbocation • Favoured by polar protic solvents (water, alcohol, acetic acid)

cards.front: Order of reactivity of alkyl halides in S<sub>N</sub>1?
cards.back: 3° > 2° > 1° > CH3X (carbocation stability). Allylic and benzylic halides are also very reactive: their carbocations are resonance-stabilised.
cards.hint: S<sub>N</sub>1 order is the reverse of S<sub>N</sub>2.

cards.front: For the same alkyl group, order of reactivity of halides in S<sub>N</sub>1 and S<sub>N</sub>2?
cards.back: R–I > R–Br > R–Cl > R–F (weaker C–X bond breaks more easily).

cards.front: Which is chiral: 1-chlorobutane or 2-chlorobutane?
cards.back: 2-Chlorobutane: C-2 carries four different groups (H, Cl, CH3, C2H5).
cards.hint: Look for a carbon with four different groups.

cards.front: What is a racemic mixture?
cards.back: An equimolar mixture of two enantiomers; optical rotation is zero (external compensation). Written as dl or (±).

cards.front: Stereochemical result of S<sub>N</sub>2 on an optically active halide?
cards.back: Inversion of configuration: the product has the opposite spatial arrangement at the stereocentre.

cards.front: Stereochemical result of S<sub>N</sub>1 on an optically active halide, and why?
cards.back: Racemisation: the planar carbocation is attacked from both faces, giving both enantiomers.

cards.front: What is meant by retention of configuration?
cards.back: The spatial arrangement of bonds at the stereocentre is the same in reactant and product (e.g. when no bond to the stereocentre is broken).

cards.front: Effect of aqueous KOH vs alcoholic KOH on a haloalkane?
cards.back: • Aqueous KOH: substitution $\rightarrow$ alcohol • Alcoholic KOH: elimination $\rightarrow$ alkene (dehydrohalogenation)
cards.hint: Alc. KOH gives alkene.

cards.front: State Saytzeff (Zaitsev) rule with an example.
cards.back: In dehydrohalogenation the more substituted alkene (more alkyl groups on C=C) is the major product. 2-Bromopentane + alc. KOH $\rightarrow$ pent-2-ene (major) + pent-1-ene

cards.front: Which type of alkyl halide favours elimination over substitution with a strong bulky base?
cards.back: Tertiary halides (and bulky bases) favour elimination; primary halides with a small nucleophile favour SN2.

cards.front: How is a Grignard reagent made, and why must water be excluded?
cards.back: $\text{RX} + \text{Mg} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \text{RMgX}$ It reacts with any proton source: $\text{RMgX} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow$ RH + Mg(OH)X
cards.hint: C–Mg bond is covalent but highly polar; carbon acts as a carbanion.

cards.front: State the Wurtz reaction.
cards.back: $2\text{RX} + 2\text{Na} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \text{R–R} + 2\text{NaX}$ Gives an alkane with double the carbons.

cards.front: Why are aryl halides much less reactive than alkyl halides towards nucleophilic substitution?
cards.back: • Resonance: C–X gets partial double bond character • C is $sp^2$: shorter, stronger bond • Phenyl cation is unstable • Electron-rich ring repels the nucleophile

cards.front: How is chlorobenzene converted to phenol industrially (Dow process)?
cards.back: Heat with aqueous NaOH at 623 K and 300 atm to get sodium phenoxide, then acidify $\rightarrow$ phenol.
cards.hint: Harsh conditions show how unreactive Ar–Cl is.

cards.front: Effect of –NO<sub>2</sub> groups at ortho/para on nucleophilic substitution in chlorobenzene?
cards.back: Increase reactivity: they withdraw electrons and stabilise the carbanion intermediate. 2,4,6-Trinitrochlorobenzene hydrolyses with just warm water.
cards.hint: Trap: meta-NO<sub>2</sub> gives no such resonance help.

cards.front: Is the halogen in haloarenes activating or deactivating for electrophilic substitution? Directing effect?
cards.back: Deactivating (–I effect dominates) but ortho/para directing (+R effect).
cards.hint: Halogens are the classic exception: deactivating yet o/p-directing.

cards.front: Products of chlorobenzene + Cl<sub>2</sub> / anhydrous FeCl<sub>3</sub>?
cards.back: 1,2-Dichlorobenzene (minor) and 1,4-dichlorobenzene (major).

cards.front: Products of nitration of chlorobenzene (conc. HNO<sub>3</sub> + conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>)?
cards.back: 1-Chloro-2-nitrobenzene (minor) + 1-chloro-4-nitrobenzene (major).

cards.front: Products of Friedel–Crafts alkylation and acylation of chlorobenzene?
cards.back: • CH3Cl / anhyd. AlCl3 $\rightarrow$ 2- and 4-chlorotoluene • CH3COCl / anhyd. AlCl3 $\rightarrow$ 2- and 4-chloroacetophenone Para isomer is major.

cards.front: What are the Wurtz–Fittig and Fittig reactions?
cards.back: • Wurtz–Fittig: ArX + RX + Na (dry ether) $\rightarrow$ Ar–R (e.g. toluene) • Fittig: 2ArX + 2Na $\rightarrow$ Ar–Ar (e.g. biphenyl)

cards.front: Uses and hazards of dichloromethane (CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>)?
cards.back: • Uses: solvent (paint remover, drug manufacture, metal cleaning), aerosol propellant • Harms the central nervous system; causes dizziness, nausea; burns skin and eyes

cards.front: Why is chloroform stored in closed, dark bottles filled to the brim?
cards.back: In air and light it oxidises to poisonous phosgene: $2\text{CHCl}_3 + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{COCl}_2 + 2\text{HCl}$

cards.front: Why does iodoform act as an antiseptic?
cards.back: Due to liberation of free iodine, not iodoform itself. It has been replaced because of its objectionable smell.
cards.hint: Trap: the antiseptic is I<sub>2</sub>, not CHI<sub>3</sub>.

cards.front: Uses and environmental effect of carbon tetrachloride?
cards.back: Used to make refrigerants and aerosol propellants (CFC feedstock). Released into air, it reaches the upper atmosphere and depletes the ozone layer.

cards.front: What are freons, and why are they harmful?
cards.back: Chlorofluorocarbons (e.g. Freon-12 = CCl2F2) used in refrigeration and AC. In the stratosphere they release Cl radicals that destroy ozone.

cards.front: Key facts about DDT?
cards.back: • p,p'-Dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane, first chlorinated insecticide (Nobel to Paul Müller, 1948) • Not metabolised quickly; stored in fatty tissue; banned in the USA in 1973

cards.front: How are monohydric alcohols classified by the carbon bearing –OH?
cards.back: • $sp^3$ C–OH: 1°, 2°, 3°, allylic and benzylic alcohols • $sp^2$ C–OH: vinylic alcohols and phenols (OH on an aromatic ring)

cards.front: IUPAC names of glycerol and ethylene glycol?
cards.back: • Glycerol: propane-1,2,3-triol • Ethylene glycol: ethane-1,2-diol

cards.front: Common names of benzene-1,2-diol, benzene-1,3-diol and benzene-1,4-diol?
cards.back: • 1,2: catechol • 1,3: resorcinol • 1,4: hydroquinone (quinol)
cards.hint: C-R-H in order 1,2 / 1,3 / 1,4: Catechol, Resorcinol, Hydroquinone.

cards.front: IUPAC names of anisole and phenetole?
cards.back: • Anisole C6H5OCH3: methoxybenzene • Phenetole C6H5OC2H5: ethoxybenzene

cards.front: C–O–H bond angle in methanol and C–O–C angle in methoxymethane?
cards.back: • Methanol C–O–H: 108.9° (less than tetrahedral: lone pair repulsion) • Methoxymethane C–O–C: 111.7° (more: repulsion between bulky alkyl groups)

cards.front: Why is the C–O bond in phenol (136 pm) shorter than in methanol (142 pm)?
cards.back: • Partial double bond character: O lone pair conjugates with the ring • The carbon bearing –OH is $sp^2$ hybridised

cards.front: Product and rule for acid-catalysed hydration of propene?
cards.back: Propan-2-ol (Markovnikov addition). Steps: protonation to a carbocation, attack by water, loss of H+.

cards.front: What does hydroboration–oxidation of propene give?
cards.back: B2H6, then H2O2 / OH− $\rightarrow$ propan-1-ol Net addition of water is anti-Markovnikov.
cards.hint: Hydroboration puts –OH on the less substituted carbon.

cards.front: Reduction of aldehydes and ketones (H<sub>2</sub>/Pd, NaBH<sub>4</sub> or LiAlH<sub>4</sub>) gives what?
cards.back: • Aldehydes $\rightarrow$ 1° alcohols • Ketones $\rightarrow$ 2° alcohols

cards.front: How are carboxylic acids reduced to alcohols in the lab and commercially?
cards.back: • Lab: LiAlH4 gives 1° alcohol directly • Commercially: acid $\rightarrow$ ester, then catalytic hydrogenation (H2/catalyst); LiAlH4 is too expensive

cards.front: Which alcohol does a Grignard reagent give with HCHO, other aldehydes and ketones?
cards.back: • HCHO $\rightarrow$ 1° alcohol • Other aldehydes $\rightarrow$ 2° alcohol • Ketones $\rightarrow$ 3° alcohol (after hydrolysis)

cards.front: Product of CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr with acetone, followed by hydrolysis?
cards.back: 2-Methylpropan-2-ol (tert-butyl alcohol), a 3° alcohol.

cards.front: How is phenol made from benzenesulphonic acid?
cards.back: Fuse with molten NaOH to get sodium phenoxide, then acidify $\rightarrow$ phenol.

cards.front: How is phenol made from aniline via a diazonium salt?
cards.back: Aniline + NaNO2/HCl at 273–278 K $\rightarrow$ benzene diazonium chloride; warm with water (or dil. acid) $\rightarrow$ phenol + N2

cards.front: Cumene process: what are the products?
cards.back: Cumene is air-oxidised to cumene hydroperoxide; dilute acid then gives phenol + acetone (useful by-product).
cards.hint: Cumene = isopropylbenzene.

cards.front: Why do alcohols and phenols boil higher than ethers or hydrocarbons of similar mass?
cards.back: Intermolecular hydrogen bonding through the –OH group.

cards.front: Effect of chain length and branching on boiling points of alcohols?
cards.back: • B.p. rises with more carbon atoms (stronger van der Waals) • B.p. falls with branching (smaller surface area)

cards.front: Why does water solubility of alcohols fall as the alkyl group grows?
cards.back: The larger hydrophobic alkyl part outweighs H-bonding of –OH with water. Lower alcohols are miscible.

cards.front: Ethanol (b.p. 351 K) vs methoxymethane (b.p. 248 K): same formula, why the gap?
cards.back: Ethanol forms intermolecular H-bonds; methoxymethane has no O–H, so it cannot.
cards.hint: Both are C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O: functional isomers.

cards.front: How do alcohols react with Na, and what is the acidity order of alcohols?
cards.back: $2\text{ROH} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow 2\text{RONa} + \text{H}_2$ Acidity: 1° > 2° > 3° (+I effect of alkyl groups makes O–H less polar).

cards.front: Are alcohols stronger or weaker acids than water?
cards.back: Weaker. Alkoxide is a stronger base than OH−: $\text{RO}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{ROH} + \text{OH}^-$
cards.hint: Alcohols act as Brønsted acids and also as bases (O lone pairs).

cards.front: Conditions for esterification of an alcohol with a carboxylic acid?
cards.back: Conc. H2SO4 catalyst; reaction is reversible, so water is removed as formed. $\text{ROH} + \text{R'COOH} \rightleftharpoons \text{R'COOR} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$

cards.front: Why is pyridine added in acylation of alcohols with acid chlorides?
cards.back: Pyridine is a base that neutralises the HCl formed, shifting the equilibrium to the right.

cards.front: How is aspirin made?
cards.back: Acetylation of salicylic acid (with acetic anhydride) $\rightarrow$ acetylsalicylic acid.

cards.front: Lucas test: reagent and observations for 1°, 2°, 3° alcohols?
cards.back: Reagent: conc. HCl + anhydrous ZnCl2 • 3°: turbidity immediately • 2°: turbidity in about 5 min • 1°: no turbidity at room temperature
cards.hint: Turbidity = insoluble alkyl chloride forming.

cards.front: Dehydration conditions for 1°, 2° and 3° alcohols?
cards.back: • Ethanol: conc. H2SO4, 443 K • 2°: 85% H3PO4, 440 K • 3°: 20% H3PO4, 358 K Ease: 3° > 2° > 1°
cards.hint: Milder conditions for 3° because its carbocation is most stable.

cards.front: Mechanism of acid dehydration of ethanol: which step is slow?
cards.back: 1. Protonation of –OH (fast) 2. Loss of water to form the carbocation (slow, rate-determining) 3. Loss of H+ to give ethene

cards.front: Reagent to oxidise a 1° alcohol only to the aldehyde?
cards.back: PCC (pyridinium chlorochromate) or CrO3 in anhydrous medium. Acidified KMnO4 goes on to the carboxylic acid.

cards.front: Oxidation behaviour of 2° and 3° alcohols?
cards.back: • 2° $\rightarrow$ ketone (e.g. chromic anhydride, CrO3) • 3° resist oxidation; strong agents (KMnO4) at high temperature give acids with fewer C atoms

cards.front: Products when 1°, 2°, 3° alcohol vapours pass over heated Cu at 573 K?
cards.back: • 1° $\rightarrow$ aldehyde • 2° $\rightarrow$ ketone (dehydrogenation) • 3° $\rightarrow$ alkene (dehydration)
cards.hint: Trap: 3° alcohols lose water, not H<sub>2</sub>.

cards.front: Why is phenol more acidic than ethanol?
cards.back: Phenoxide ion is resonance-stabilised: negative charge spreads into the ring. Alkoxide has no such delocalisation. Phenol reacts with NaOH; ethanol does not.
cards.hint: Trap: phenol is too weak to release CO<sub>2</sub> from NaHCO<sub>3</sub>.

cards.front: pK<sub>a</sub> of ethanol, phenol and picric acid (NCERT)?
cards.back: • Ethanol: 15.9 • Phenol: 10.0 • 2,4,6-Trinitrophenol: 0.71
cards.hint: Lower pK<sub>a</sub> = stronger acid.

cards.front: Effect of –NO<sub>2</sub> and –CH<sub>3</sub> groups on acidity of phenol?
cards.back: • EWG (–NO2) at o/p: increases acidity • EDG (–CH3): decreases acidity e.g. p-nitrophenol > phenol > p-cresol

cards.front: Acidity order of o-, m- and p-nitrophenol?
cards.back: p-nitrophenol (7.1) > o-nitrophenol (7.2) > m-nitrophenol (8.3) > phenol (10.0) [pKa values]
cards.hint: Meta-NO<sub>2</sub> acts only by –I, no resonance withdrawal.

cards.front: How does the –OH group affect electrophilic substitution of the benzene ring?
cards.back: Activating and ortho/para directing: O lone pair raises electron density at o and p positions (+R).

cards.front: Products of phenol + dilute HNO<sub>3</sub> at 298 K, and how are they separated?
cards.back: o- and p-nitrophenol. Separated by steam distillation: o-isomer is steam volatile (intramolecular H-bond); p-isomer is not (intermolecular H-bond).

cards.front: Product of phenol with conc. HNO<sub>3</sub>?
cards.back: 2,4,6-Trinitrophenol (picric acid), in poor yield.

cards.front: Phenol + bromine water vs Br<sub>2</sub> in CS<sub>2</sub> at low temperature?
cards.back: • Bromine water: 2,4,6-tribromophenol, white precipitate • Br2 in CS2/CHCl3, low T: o- and p-bromophenol (mono)
cards.hint: Polar solvent ionises phenol more, so ring gets fully brominated.

cards.front: State Kolbe's reaction.
cards.back: Sodium phenoxide + CO2, then acid $\rightarrow$ salicylic acid (2-hydroxybenzoic acid). Phenoxide is more reactive than phenol toward the weak electrophile CO2.
cards.hint: Salicylic acid is the starting material for aspirin.

cards.front: State the Reimer–Tiemann reaction.
cards.back: Phenol + CHCl3 + aq. NaOH, then acid $\rightarrow$ salicylaldehyde (–CHO at ortho). Intermediate: substituted benzal chloride.
cards.hint: Reimer–Tiemann gives aldehyde; Kolbe gives acid.

cards.front: What does phenol give on heating with zinc dust?
cards.back: Benzene (zinc dust removes the –OH).

cards.front: Product of oxidation of phenol with chromic acid?
cards.back: Benzoquinone (a conjugated diketone). Phenols slowly darken in air due to quinone formation.

cards.front: What is the Williamson ether synthesis?
cards.back: $\text{R–X} + \text{R'–O}^-\text{Na}^+ \rightarrow \text{R–O–R'} + \text{NaX}$ An SN2 reaction; works best with primary alkyl halides.
cards.hint: A 3° halide with alkoxide gives alkene, not ether.

cards.front: Correct reactants to make tert-butyl methyl ether by Williamson synthesis?
cards.back: Sodium tert-butoxide + CH3Br. Using (CH3)3CBr + CH3ONa gives 2-methylpropene by elimination instead.
cards.hint: Trap: put the 3° group on the alkoxide, never on the halide.

cards.front: How is anisole made by Williamson synthesis?
cards.back: Sodium phenoxide + CH3Br (or CH3I). Aryl halides cannot be used: they resist nucleophilic substitution.

cards.front: Ethanol + conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> at 413 K vs 443 K?
cards.back: • 413 K: ethoxyethane (diethyl ether), SN2 on protonated alcohol • 443 K: ethene Method suits only 1° alcohols.
cards.hint: Lower temperature favours ether, higher favours alkene.

cards.front: How do boiling point and water solubility of ethers compare with alcohols?
cards.back: • B.p. much lower than isomeric alcohols, close to alkanes (no H-bonding between ether molecules) • Solubility similar to alcohols of same mass (ether O H-bonds with water)

cards.front: Cleavage of a methyl alkyl ether (1° or 2° alkyl) by HI: which halide forms?
cards.back: Methyl iodide + the other alcohol: I− attacks the smaller alkyl group (SN2). Reactivity: HI > HBr > HCl.

cards.front: Products of (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C–O–CH<sub>3</sub> with HI?
cards.back: (CH3)3C–I + CH3OH. Cleavage goes by SN1 via the stable tert-butyl carbocation.
cards.hint: Trap: with a 3° group the halide forms on the 3° carbon.

cards.front: Products of anisole with HI?
cards.back: Phenol + CH3I. The O–aryl bond has partial double bond character, so iodobenzene is not formed.

cards.front: Bromination of anisole: conditions and major product?
cards.back: Br2 in ethanoic acid, even without FeBr3 (–OCH3 activates the ring) $\rightarrow$ p-bromoanisole (major) + o-isomer.

cards.front: Products of Friedel–Crafts acylation and nitration of anisole?
cards.back: • CH3COCl/AlCl3 $\rightarrow$ 2- and 4-methoxyacetophenone • Conc. HNO3/H2SO4 $\rightarrow$ 2- and 4-nitroanisole Para isomer is major.

cards.front: Common and IUPAC names of HCHO, CH<sub>3</sub>CHO and CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub>?
cards.back: • HCHO: formaldehyde, methanal • CH3CHO: acetaldehyde, ethanal • CH3COCH3: acetone, propanone

cards.front: IUPAC names of acetophenone and benzophenone?
cards.back: • C6H5COCH3: 1-phenylethanone • C6H5COC6H5: diphenylmethanone

cards.front: Hybridisation and geometry of the carbonyl carbon?
cards.back: $sp^2$, trigonal planar, bond angles about 120°. C is electrophilic ($\delta^+$); O is nucleophilic ($\delta^-$, Lewis base).

cards.front: How are aldehydes and ketones made from alkenes by ozonolysis?
cards.back: Alkene + O3, then Zn dust / H2O $\rightarrow$ aldehydes and/or ketones (C=C is cleaved).

cards.front: Product of hydration of ethyne vs propyne (H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + HgSO<sub>4</sub>)?
cards.back: • Ethyne $\rightarrow$ ethanal • Propyne (and other alkynes) $\rightarrow$ ketones (propanone)
cards.hint: Only ethyne gives an aldehyde.

cards.front: State the Rosenmund reduction.
cards.back: $\text{RCOCl} + \text{H}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Pd–BaSO}_4} \text{RCHO} + \text{HCl}$ Catalyst is poisoned Pd on BaSO4 so the aldehyde is not reduced further.

cards.front: State the Stephen reaction.
cards.back: Nitrile + SnCl2 / HCl $\rightarrow$ imine, then hydrolysis $\rightarrow$ aldehyde.
cards.hint: Stephen starts from a nitrile; Rosenmund from an acid chloride.

cards.front: Which reagent reduces nitriles and esters to aldehydes?
cards.back: DIBAL-H (diisobutylaluminium hydride), followed by hydrolysis.

cards.front: State the Etard reaction.
cards.back: Toluene + chromyl chloride (CrO2Cl2) in CS2 $\rightarrow$ chromium complex $\rightarrow$ hydrolysis $\rightarrow$ benzaldehyde
cards.hint: Chromyl chloride stops oxidation of –CH<sub>3</sub> at the aldehyde stage.

cards.front: Toluene to benzaldehyde using CrO<sub>3</sub>: reagent and intermediate?
cards.back: CrO3 in acetic anhydride gives benzylidene diacetate, which is hydrolysed by aqueous acid to benzaldehyde.

cards.front: How is benzaldehyde made by side-chain chlorination of toluene?
cards.back: Toluene + Cl2 / hν $\rightarrow$ benzal chloride (C6H5CHCl2) $\rightarrow$ hydrolysis at 373 K $\rightarrow$ benzaldehyde

cards.front: State the Gatterman–Koch reaction.
cards.back: Benzene + CO + HCl, anhydrous AlCl3 or CuCl $\rightarrow$ benzaldehyde

cards.front: How are ketones made from acyl chlorides using dialkylcadmium?
cards.back: $2\text{R'COCl} + \text{R}_2\text{Cd} \rightarrow 2\text{R'COR} + \text{CdCl}_2$ R2Cd comes from Grignard reagent + CdCl2.

cards.front: Product of a nitrile with a Grignard reagent, then hydrolysis?
cards.back: A ketone, e.g. CH3CH2CN + C6H5MgBr $\rightarrow$ propiophenone (1-phenylpropan-1-one)

cards.front: How are aromatic ketones made from benzene?
cards.back: Friedel–Crafts acylation: benzene + RCOCl (or anhydride), anhydrous AlCl3 $\rightarrow$ aryl ketone C6H5COR

cards.front: Boiling points of aldehydes/ketones vs alcohols and ethers of similar mass?
cards.back: Alcohols > aldehydes/ketones > ethers ≈ hydrocarbons. Carbonyls have dipole–dipole attraction but no intermolecular H-bonding.

cards.front: Why are methanal, ethanal and propanone miscible with water?
cards.back: They form hydrogen bonds with water. Solubility falls rapidly as the alkyl chain grows.

cards.front: Why are aldehydes more reactive than ketones in nucleophilic addition?
cards.back: • Steric: two alkyl groups crowd the ketone carbon • Electronic: two +I alkyl groups make ketone carbon less electrophilic

cards.front: Describe the mechanism of nucleophilic addition to C=O.
cards.back: Nucleophile attacks the $sp^2$ carbon perpendicular to the plane $\rightarrow$ tetrahedral alkoxide ($sp^3$) $\rightarrow$ takes H+ to give the product.

cards.front: Why is benzaldehyde less reactive than propanal in nucleophilic addition?
cards.back: Resonance with the ring donates electron density to C=O, making the carbonyl carbon less electrophilic.

cards.front: Addition of HCN to aldehydes/ketones: catalyst and product?
cards.back: Base catalyst (generates CN−, the stronger nucleophile) $\rightarrow$ cyanohydrin

cards.front: How is NaHSO<sub>3</sub> addition used to purify aldehydes?
cards.back: Forms a crystalline bisulphite adduct; it is reversed by dilute acid or alkali to regenerate the pure aldehyde.
cards.hint: Equilibrium favours the adduct for most aldehydes, not most ketones (steric).

cards.front: What does an aldehyde form with alcohol + dry HCl? A ketone with ethylene glycol?
cards.back: • Aldehyde + alcohol: hemiacetal $\rightarrow$ acetal • Ketone + ethylene glycol: cyclic ethylene glycol ketal
cards.hint: Dry HCl protonates the carbonyl O, making C more electrophilic.

cards.front: Products of C=O with hydroxylamine, hydrazine and semicarbazide?
cards.back: • NH2OH $\rightarrow$ oxime • NH2NH2 $\rightarrow$ hydrazone • NH2NHCONH2 $\rightarrow$ semicarbazone

cards.front: What does 2,4-DNP reagent give with aldehydes and ketones?
cards.back: 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazones: yellow, orange or red solids used to identify carbonyl compounds.

cards.front: Clemmensen vs Wolff–Kishner reduction?
cards.back: Both convert C=O to CH2: • Clemmensen: Zn–Hg / conc. HCl • Wolff–Kishner: NH2NH2, then KOH in ethylene glycol, heat
cards.hint: Clemmensen = acidic; Wolff–Kishner = basic.

cards.front: What is Tollens' reagent and its test result with aldehydes?
cards.back: Ammoniacal silver nitrate. Aldehyde is oxidised to carboxylate and a silver mirror forms. Ketones do not respond.

cards.front: Fehling's test: composition and positive result?
cards.back: Fehling A (aq. CuSO4) + Fehling B (alkaline sodium potassium tartrate). Aldehyde gives a reddish-brown Cu2O precipitate.
cards.hint: Trap: aromatic aldehydes (benzaldehyde) do not give Fehling's test.

cards.front: Which compounds give the iodoform test, and what is seen?
cards.back: Compounds with CH3CO– or CH3CH(OH)– group, with NaOI (I2 + NaOH) $\rightarrow$ yellow CHI3 precipitate
cards.hint: The haloform reaction does not affect a C=C in the molecule.

cards.front: Which give a positive iodoform test: methanol, ethanol, propanal, propan-2-ol, acetophenone, benzaldehyde?
cards.back: Positive: ethanol, propan-2-ol, acetophenone Negative: methanol, propanal, benzaldehyde
cards.hint: Ethanol works: it is oxidised to CH<sub>3</sub>CHO first.

cards.front: Why are α-hydrogens of aldehydes and ketones acidic?
cards.back: Electron-withdrawing C=O plus resonance stabilisation of the enolate (carbanion) formed on losing H+.

cards.front: Aldol condensation: condition and products from ethanal?
cards.back: Needs at least one α-H; dilute NaOH. Ethanal $\rightarrow$ 3-hydroxybutanal (aldol) $\xrightarrow{\Delta}$ but-2-enal (α,β-unsaturated)
cards.hint: Aldol = ald(ehyde) + (alcoh)ol in one molecule.

cards.front: How many products does cross aldol of ethanal and propanal give?
cards.back: Four: two self-aldol and two cross-aldol products (both have α-H).

cards.front: Product of cross aldol of benzaldehyde with acetophenone?
cards.back: 1,3-Diphenylprop-2-en-1-one (benzalacetophenone). Benzaldehyde has no α-H, so it acts only as the acceptor.

cards.front: State the Cannizzaro reaction with an example.
cards.back: Aldehydes without α-H + conc. alkali undergo self oxidation–reduction: $2\text{HCHO} + \text{conc. KOH} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{OH} + \text{HCOOK}$
cards.hint: Disproportionation: one molecule reduced to alcohol, one oxidised to acid salt.

cards.front: Directing effect of –CHO in electrophilic substitution of benzaldehyde?
cards.back: Deactivating, meta-directing. Nitration gives m-nitrobenzaldehyde.

cards.front: What is formalin and its uses?
cards.back: ~40% aqueous methanal; used to preserve biological specimens and to make bakelite and other resins.

cards.front: Origin of the names formic acid and acetic acid?
cards.back: • Formic acid (HCOOH): from ants (Latin formica) • Acetic acid (CH3COOH): from vinegar (Latin acetum)

cards.front: Why is the carboxyl carbon less electrophilic than a carbonyl carbon?
cards.back: Resonance: the –OH lone pair delocalises onto C=O, so carboxylic acids do not give typical aldehyde/ketone addition reactions.

cards.front: Reagents to oxidise 1° alcohols or aldehydes to carboxylic acids?
cards.back: KMnO4 (neutral, acidic or alkaline), K2Cr2O7 or CrO3 in acid (Jones reagent).

cards.front: Oxidation of alkylbenzenes with KMnO<sub>4</sub>: what is the rule?
cards.back: The whole side chain becomes –COOH, whatever its length, giving benzoic acid. 1° and 2° alkyl groups react; 3° alkyl is not oxidised.
cards.hint: Trap: tert-butylbenzene does not give benzoic acid this way.

cards.front: How is a carboxylic acid made from a Grignard reagent?
cards.back: RMgX + CO2 (dry ice), then H3O+ $\rightarrow$ RCOOH (one carbon more than R).

cards.front: Why do carboxylic acids boil higher than alcohols of similar mass?
cards.back: More extensive H-bonding; acids exist as dimers even in the vapour phase and in aprotic solvents.

cards.front: Test to tell a carboxylic acid from a phenol?
cards.back: NaHCO3: carboxylic acids give brisk effervescence of CO2; phenols do not react.

cards.front: Why are carboxylic acids more acidic than phenols?
cards.back: Carboxylate negative charge is shared by two equivalent, electronegative O atoms; in phenoxide it is spread onto less electronegative carbons.

cards.front: Acidity order of HCOOH, CH<sub>3</sub>COOH and C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COOH?
cards.back: HCOOH > C6H5COOH > CH3COOH CH3 (+I) weakens acetic acid; phenyl on an $sp^2$ carbon makes benzoic acid stronger.
cards.hint: HCOOH has no electron-donating alkyl group, so it is strongest.

cards.front: Acidity order of fluoro-, chloro-, bromo- and iodoacetic acid?
cards.back: FCH2COOH > ClCH2COOH > BrCH2COOH > ICH2COOH (–I effect falls with electronegativity).

cards.front: Acidity order of mono-, di- and trichloroacetic acid?
cards.back: Cl3CCOOH > Cl2CHCOOH > ClCH2COOH. More –I groups stabilise the carboxylate more.

cards.front: Which is the strongest acid: 2-, 3- or 4-chlorobutanoic acid?
cards.back: 2-Chlorobutanoic acid. –I effect fades with distance, so 2- > 3- > 4-.
cards.hint: Closer to –COOH means stronger –I effect.

cards.front: Which reagent is preferred to convert RCOOH to RCOCl, and why?
cards.back: SOCl2: by-products SO2 and HCl are gases that escape, giving pure acyl chloride. PCl5 and PCl3 also work.

cards.front: Which reagents reduce –COOH to a 1° alcohol? Which do not?
cards.back: • Yes: LiAlH4, diborane (B2H6) • No: NaBH4 B2H6 leaves ester, nitro and halo groups untouched.

cards.front: Decarboxylation with soda lime: reagent and product?
cards.back: Sodium carboxylate heated with soda lime (NaOH + CaO, 3:1) $\rightarrow$ alkane with one carbon less.

cards.front: What does Kolbe electrolysis of a sodium carboxylate give?
cards.back: An alkane with double the alkyl group (R–R), e.g. CH3COONa $\rightarrow$ ethane.
cards.hint: Soda lime: lose one carbon. Kolbe electrolysis: join two R groups.

cards.front: State the Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky (HVZ) reaction.
cards.back: Acid with an α-H + X2 / red phosphorus, then H2O $\rightarrow$ α-halocarboxylic acid
cards.hint: Only the α-hydrogen is replaced; no α-H means no HVZ.

cards.front: Why does benzoic acid not undergo Friedel–Crafts reaction?
cards.back: –COOH is deactivating, and the catalyst AlCl3 bonds to the carboxyl group. Nitration and bromination occur at the meta position.

cards.front: Hybridisation and shape around N in amines?
cards.back: $sp^3$ N, pyramidal • Three bonds + one lone pair • C–N–C angle in trimethylamine ≈ $108^\circ$
cards.hint: Lone pair occupies the fourth $sp^3$ orbital, like NH<sub>3</sub>.

cards.front: How are amines classified as 1°, 2° and 3°?
cards.back: By the number of H atoms of NH3 replaced by alkyl/aryl groups • 1°: RNH2 • 2°: R2NH • 3°: R3N
cards.hint: Trap: unlike alcohols, 1°/2°/3° here is NOT about the carbon bearing N.

cards.front: IUPAC names of CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>NH and (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>N?
cards.back: • Methanamine • N-Methylmethanamine • N,N-Dimethylmethanamine
cards.hint: Largest alkyl = parent alkanamine; others are N-prefixes.

cards.front: IUPAC name of aniline and of H<sub>2</sub>N–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–NH<sub>2</sub>?
cards.back: • Aniline = benzenamine • H2NCH2CH2NH2 = ethane-1,2-diamine
cards.hint: With diamine the terminal 'e' of the alkane is retained.

cards.front: Reagents for reducing nitrobenzene to aniline?
cards.back: • H2 / finely divided Ni, Pd or Pt • Sn + HCl or Fe scrap + HCl

cards.front: Why is Fe scrap + HCl preferred for reducing nitro compounds?
cards.back: FeCl2 formed hydrolyses to release HCl, so only a small amount of HCl is needed to start the reaction.

cards.front: What is ammonolysis of alkyl halides?
cards.back: Heating R–X with ethanolic NH3 in a sealed tube at 373 K → nucleophilic substitution gives 1° amine, which can react further.

cards.front: Main drawback of ammonolysis and how to favour the 1° amine?
cards.back: Gives a mixture of 1°, 2°, 3° amines and quaternary ammonium salt • Large excess of NH3 favours the 1° amine

cards.front: Product of reducing a nitrile R–C≡N with LiAlH<sub>4</sub> (or H<sub>2</sub>/Ni)?
cards.back: 1° amine R–CH2–NH2 • Amine has one carbon more than the starting alkyl halide → used for ascent of series
cards.hint: R–X + CN<sup>–</sup> then reduce = add one C.

cards.front: Product of reducing an amide RCONH<sub>2</sub> with LiAlH<sub>4</sub> followed by H<sub>2</sub>O?
cards.back: R–CH2–NH2 (1° amine with the same number of C as the amide)
cards.hint: Contrast: Hoffmann bromamide gives one C less.

cards.front: Steps of Gabriel phthalimide synthesis?
cards.back: • Phthalimide + ethanolic KOH → potassium phthalimide • + R–X → N-alkylphthalimide • Alkaline hydrolysis → 1° amine

cards.front: Why can't aromatic 1° amines be made by Gabriel synthesis?
cards.back: Aryl halides do not undergo nucleophilic substitution with the phthalimide anion.
cards.hint: Gabriel = only 1° ALIPHATIC amines; no 2°/3°.

cards.front: Hoffmann bromamide degradation: reagents and product?
cards.back: Amide + Br2 + NaOH (aq/ethanolic) → 1° amine with one C less • RCONH2 $\rightarrow$ RNH2 (+ Na2CO3, NaBr, H2O)
cards.hint: Moles of NaOH used per mole amide: 4.

cards.front: Key mechanistic step in Hoffmann bromamide degradation?
cards.back: Migration of the alkyl/aryl group from the carbonyl carbon to the nitrogen atom.

cards.front: Which preparation methods change the carbon count of the amine?
cards.back: • Nitrile reduction: +1 C (vs alkyl halide) • Hoffmann bromamide: –1 C (vs amide) • Amide reduction, Gabriel: no change

cards.front: Physical state and smell of lower aliphatic amines; colour change of aniline on storage?
cards.back: • Lower aliphatic amines: gases with fishy smell • Aniline: colourless liquid that becomes coloured on storage due to atmospheric oxidation

cards.front: Boiling point order of isomeric 1°, 2° and 3° amines?
cards.back: 1° > 2° > 3° • 1° has two N–H for H-bonding; 3° has no N–H, so no intermolecular H-bonding

cards.front: Why are amines basic?
cards.back: N has an unshared electron pair → acts as a Lewis base; amines form salts with acids, e.g. RNH2 + HCl $\rightarrow$ RNH3+Cl–

cards.front: Why are aliphatic amines more basic than NH<sub>3</sub>?
cards.back: Alkyl groups have +I effect: increase electron density on N and stabilise the substituted ammonium ion.

cards.front: Basicity order of methylamines in the gas phase?
cards.back: (CH3)3N > (CH3)2NH > CH3NH2 > NH3 • Only +I effect operates: 3° > 2° > 1°

cards.front: Basicity order of methyl-substituted amines in aqueous solution?
cards.back: (CH3)2NH > CH3NH2 > (CH3)3N > NH3 • i.e. 2° > 1° > 3° > NH3
cards.hint: Methyl: 2-1-3. Ethyl: 2-3-1.

cards.front: Basicity order of ethyl-substituted amines in aqueous solution?
cards.back: (C2H5)2NH > (C2H5)3N > C2H5NH2 > NH3 • i.e. 2° > 3° > 1°
cards.hint: Trap: methyl and ethyl series give different orders.

cards.front: Why is aniline a much weaker base than NH<sub>3</sub> and alkylamines?
cards.back: N lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring (resonance), so less available • Anilinium ion has fewer resonance structures than aniline, so protonation is unfavourable
cards.hint: pK<sub>b</sub>: aniline 9.38 vs NH<sub>3</sub> 4.75.

cards.front: Effect of substituents on the basicity of aniline?
cards.back: • Electron-releasing (–CH3, –OCH3) increase basicity • Electron-withdrawing (–NO2, –X, –COOH) decrease basicity

cards.front: Arrange in increasing basicity: aniline, p-toluidine, p-nitroaniline.
cards.back: p-Nitroaniline < aniline < p-toluidine
cards.hint: –NO<sub>2</sub> pulls the lone pair away; –CH<sub>3</sub> pushes density in.

cards.front: Which is more basic: benzylamine (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) or aniline? Why?
cards.back: Benzylamine ($pK_b$ 4.70 vs 9.38) • –NH2 is on a CH2, not directly on the ring, so no lone-pair delocalisation

cards.front: Product when a 1° amine reacts repeatedly with excess alkyl halide?
cards.back: Successive alkylation: 1° → 2° → 3° → quaternary ammonium salt R4N+X–

cards.front: What is acylation of amines and why is pyridine added?
cards.back: 1°/2° amines + acid chloride, anhydride or ester → amide (H of N–H replaced by acyl) • Pyridine (stronger base) removes HCl, shifting equilibrium forward
cards.hint: 3° amines have no N–H, so no acylation.

cards.front: Product of aniline + acetic anhydride (or acetyl chloride)?
cards.back: Acetanilide (N-phenylethanamide), C6H5NHCOCH3

cards.front: Carbylamine reaction: reagents, product and use?
cards.back: 1° amine + CHCl3 + alcoholic KOH, heat → isocyanide (carbylamine) with foul smell • Test for 1° amines (aliphatic and aromatic); 2°, 3° do not respond
cards.hint: Also called the isocyanide test.

cards.front: Reaction of aliphatic 1° amines with nitrous acid?
cards.back: Form unstable aliphatic diazonium salts → alcohol + N2 gas • Quantitative N2 evolution is used to estimate amino acids and proteins
cards.hint: HNO<sub>2</sub> is made in situ from NaNO<sub>2</sub> + mineral acid.

cards.front: Reaction of aromatic 1° amines with nitrous acid?
cards.back: At 273–278 K (cold) → arenediazonium salt, e.g. benzenediazonium chloride (diazotisation)

cards.front: Hinsberg test: reagent and result with 1° amine?
cards.back: Benzenesulphonyl chloride (C6H5SO2Cl) • 1° → N-alkylbenzenesulphonamide, soluble in alkali (acidic H on N, due to strong electron-withdrawing SO2)
cards.hint: Today p-toluenesulphonyl chloride often replaces it.

cards.front: Hinsberg test: result with 2° and 3° amines?
cards.back: • 2° → N,N-dialkylbenzenesulphonamide, insoluble in alkali (no H on N) • 3° → no reaction
cards.hint: Soluble = 1°, insoluble solid = 2°, nothing = 3°.

cards.front: Why is –NH<sub>2</sub> in aniline strongly o/p-directing and activating?
cards.back: N lone pair is donated into the ring (+R effect), raising electron density at ortho and para positions.

cards.front: Product of aniline + bromine water at room temperature?
cards.back: 2,4,6-Tribromoaniline, a white precipitate
cards.hint: Too reactive: all three o/p positions get substituted.

cards.front: How is p-bromoaniline (monobromination) prepared from aniline?
cards.back: • Acetylate → acetanilide (activation reduced) • Br2/CH3COOH → p-bromoacetanilide • Hydrolyse → p-bromoaniline
cards.hint: Acetyl lowers activation: the N lone pair is also delocalised onto the C=O by resonance.

cards.front: Why does direct nitration of aniline give a large amount of meta product?
cards.back: In strong acid aniline is protonated to anilinium ion (–NH3+), which is meta-directing • Also tarry oxidation products form
cards.hint: Approx: para 51%, meta 47%, ortho 2%.

cards.front: How is p-nitroaniline obtained as the major product?
cards.back: Protect –NH2 by acetylation → nitrate acetanilide → hydrolyse the p-nitroacetanilide

cards.front: Product of sulphonation of aniline?
cards.back: Aniline + conc. H2SO4 → anilinium hydrogensulphate; heat at 453–473 K → sulphanilic acid (p-aminobenzenesulphonic acid), exists as a zwitterion

cards.front: Why doesn't aniline undergo Friedel–Crafts reaction?
cards.back: Aniline (Lewis base) forms a salt with AlCl3 (Lewis acid); N acquires + charge and strongly deactivates the ring.
cards.hint: Trap: it's not that –NH<sub>2</sub> is deactivating; the complex is.

cards.front: What is diazotisation? Conditions?
cards.back: Conversion of aromatic 1° amine to diazonium salt using NaNO2 + HCl at 273–278 K • C6H5NH2 $\rightarrow$ C6H5N2+Cl–
cards.hint: Salt is used immediately; it is unstable when warm.

cards.front: Why are arenediazonium salts more stable than alkyldiazonium salts?
cards.back: Resonance (dispersal of + charge over the benzene ring) stabilises the arenediazonium ion; alkyldiazonium salts are highly unstable.

cards.front: Physical nature of benzenediazonium chloride vs its fluoroborate?
cards.back: • Chloride: colourless crystalline solid, soluble in water, stable in cold, reacts with water on warming • Fluoroborate: water-insoluble, stable at room temperature

cards.front: Sandmeyer reaction: reagents and products?
cards.back: ArN2+X– with • CuCl/HCl → ArCl • CuBr/HBr → ArBr • CuCN/KCN → ArCN
cards.hint: Sandmeyer uses Cu(I) salts.

cards.front: Gattermann reaction vs Sandmeyer reaction?
cards.back: Gattermann: Cu powder + HCl/HBr → ArCl/ArBr • Sandmeyer gives better yield

cards.front: Reagent to replace –N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> by iodine?
cards.back: Treat with KI solution → ArI (iodobenzene)
cards.hint: Iodine cannot be introduced well by direct iodination.

cards.front: How is fluorobenzene prepared from a diazonium salt?
cards.back: With fluoroboric acid (HBF4) → ArN2+BF4–; heating gives ArF + BF3 + N2
cards.hint: Balz–Schiemann type route.

cards.front: Reagents that replace –N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> by –H?
cards.back: Mild reducing agents: hypophosphorous acid (H3PO2) or ethanol → arene (e.g. benzene)
cards.hint: Ethanol is itself oxidised to ethanal.

cards.front: How is phenol obtained from benzenediazonium chloride?
cards.back: Warm the aqueous solution (temperature allowed to rise to 283 K): salt is hydrolysed to phenol + N2 + HCl

cards.front: How is nitrobenzene made from benzenediazonium salt?
cards.back: Diazonium fluoroborate heated with aq. NaNO2 + Cu powder → nitrobenzene

cards.front: Product of benzenediazonium chloride + phenol (alkaline medium)?
cards.back: p-Hydroxyazobenzene, an orange dye (azo coupling at para position)
cards.hint: Coupling = electrophilic substitution; N<sub>2</sub> is retained.

cards.front: Product of benzenediazonium chloride + aniline (coupling)?
cards.back: p-Aminoazobenzene, a yellow dye
cards.hint: Phenol → orange; aniline → yellow.

cards.front: Why are diazonium salts important in synthesis?
cards.back: They introduce –F, –I, –CN, –OH, –NO2, –H into the ring, giving aryl fluorides, iodides, cyanobenzene etc. that are hard to make by direct substitution.

cards.front: How to distinguish aniline from benzylamine?
cards.back: HNO2 (NaNO2 + HCl) cold, then β-naphthol • Aniline → orange-red azo dye • Benzylamine → N2 effervescence (aliphatic-type amine), no dye

cards.front: Define carbohydrates.
cards.back: Optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, or compounds that give them on hydrolysis.
cards.hint: Trap: C<sub>x</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>y</sub> fails (rhamnose C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>5</sub> is a carb; acetic acid fits but isn't).

cards.front: Classification of carbohydrates by hydrolysis?
cards.back: • Monosaccharides: not hydrolysed further (glucose, fructose) • Oligosaccharides: 2–10 units (sucrose) • Polysaccharides: many units (starch, cellulose)

cards.front: What are reducing sugars? Which common sugars are non-reducing?
cards.back: Reduce Fehling's and Tollens' reagents; all monosaccharides are reducing • Sucrose is non-reducing (reducing groups of both units are bonded)

cards.front: How are monosaccharides named as aldose/ketose?
cards.back: By carbonyl type + number of C • Glucose = aldohexose • Fructose = ketohexose

cards.front: Preparation of glucose from sucrose?
cards.back: Boil sucrose with dil. HCl or H2SO4 in alcoholic solution → glucose + fructose (equal amounts)

cards.front: Commercial preparation of glucose from starch?
cards.back: Hydrolysis of starch by boiling with dil. H2SO4 at 393 K under 2–3 atm pressure

cards.front: Glucose + HI (prolonged heating) gives? What does it prove?
cards.back: n-Hexane • All six C atoms are in a straight chain

cards.front: Glucose + NH<sub>2</sub>OH and + HCN give? Conclusion?
cards.back: Oxime and cyanohydrin respectively • Shows presence of a carbonyl (>C=O) group

cards.front: Glucose + bromine water gives? Conclusion?
cards.back: Gluconic acid (6-C carboxylic acid) • Carbonyl group is an aldehyde (–CHO)
cards.hint: Br<sub>2</sub> water is a mild oxidant: only –CHO is oxidised.

cards.front: Glucose + acetic anhydride gives? Conclusion?
cards.back: Glucose pentaacetate • Five –OH groups, on different C atoms (glucose is stable)

cards.front: Glucose + nitric acid gives? Conclusion?
cards.back: Saccharic acid (glucaric acid, a dicarboxylic acid) • Glucose has a primary alcohol (–CH2OH) group
cards.hint: Both ends oxidised: –CHO and –CH<sub>2</sub>OH become –COOH.

cards.front: Which facts could the open-chain structure of glucose NOT explain?
cards.back: • No Schiff's test; no NaHSO3 addition product • Pentaacetate doesn't react with NH2OH (no free –CHO) • Exists as two forms, α and β

cards.front: Melting points / crystallisation of α- and β-D-glucose?
cards.back: • α: m.p. 419 K, from concentrated solution at 303 K • β: m.p. 423 K, from hot saturated solution at 371 K

cards.front: How does the cyclic (pyranose) form of glucose arise?
cards.back: –OH at C-5 adds to the –CHO (C-1) → six-membered hemiacetal ring • Called pyranose (analogy with pyran)

cards.front: What are anomers? Name the anomeric carbon of glucose.
cards.back: Cyclic isomers differing only in configuration at the hemiacetal carbon → α and β forms • Anomeric carbon of glucose = C-1

cards.front: What does D or L in D-glucose indicate?
cards.back: Relative configuration: –OH on the lowest asymmetric C (C-5) on the right, like (+)-glyceraldehyde • Not related to the sign of optical rotation
cards.hint: Trap: D ≠ (+). D-fructose is laevorotatory.

cards.front: Fructose: formula, carbonyl group position, optical rotation?
cards.back: C6H12O6, ketone at C-2 • Natural form is D-(–)-fructose (laevorotatory)

cards.front: Ring form of fructose?
cards.back: Five-membered furanose ring: –OH at C-5 adds to the C-2 keto group
cards.hint: Furan has 5 atoms; pyran has 6.

cards.front: What is a glycosidic linkage?
cards.back: Oxide (–O–) linkage joining two monosaccharide units through an oxygen atom, formed with loss of water.

cards.front: Composition and linkage of sucrose?
cards.back: α-D-glucose + β-D-fructose, linked C-1 (glucose) to C-2 (fructose) • Both reducing groups involved → non-reducing
cards.hint: Glycosidic bond joins C-1 of glucose to C-2 of fructose: both anomeric carbons used.

cards.front: Why is hydrolysed sucrose called invert sugar?
cards.back: Sucrose is dextrorotatory; hydrolysis gives glucose ($+52.5^\circ$) and fructose ($-92.4^\circ$), net laevorotatory • Sign of rotation inverts

cards.front: Composition and linkage of maltose?
cards.back: Two α-D-glucose units, linked C-1 to C-4 • Reducing sugar (free aldehyde possible at C-1 of second unit)
cards.hint: Malt = glucose + glucose, α(1→4).

cards.front: Composition and linkage of lactose?
cards.back: β-D-galactose + β-D-glucose, linked C-1 of galactose to C-4 of glucose • Milk sugar, reducing

cards.front: Two components of starch: proportion and solubility?
cards.back: • Amylose: 15–20%, water-soluble • Amylopectin: 80–85%, water-insoluble
cards.hint: Amylopectin is the major (insoluble) part.

cards.front: Structure of amylose vs amylopectin?
cards.back: • Amylose: unbranched chain of 200–1000 α-D-glucose, C1–C4 links • Amylopectin: branched; C1–C4 chain with C1–C6 branch points

cards.front: Structure of cellulose?
cards.back: Straight chain of β-D-glucose units joined by C1–C4 glycosidic links • Major constituent of plant cell walls
cards.hint: Starch = α links; cellulose = β links. Humans can't digest cellulose.

cards.front: What is glycogen and where is it stored?
cards.back: Animal starch; structure like amylopectin but more highly branched • Stored in liver, muscles and brain

cards.front: Importance of carbohydrates?
cards.back: • Major energy source; storage as starch (plants) and glycogen (animals) • Cellulose in plant cell walls • D-ribose / 2-deoxyribose in nucleic acids

cards.front: General structure of α-amino acids?
cards.back: An –NH2 and a –COOH group on the same (α) carbon, plus a variable side chain R

cards.front: Essential vs non-essential amino acids?
cards.back: • Non-essential: synthesised in the body • Essential: must be obtained through diet (e.g. valine, leucine, lysine)

cards.front: Classify amino acids as acidic, basic or neutral.
cards.back: By relative number of –NH2 and –COOH • Equal → neutral • More –NH2 → basic • More –COOH → acidic

cards.front: Which natural amino acid is optically inactive?
cards.back: Glycine (R = H, no chiral carbon) • All others are optically active, mostly L-configuration

cards.front: What is a zwitterion?
cards.back: Dipolar ion H3N+–CHR–COO– formed in aqueous solution, carboxyl loses H+ and amino group gains it • Makes amino acids amphoteric, high m.p., water-soluble

cards.front: What is a peptide bond?
cards.back: Amide linkage –CO–NH– formed between –COOH of one amino acid and –NH2 of another, with loss of water
cards.hint: Dipeptide has one peptide bond; n amino acids give (n–1) bonds.

cards.front: Polypeptide vs protein (NCERT criterion)?
cards.back: • Polypeptide: more than ten amino acids • Protein: polypeptide with > 100 amino acids, molar mass > 10,000 u

cards.front: Fibrous vs globular proteins?
cards.back: • Fibrous: parallel fibre-like chains, insoluble in water (keratin, myosin) • Globular: coiled spherical, water-soluble (insulin, albumins)
cards.hint: Fibrous = structural; globular = functional (enzymes, hormones).

cards.front: What is the primary structure of a protein?
cards.back: The specific sequence of amino acids in the polypeptide chain • A change in even one amino acid creates a different protein

cards.front: Describe the α-helix (secondary structure).
cards.back: Chain twisted into a right-handed helix, held by H-bonds between –NH and >C=O of adjacent turns

cards.front: Describe the β-pleated sheet.
cards.back: Chains stretched out side by side and joined by intermolecular H-bonds, giving a pleated sheet

cards.front: Forces stabilising secondary and tertiary structure of proteins?
cards.back: H-bonds, disulphide linkages, van der Waals and electrostatic forces
cards.hint: Tertiary = overall folding into fibrous or globular shape.

cards.front: What is the quaternary structure of a protein?
cards.back: Spatial arrangement of two or more polypeptide subunits with respect to each other
cards.hint: Only proteins with more than one subunit (e.g. haemoglobin) have it.

cards.front: What is denaturation of proteins? Which structure survives?
cards.back: Loss of biological activity due to heat or pH change: 2° and 3° structures destroyed • Primary structure remains intact

cards.front: Two everyday examples of protein denaturation?
cards.back: • Coagulation of egg white on boiling • Curdling of milk (lactic acid from bacteria)

cards.front: Fat-soluble vs water-soluble vitamins?
cards.back: • Fat-soluble: A, D, E, K, stored in liver and adipose tissue • Water-soluble: B group and C, excreted in urine, so need regular supply
cards.hint: Exception: vitamin B<sub>12</sub> can be stored.

cards.front: Deficiency diseases of vitamins A and D?
cards.back: • A: xerophthalmia, night blindness • D: rickets (children), osteomalacia (adults)
cards.hint: A for eyes (night blindness); D for bones.

cards.front: Deficiency diseases of vitamins B<sub>1</sub>, B<sub>2</sub>, B<sub>6</sub>, B<sub>12</sub>?
cards.back: • B1: beriberi • B2: cheilosis, digestive disorders • B6: convulsions • B12: pernicious anaemia
cards.hint: B1 beriberi; B12 pernicious anaemia.

cards.front: Deficiency diseases of vitamins C, E and K?
cards.back: • C: scurvy (bleeding gums) • E: increased fragility of RBCs, muscular weakness • K: increased blood clotting time

cards.front: Nucleotide vs nucleoside?
cards.back: • Nucleoside = base + pentose sugar (base at C-1') • Nucleotide = nucleoside + phosphate (at C-5')
cards.hint: Nucleo-T-ide has the phosphaTe.

cards.front: Sugar and bases in DNA vs RNA?
cards.back: • DNA: β-D-2-deoxyribose; A, G, C, T • RNA: β-D-ribose; A, G, C, U
cards.hint: Purines: A, G. Pyrimidines: C, T, U.

cards.front: Linkage joining nucleotides in a nucleic acid chain?
cards.back: Phosphodiester linkage between 5' and 3' carbons of the pentose sugars
cards.hint: Backbone = alternating sugar and phosphate.

cards.front: Structure of DNA and base pairing?
cards.back: Double helix (Watson and Crick); two strands held by H-bonds between complementary bases • A pairs with T, G pairs with C

cards.front: Structure of RNA and its three types?
cards.back: Single-stranded (may fold) • m-RNA, r-RNA, t-RNA

cards.front: Biological functions of DNA and RNA?
cards.back: • DNA: chemical basis of heredity; reserves genetic information; replication • RNA: carries out protein synthesis

cards.front: What are hormones (general idea)?
cards.back: Chemical messengers produced by endocrine (ductless) glands, released into blood and acting on distant target cells

cards.front: Chemical classes of hormones with examples?
cards.back: • Steroids: estrogens, androgens • Polypeptides: insulin, endorphins • Amino acid derivatives: epinephrine, thyroxine
cards.hint: Insulin and glucagon together keep blood glucose in a narrow range.
